World.title: FCMB Deepens Agritech with AI Advisory in Local Languages
World.content:
First City Monument Bank has unveiled plans to deepen its agritech strategy by deploying AI-powered advisory services in major Nigerian languages, as part of efforts to improve access to finance and support for smallholder farmers.

According to the bank’s Agritech Alumni Impact Report covering 2018 to 2026, the bank will continue to support the growth and scale-up of innovative AgTech companies developing solutions across the agricultural value chain, including AI-powered platforms that provide farmers with real-time advisory and support in local languages such as Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo.

The initiative comes amid growing concerns over food security, agricultural productivity and the continued exclusion of farmers from formal financial systems across Africa.

FCMB noted that although agriculture contributes about 24 per cent of Nigeria’s GDP, only six per cent of farmers in Africa currently have access to formal credit. The Bank said this long-standing financing gap continues to inform the development of broader, more inclusive lending models that leverage relevant AgTech solutions, including weather data, soil intelligence, and USSD-enabled technology platforms.

The report stated that the bank’s agritech programme has evolved from a startup-focused competition into a broader ecosystem connecting innovators, investors and development partners.

FCMB said the strategy reflects a shift from traditional lending toward building “a de-risked, data-driven, and sovereign future for food and agriculture in Africa.”

World.title: RockPay Targets Digital Payments through Social Finance
World.content:
Finacial technology company, RockPay, has launched its digital finance platform in the country, offering users a single platform for making payments, growing businesses and raising funds for personal and community needs.

RockPay, which is designed for individuals, businesses and communities, brings together peer-to-peer transfers, payment requests, QR code payments, payment links and business profiles, while also providing a donation feature for fundraising.

Speaking on the launch, Francis Osaji, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of RockPay, said the platform was created to solve everyday challenges faced by Nigerians.

“RockPay was built to connect businesses with customers, simplify digital payments, and make it easier for people to raise money for the things that matter most. We wanted to create a platform where accepting payments, supporting causes, and growing businesses feel as natural as using social media,” he said.

“RockPay addresses the growing need for a more connected financial experience by eliminating the need to use multiple applications for payments, fundraising, and business transactions. Through searchable business profiles, QR code payments, payment links, and transparent fundraising campaigns, users can seamlessly transact while building stronger relationships with customers and their communities.

“RockPay is more than a payment app, it is a complete solution provider built essentially to help small businesses grow, socialise, give them real market visibility, and raise funds with ease. Whether you are a business owner looking to get discovered and accept payments faster through your business profile, QR codes and payment links, or an individual who wants to raise money for school fees, medical bills or a community project through our verified donation feature, RockPay was built for you,” he added.

World.title: Lighting Up Africa: Genesis Energy on Building Africa’s Industrial Future Beyond Capital
World.content:
Oluchi Chibuzor

Africa’s energy story is entering a pivotal chapter. The question is no longer whether the continent has the resources or ambition to industrialise, but whether it can build the infrastructure, mobilise investment and forge the partnerships required to turn that potential into sustained economic growth.

That question was at the heart of the 2026 Africa Energy Forum (AEF) in Cape Town, held under the theme, ‘Building Africa’s Industrialised Future’. Bringing together policymakers, investors, developers, financiers and technology leaders, the forum focused on a fundamental challenge: how Africa can move from ambition to execution and from abundant resources to lasting value creation.

For Genesis Energy, the conversations reinforced a view that has shaped its approach to energy development across the continent. The company sponsored a hosted boardroom on “Financing Africa’s Gas Infrastructure Deficit,” convening senior leaders including Lagos State Commissioner for Energy and Mineral Resources, Hon. Biodun Ogunleye; Samir Salé, Country Managing Director for Mozambique at Globeleq; and Nthato Minyuku, Head of Africa Government Affairs, Market Development & Growth at Siemens Energy.

Additionally, Genesis also participated in high-level closed-door executive sessions and a panel examining “How has the recent Geopolitics impacted international attitudes to Gas,” bringing a development and investment perspective to the changing global energy landscape.

Across discussions on regional gas infrastructure, energy technology, global market dynamics and integrated energy systems, Genesis Energy executives explored what this means in practice — and what it will take to build energy systems capable of supporting Africa’s next phase of industrial growth. A main takeaway from AEF 2026 was that Africa’s infrastructure gap is increasingly seen as its most promising investment opportunity. The continent’s advantage isn’t just in natural resources but in modern infrastructure above ground. Forward-thinking investors are moving beyond isolated projects.

Maximising Domestic Value with Local Gas Chains

Discussions on natural gas revealed a key shift in the regional narrative. The debate is no longer about whether natural gas plays a role, but how Africa can maximize local economic benefits from its resources.

Executive Vice President of Project Development and Investment at Genesis Energy, Melissa Fadzai Sikwila, emphasised the importance of local value creation saying: “There is an enormous amount of gas in Nigeria, for example, that gets wasted because of a lack of domestic liquefaction plants. The industry has to learn fast and fail forward.”

Processing and using gas locally opens immediate opportunities for power, manufacturing, jobs, and economic independence. Landmark projects like Genesis Energy’s 84MW gas-fired IPP at Port Harcourt Refinery in Nigeria demonstrate how replacing expensive diesel and HFO with cleaner, locally processed gas sustains economic value within host countries. A key theme emerging from the discussion was that the greatest barriers to scaling energy infrastructure in Africa are no longer just technical, they are commercial, financial, and institutional.

The discussion reinforced that Africa’s energy transition will be driven as much by collaboration as by technology. As projects increase in scale and complexity, success depends on creating ecosystems where governments, developers, investors, DFIs, regulators and technology providers work together to structure bankable projects and allocate risk effectively. While the technology to deliver reliable, clean energy already exists, unlocking investment requires innovative financing, coordinated planning and strategic partnerships. This shift highlights that the future of energy development in Africa is not just about deploying technology—it is about building the commercial and institutional frameworks that enable projects to move from concept to reality.

Turning Energy Potential into Progress

The conversations at AEF 2026 reinforced a conviction that has shaped Genesis Energy’s work across Africa for more than two decades: unlocking the continent’s potential requires more than capital. It requires the infrastructure, partnerships and execution to turn viable projects into reliable energy that powers businesses, communities and economies. This aligns with its vision of: LIGHTING UP AFRICA, ONE COMMUNITY AT A TIME.

From gas-to-power and solar to battery storage and other clean energy solutions, Genesis continues to develop, finance and operate energy infrastructure across the continent. With more than 300MW in operational and implementation projects and a development pipeline exceeding 4GW, the company remains focused on building the dependable clean energy ecosystem needed to drive Africa’s sustainable growth.

World.title: Insecurity in Nigeria: Lessons from Maritime Sector
World.content:
Emmanuel Alfred

On Friday, July 10, 2026, there was widespread jubilation across Nigeria following the release of pupils and teachers abducted from Oriire Local Government Area of Oyo State after spending 56 days in captivity. This successful rescue operation highlights important considerations not only for the immediate context but also for addressing the broader issue of insecurity in the country.

Discussions about insecurity in Nigeria typically focus on familiar strategies such as increasing troop deployments, acquiring weapons, addressing intelligence failures and conducting military operations. However, there is another dimension of Nigeria’s security landscape that deserves our attention: the nation’s maritime domain. Exploring this dimension could offer valuable insights and innovative approaches to enhancing security in Nigeria.

For many years, piracy and armed attacks in the Gulf of Guinea posed serious threats to shipping, trade and the wider Nigerian economy. Nigeria’s waters became notorious for kidnapping at sea, attacks on vessels, smuggling operations and the criminal enterprises that profited from these activities. Today, however, the picture is considerably different. Remarkably, the Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency (NIMASA) reported no piracy incidents in Nigerian waters in 2025. This achievement is commendable, although it should not be misconstrued as a permanent elimination of the threat.

The critical question to consider is not whether Nigeria has totally “won’’ the battle against maritime insecurity, but rather what strategies were employed at sea that could inform approaches to addressing insecurity on land. The answer may lie less in the sheer number of security personnel deployed and more in the organisational structure of the security system itself.

Intelligence before force

One of the clearest lessons from maritime experience is the importance of understanding a threat before determining how best to respond. Nigeria invested significantly in enhancing maritime domain awareness, surveillance and intelligence capabilities, including the C4i Centre associated with the Deep Blue Project. Rather than simply deploying more security personnel at sea, Nigeria has focused on improving its capacity to see, track and understand activities across its maritime space. This distinction is crucial; effective security encompasses not only swift responses to attacks but also understanding the networks underpinning criminal activities, including individuals involved, their operational areas, movement patterns, sponsors and where their proceeds go.

Kidnapping, banditry, armed robbery and other forms of organised crime on land operate in much the same way. They often involve financiers, informants, transporters, safe houses, weapons suppliers and escape route planners. If criminals operate as networks while security forces respond mainly to individual incidents, the state will remain largely reactive. Lesson from Nigeria’s maritime experience suggests a more proactive approach: build intelligence systems capable of identifying and disrupting criminal networks, rather than simply reacting to their latest attacks.

Security gaps, often institutional gaps

The challenges posed by criminal networks often reflect institutional gaps within security frameworks. Criminal networks do not respect administrative boundaries. At sea, criminal networks can operate across territorial waters and jurisdictions, which requires Nigeria to collaborate with neighbouring countries and regional institutions. Likewise, criminal groups do not cease operating simply because they cross into another state. Yet, Nigeria’s security architecture remains heavily influenced by administrative boundaries and institutional jurisdictions. The point here is not solely whether each security agency is sufficiently staffed or equipped, but whether they effectively share intelligence, coordinate operations and together pursue criminal networks across jurisdictions. Experiences from Nigeria’s maritime context highlight a crucial principle: security institutions should be designed around the behaviour and dynamics of threats, rather than being confined to the limitations of government agency boundaries. When threats are interconnected, but institutions operate in isolation, security gaps inevitably emerge.

Make crime difficult and less profitable

Effective security measures cannot depend on force alone. While arresting criminals is important, there must also be a credible prospect of prosecution and punishment to deter future offences. Piracy is ultimately an economic enterprise, driven by the perception that the rewards appear to outweigh the risks. As part of its maritime response, Nigeria has implemented not only surveillance and security operations but also a stronger legal framework. The Suppression of Piracy and Other Maritime Offences Act 2019 significantly strengthened the prosecution of maritime crimes, and subsequent judicial enforcement has demonstrated that maritime offences can attract serious legal consequences. Insecurity has intersected with poverty, unemployment, environmental degradation, weak institutions and limited economic opportunities. While these factors may create conditions in which criminality thrives, they do not justify or excuse it. The state must simultaneously address underlying vulnerabilities and increase the risks and consequences associated with crime.

Prioritisation and effective coordination

Perhaps the most valuable lesson gleaned from the maritime sector is not any single piece of equipment, law or security operation. It is prioritisation and effective coordination. Complex security problems rarely have single-agency solutions. Nigeria’s maritime security architecture brings together surveillance, intelligence, naval and other security operations, maritime regulation, legal enforcement and regional cooperation. The existence of multiple security agencies with considerable capabilities underscores the significance of connecting these resources toward a common security objective. Although Nigeria has soldiers, police officers, intelligence personnel, surveillance technologies, and laws, the effectiveness of these resources can diminish if information sharing between institutions is slow, responsibilities overlap, or agencies pursue disconnected objectives. Therefore, Nigeria’s security problem may sometimes stem from a lack of integrated security systems, rather than a shortage of personnel or agencies. The maritime experience demonstrates that a well-structured institutional framework is as critical as having adequate manpower and equipment.

Suppression not permanent victory

There is, however, a danger in drawing overly optimistic conclusions from the maritime experience. A noted decline in piracy does not mean that the conditions facilitating such crimes have been eliminated. Criminal groups adapt, change routes, evolve tactics, and explore new opportunities. The same is true on land. Security gains can be reversed if institutions become complacent, funding declines, intelligence systems deteriorate or underlying economic and governance problems are ignored. The objective should therefore not simply be to reduce attacks temporarily, but to build institutions capable of detecting emerging threats, adapting to changing tactics and maintaining sustained pressure on criminal networks. Achieving this level of sustainable security is a challenge, but it is essential for long-term stability and safety.

Why It Matters

The issue of insecurity in Nigeria extends beyond immediate safety concerns and has significant socio-economic implications for every citizen. When farmers encounter dangers in accessing their farms, agricultural production suffers, leading to food shortages and rising prices. When transport routes become dangerous, logistics costs increase, impacting businesses and consumers alike. When businesses spend more on private security and insurance to mitigate risks, productive capital is diverted from growth and expansion initiatives. When investors perceive the country as unsafe, investment decisions change. When citizens are unable to move freely or conduct business safely and confidently, the very foundation of the economy is jeopardised.

This is why the maritime experience matters even to citizens who may never set foot on a commercial vessel. While piracy and land-based banditry are not identical threats, experiences in combating maritime insecurity reveal that complex security challenges can be significantly reduced when the government integrates intelligence, specialised capabilities, legal instruments, institutional coordination and sustained attention. The Oyo rescue operation appears to have employed some of the very principles this article advocates: intelligence, multi-agency collaboration, specialised capabilities and sustained targeting of a criminal network.

Therefore, the more important question is whether Nigeria can adapt proven maritime security strategies to address the security challenges faced on land. Can Nigeria transform exceptional multi-agency successes into a routine, institutionalised national security framework? Rather than relying on new slogans, there is an urgent need for an honest, systematic evaluation of successful security measures and exploration of how these lessons can be applied to different contexts. By harnessing successful approaches from its maritime sector, Nigeria has the potential to significantly make its roads, farms, schools, communities and cities safer. Ultimately, security is not a one-time event, but a dynamic system. Sustainable security depends on designing a robust framework, capable of learning, adapting and enduring over time, ensuring safety for all citizens.

Dr. Emmanuel Alfred, a Maritime Affairs Analyst wrote from Lagos

World.title: Foremost Capital Secures Investment Grade Rating of BBB+
World.content:
DataPro, a leading credit rating agency and compliance consulting firm in Nigeria, has rated Foremost Capital Limited with BBB+ in its assessment of the company’s key performance indices, marking a major feat in its operations in less than two years.

The latest rating of the company, is an important independent recognition of its financial and operational standards, sending signals to clients, investors, counterparties, regulators and the wider market that the management remains fully committed to world-class standards at all levels of its business operations.

Specifically, the DataPro BBB+ rating of the company provides an independent assessment of its financial strength and operating capacity, a strong liquidity position, supporting its ability to meet financial obligations and manage client investment activities, and improvements in the company’s capitalisation, profitability, asset base and overall financial position.

Similarly, with the company’s assets under management growth of 250% from July to December 2025, the rating demonstrates its growing presence and capacity within the investment management industry, a stable outlook and provides a positive indication of the company’s direction and potential for continued improvement.

Commenting on the company’s latest performance feat, the Managing Director/CEO, Emmanuel Akehomen, said: “This BBB+ rating from DataPro is a significant milestone, validating our robust governance, liquidity and operational resilience. For our clients, it serves as an independent assurance of our stability and capacity for sustainable growth.

“We intend to leverage this strengthened market credibility to attract high-value mandates and optimize portfolio performance. Moving forward, we remain committed to deepening our market share through disciplined risk management and innovative investment strategies that consistently deliver superior, long-term value for our investors,” he added.
