World.title: Russia likely to mobilize at least 300,000 more troops to Ukraine war, Zelensky warns
World.content:
Russia is likely to mobilize another 300,000 troops later this year, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, as it tries to complete the capture of a long-coveted region of east Ukraine.

In wide-ranging remarks released Sunday, Zelensky said he expected that the Russians would end the year occupying the same amount of Ukrainian territory as at the beginning of the year, despite enormous losses of manpower.

“Russia has lost 267,000 personnel since the start of the year, including around 155,000 killed to date,” Zelensky claimed.

The figure is impossible to confirm but in line with estimates by Western officials.

Russian parliamentary elections take place next month, and there has been speculation about a fresh mobilization despite a 2022 draft triggering protests and an exodus of young men.

“We are confident that following the elections, they will carry out a mobilization. We believe this will not take place in the major cities,” Zelensky said.

Zelensky said he believed Putin would “deploy the 300,000 newly mobilized troops depending on the situation in the east of our country,” and had told his generals to complete the occupation of Donetsk by the end of the year.

“They’ll lose all 300,000 of these newly mobilized Russians there; we’ll wipe them out,” Zelensky asserted.

Ukrainian units are defending some 20% of Donetsk, including a belt of strategic industrial towns such as Slaviansk and Kramatorsk.

Zelensky said it was impossible for the Russians to complete the capture of Donetsk region. He suggested the Russians might also attempt an incursion into the northern Ukrainian regions of Kharkiv and Sumy.

“They do not yet have troops in the Bryansk region (which borders northern Ukraine), but we can see military equipment along the borders with the Russian Federation.”

Musk, Kushner, and air defenses

On air defenses, Zelensky contrasted the number of Patriot missiles supplied in 2023 – which was 675 – with the forecast number of 264 this year. Ballistic missile attacks have increased civilian casualties and infrastructure damage across Ukraine – and Patriots are the only means of shooting them down.

A Ukrainian soldier fires a howitzer towards Russian troops on the front line in Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukraine June 23, 2026. Stringer/Reuters

“As you can see, there is, unfortunately, a downward trend, and this depends primarily on the American side,” he said.

Last month, US President Donald Trump suggested Ukraine would be permitted to build Patriot missiles on license, but later backed away from the idea.

If the US would supply up to 10% of its Patriot missile stocks to Ukraine, Kyiv would pay for them, Zelensky said. Such a commitment “could make a huge difference, both in terms of saving lives and diplomatically as well.”

Ukraine faces the same problem in acquiring Aster air defense missiles from Europe, according to Zelensky, despite a recent pledge by French president Emmanuel Macron.

“There aren’t enough ‘Aster’ missiles, even though they are being produced,” he said – though added a licensing agreement would accelerate supplies.

In the meantime, Ukraine is hunting the sites in Russia from where ballistic missiles are launched, according to Zelensky.

Russia’s military industries may be capable of building about 1,300 ballistic missiles a year, Zelensky said. “There are specific objectives regarding strikes on military targets and other anti-ballistic sanctions,” he said.

Volodymyr Zelensky stands in front of a Patriot anti-aircraft missile system during a visit to a military training area in Germany in 2024. Jens Büttner/Pool/Getty Images

Ukraine has developed an arsenal of long-range drones and its own cruise missiles which are being used against a widening array of targets inside Russia.

He also spoke about Kyiv’s efforts to get permission to use Starlink satellite imagery of Russian territory.

Elon Musk, who owns Starlink, said he “believed that this could lead to a major escalation against the Russian Federation on Ukraine’s part,” according to Zelensky.

“He said he was in favor of ending the war, not prolonging it” – and discussions with Washington were continuing.

As for negotiations, Zelensky suggested that the window of opportunity for ending the war stretched through the end of next summer, when the US presidential election campaign would begin.

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were “finding it very difficult to find a format whereby the Russians would agree to end this war without Ukraine having to withdraw from Donbas or accept other unacceptable solutions.”

“Jared, Steve and I agreed to summarize all these discussions on a single page – setting out the realistic options for ending the war. This is what the Americans want to discuss with us and with the Russians.”

World.title: A closer look at the Strait of Hormuz after Iran issues new threat
World.content:
As we’ve been reporting, Iran’s security chief has threatened to halt oil flow out of the Strait of Hormuz, according to state-affiliated Press TV.

Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, threatened to shut down all traffic through the critical waterway should any neighboring countries enter the US’ expected economic crackdown.

A narrow waterway that bypasses Iran and Oman, the Strait of Hormuz is the main route for shipping crude from oil-rich countries such as Saudi Arabia and Kuwait to the rest of the world.

The strait has remained a major flashpoint since it was effectively closed by Tehran following airstrikes by the US and Israel on February 28.

Iran controls the strait’s northern side. About 20 million barrels of oil, or about one-fifth of daily global production, used to flow through the strait every day, according to the US Energy Information Administration, which calls the channel a “critical oil chokepoint.”

The strait also carries about one-fifth of global trade in liquefied natural gas, largely from Qatar. Some producers, including Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, have found alternative routes for their exports.

World.title: Top security official’s comments are a fresh sign of Iran’s readiness to go on the offense
World.content:
One of the most powerful figures in Iran has said that the US campaign of maximum economic pressure will fail — in a further sign that Iran’s hardline leadership is unwilling to compromise despite a deepening economic crisis.

“The world has realized that (US President Donald) Trump’s bluster is nothing but empty talk,” said the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, in an interview yesterday.

Rezaei’s remarks are another indication of the control exerted by Tehran’s hardliners and their growing readiness to adopt a more offensive posture.

“We will see changes in the conduct of the war, in diplomacy, and in political and social affairs, and new capabilities will be brought into play,” he added.

Rezaei, who is an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamanei, said Iran will not yield to US pressure, adding the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until Washington meets its commitments.

Shipping data suggests that more crude oil is leaving the Gulf via a southern route close to the coast with Oman, a threat to the leverage Iran has exercised in recent months.

Rezaei was a senior commander during the war with Iraq in the 1980s — a foundational moment in the creation of the Islamic Republic. He was named as the new security chief this month in what was seen as a shift to a more aggressive approach to that under the late supreme leader.

In his comments, the most substantial since taking on the new role, Rezaei also claimed the US’ attack on Iran had encouraged countries to seek protection by acquiring nuclear weapons.

World.title: Trump’s 75-country immigrant visa ban struck down by judge
World.content:
The Trump administration’s ban on visas for immigrants from 75 countries was struck down by a federal judge on Friday, who ruled it was “contrary to law” and outside the statutory authority of Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

In January, the State Department paused the issuance of immigrant visas from almost 40% of the world’s nations – including Brazil, Colombia, Egypt, Haiti, Somalia and Russia – in a move that it said would prevent the entry of people who would “take welfare and public benefits.”

Judge Jeannette Vargas of the Federal District Court in Manhattan took issue with the State Department’s rationale for the policy, reversing any visa denial based solely on it – in another setback to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

Under the law, an immigrant can only be turned away as a likely “public charge” (someone expected to depend on government support) after a consular officer weighs that person’s own finances, age, health, skills and family situation.

Judge Vargas found that, in practice, US officers were ordered to reject visas for applicants, even those who could support themselves, solely based on the country they came from.

The visa ban halted permanent-residence visas for people joining family members or taking jobs in the US, but did not apply to nonimmigrant visas such as tourist or student visas.

A cable that Rubio sent to every diplomatic and consular post, and which was entered into the case record, directed officers to refuse applicants even when someone “provides additional evidence that demonstrates he or she overcomes the public charge refusal.”

“The outcome is predetermined,” Vargas wrote. “The visa will be refused.” The policy, she said, ran afoul of a 1965 law barring discrimination by nationality in granting visas, and of a separate provision denying the secretary of state any say over how consular officers decide individual cases.

Denials that rested on other legal grounds stand, even where an officer also cited the ban, leaving the number of reversals expected unclear.

President Donald Trump, alongside US Secretary of State Marco Rubio (left), speaks during a Cabinet meeting at Camp David in Maryland, on July 31. Aaron Schwartz/AFP/Getty Images

Most of the 75 countries are non-European, spanning the Caribbean, sub-Saharan Africa, the Balkans, the Middle East, Central Asia and Southeast Asia, and count several US partners among them, including Jordan, Egypt and Georgia. The State Department drew its list from Council of Economic Advisers data, targeting nations where more than 30 percent of immigrant households received some form of public assistance.

Among the plaintiffs were six US citizens who filed family-based petitions and said the ban blocked relatives in Ghana, Jamaica, Guatemala and Ethiopia from obtaining visas. Five Colombians who had applied through job-based visas, one of whom received a denial notice that cited the policy, were also part of the case.

The administration did win on one narrower point, with the judge agreeing the policy was not the kind of formal rule that must be opened to public comment before being implemented.

In arguing their case, the administration’s legal team leaned on a 2018 Supreme Court decision upholding the third version of Trump’s first-term travel ban, which barred entry by nationals of several countries, most of them majority-Muslim. But Vargas said that case turned on the president’s power to decide who may enter the country, whereas the visa ban case rested on a different question: whether a visa may be issued at all.

Vargas, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, gave both sides until September 11 to propose how to resolve what remains of the case. The administration can appeal the ruling.

CNN has reached out to the Justice Department and the White House for comment.

World.title: NFSA: Egypt’s food exports reach 208,000 tons in one week,
World.content:
Egypt exported 4,370 food shipments totaling 208,000 tons between August 15 and 21, 2026, shipped by 1,410 exporting companies and covering around 758 food products, the National Food Safety Authority (NFSA) said on Sunday, August 23, 2026.

In its 31st weekly report for 2026, the authority said the exports included vegetables and tubers, fruits, preserved fruit and vegetable products, flour and grain products, and various other food items.

Vegetable exports totaled 50,000 tons across 45 varieties. Sweet potatoes topped the list at 20,000 tons, followed by onions at 10,000 tons and potatoes at 5,000 tons.

Fruit exports reached 36,000 tons across 34 varieties, led by strawberries at 13,000 tons, followed by citrus fruits at 7,000 tons and mangoes at 6,000 tons.

Tunisia was the largest importer of Egyptian food products during the week, followed by Italy, Syria, Saudi Arabia and the Netherlands, among 182 countries importing Egyptian food products.

Alexandria Port ranked first in the number of food export consignments, with 740 shipments, followed by Safaga Port with 703 and Damietta Port with 630.

As for food imports, Egypt received 1,917 food consignments totaling around 220,000 tons, imported by 858 companies. The shipments included wheat, soybeans and various oils.

Russia topped the list of food suppliers to Egypt during the week, followed by Indonesia, the United States, Australia and China, among 84 countries exporting food products to the Egyptian market.

Alexandria Port also ranked first in food import consignments with 679 shipments, followed by Cairo International Airport with 381 and Port Said Port with 220.

World.title: 262nd aid convoy enters Gaza via Rafah terminal
World.content:
The 262nd convoy of the “Zad Al-Ezza: From Egypt to Gaza” humanitarian aid campaign entered the Gaza Strip on Sunday, August 23, 2026, through the Rafah land crossing toward the Karm Abu Salem crossing in southern Gaza, following a two-day halt on Friday and Saturday for the weekly weekend break.

The convoy’s trucks are carrying humanitarian and relief supplies, including meat, food baskets, flour, medical supplies, relief materials, petroleum products and fuel.

The trucks are being inspected by Israeli authorities at the Karm Abu Salem crossing before being allowed to enter the Gaza Strip.

The Egyptian Red Crescent has maintained its presence along the border since the beginning of the crisis, remaining on standby at all logistical centers and continuing efforts to facilitate the entry of humanitarian and relief aid. More than 75,000 volunteers have contributed to the organization’s efforts.

World.title: Farida Osman wins bronze in 50m butterfly at Taranto 2026
World.content:
Egyptian swimmer Farida Osman won the bronze medal in the women’s 50m butterfly at the Taranto 2026 Mediterranean Games after finishing the race in 26.32 seconds, giving Egypt its second medal at the Games.

Osman’s bronze came after Abdelrahman Sameh won the gold medal in the men’s 50m butterfly in 23.18 seconds, securing Egypt’s first gold medal of the Games and breaking the competition record.

The 20th edition of the Mediterranean Games is being held in the Italian city of Taranto and will continue through Sept 3, with 3,803 athletes from 26 countries taking part.

The Egyptian delegation is competing in 23 sports, including archery, athletics, badminton, 3×3 basketball, boxing, canoeing and kayaking, equestrian, fencing, swimming, gymnastics, handball, judo, karate, padel, rowing, sailing, shooting, table tennis, volleyball, weightlifting, wrestling, fin swimming and inline skating.

The Egyptian delegation is seeking to continue its medal-winning run and achieve strong results at the Games, maintaining Egypt’s position among the leading medal-winning countries in Mediterranean Games history.

Egypt ranks sixth among the countries with the most medals in the history of the Mediterranean Games, with a total of 620 medals, including 156 gold, 209 silver and 255 bronze.

World.title: Liberia: Jewel Howard Taylor Rushed to GIMS Hospital After Medical Emergency in Police Custody
World.content:
MONROVIA, LIBERIA — Former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor has been rushed to GIMS Hospital in Sophie, Monrovia, after reportedly experiencing a medical emergency while in police custody.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Taylor was transported to the medical facility Thursday evening under heavy police escort after health practitioners reportedly observed a significant rise in her blood pressure.

The medical emergency occurred as authorities were preparing to transfer the former vice president to the Monrovia City Court, where she was expected to face proceedings stemming from allegations of drug trafficking and money laundering.

FrontPageAfrica has gathered that medical personnel were called to the Liberia National Police Headquarters after concerns were raised about Taylor’s condition. She has remained in police custody since her arrest.

She was subsequently placed in a heavily escorted police convoy and taken to GIMS Hospital for further medical evaluation and treatment.

Her expected court appearance has now been thrown into uncertainty as doctors assess her condition.

The development comes amid heightened security surrounding the former vice president, whose arrest and detention have generated significant public attention.

Police Spokesman Sam Collins confirmed Taylor’s transfer to the medical facility but did not provide details about her current condition or say whether she would be taken to court following treatment.

FrontPageAfrica is continuing to follow the developing situation.

World.title: 20 Deportees Arrive in Liberia as U.S. Transfer Deal Takes Effect
World.content:
Monrovia — The first batch of 20 deportees from the United States arrived in Liberia on Thursday through Roberts International Airport, marking the start of an arrangement under which the Liberian Government says up to 1,200 people could be transferred to the country over the next year.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The arrivals are part of an agreement between Liberia and the United States for the “dignified, safe and timely” transfer of persons being removed from the United States.

Information Minister Jerolinmek Piah said the arrangement is based on an exchange of notes between the two governments dated September 4 and September 10, 2025.

According to Piah, Liberia has agreed to accept up to 1,200 people within a year. The individuals are third-country nationals, including citizens or nationals of African and Western Hemisphere countries, some of whom may wish to seek asylum in Liberia.

The government said those transferred under the arrangement must be medically authorized to travel.

Authorities said preparations had been made for the first group’s reception at Roberts International Airport and their stay in Liberia, describing the arrangement as part of efforts to provide a safe place for the individuals while strengthening bilateral relations between Liberia and the United States.

However, the arrival of the first group was conducted with tight security and limited public access.

FrontPage Africa reporters at Roberts International Airport observed the 20 deportees being shielded from public view before they were quietly escorted onto a minibus and transported toward Monrovia.

The group was accompanied by officers of the Liberia National Police and the Liberia Immigration Service.

The government has not publicly disclosed the identities of the deportees, their countries of origin, or details regarding where they will be accommodated during their stay in Liberia.

The arrival comes days after the Liberian Government formally announced the transfer arrangement, saying it had made the necessary preparations to receive the first group.

The government has maintained that the arrangement is intended to ensure the safe and dignified reception of persons being removed from the United States while deepening cooperation between the two countries.

The transfer of up to 1,200 people over a one-year period is expected to place Liberia at the center of growing international attention over U.S. deportation arrangements involving third-country nationals.

World.title: Former VP Taylor Remains at LNP Holding Cell Amid Reported Health Concerns
World.content:
Former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor remains at the Liberia National Police’s withholding cell as of Thursday, August 20, amid reports that she may not be transferred to the Monrovia City Court today.

By Willie N. Tokpah

The development follows reports that the former Vice President is experiencing very high blood pressure, reportedly as the joint security prepared to transfer her to court for further proceedings.

FrontPageAfrica Judicial Bureau Chief, monitoring developments at the police headquarters, observed medical practitioners being taken into the withholding cell where Madam Taylor is being held.

The medical personnel were reportedly brought in to assess her condition and assist in stabilizing her blood pressure.

Information gathered from the corridor of the Liberia National Police Headquarters indicates that authorities may continue monitoring Taylor’s condition throughout the day.

Her transfer to court could depend on whether her condition stabilizes sufficiently to permit the movement.

Meanwhile, security personnel remain stationed at the Monrovia City Court, where preparations had reportedly been made for Taylor’s appearance.

As of the latest observation, there has been no official confirmation of a new transfer time. Authorities are expected to determine the next course of action based on her medical condition and prevailing security considerations.

World.title: Mwamba Urges AU to Save Zambia’s Democracy
World.content:
SAVE ZAMBIA’S DEMOCRACY, MWAMBA URGES AU

…Former envoy urges Ndayishimiye to intervene before August 25 petition deadline

Former Zambian Permanent Representative to the African Union, Ambassador Emmanuel Mwamba, has asked the continental body to urgently intervene in the country’s post-election crisis. Mr Mwamba has warned that the constitutional window for challenging the August 13 presidential election expires tomorrow.

In an urgent letter dated August 23, 2026, addressed to AU Chairperson Évariste Ndayishimiye, who is also President of Burundi, through African Union Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Amb. Mwamba said events following the election had now directly engaged the AU’s values, instruments and its own election observation mission.

“The facts set out below were not then on the public record. They are now, and most of them stand admitted by the Government of Zambia itself,” Amb Mwamba wrote.

He referred to the killing of former Cabinet Minister Mutotwe Kafwaya, the reported refuge taken by presidential candidates Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu at United Nations premises, and obstruction of an election petition.

Amb Mwamba, writing for and on behalf of the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance/NRPUP, whose presidential candidate Mr Mundubile was declared runner-up, urged the AU chairperson to exercise his good offices with President Hakainde Hichilema and consider sending a special envoy to Lusaka. He also called for the AU Peace and Security Council to be seized of the situation, arguing that developments had become sufficiently serious to warrant continental intervention.

The former diplomat said the Electoral Commission of Zambia’s suspension of counting and announcement of results on August 14 had raised serious concerns over the transparency of the tabulation process. He said party agents and accredited monitors were withdrawn during the suspension, while the head of the SADC Election Observation Mission stated that his mission was not in a position to observe the counting and collation of results during that period.

He further cited an EU Election Observation Mission update which, he said, found that the conduct of tabulation deteriorated significantly after the suspension, including a decline in verification that electronically entered figures matched paper tally sheets, from 100 percent to 81 percent of observations.

Amb Mwamba said the EU mission also observed returning officers appearing to wait for instructions from ECZ headquarters before announcing results, while a heavy military presence at totalling centres allegedly intimidated participants and reduced the presence of agents and observers. He said an armed group took almost all polling-station result forms from the Makeni Totalling Centre in Lusaka on August 15, and that credible witnesses reported raids on totalling centres in Kabwe by ruling-party cadres.

“We believe the declared figures do not reflect the ballots cast,” Amb. Mwamba said, adding that the claim could be tested through arithmetic against signed result forms held by party agents. He said the alliance had already tendered copies of its result forms to all observer missions, including the AU’s own mission.

Mr Mwamba also placed the killing of Mr Kafwaya at the centre of his appeal to the AU. He said an armed operation was conducted at Mr Mundubile’s Kabulonga residence on the night of August 14, hours after the opposition candidate had held a consultative meeting with the Joint AU-COMESA Election Observation Mission. Amb. Mwamba said Mr Kafwaya, a former Cabinet minister and Alliance finance chairperson, was shot and died that night.

He said the Government denied for five days that the operation had occurred, before the Central Joint Operations Committee, under the signature of Inspector General of Police Graphel Musamba, confirmed on August 19 that the operation had taken place and that Mr Kafwaya had been killed.

“Whatever else is disputed in Zambia today, this is not: the State killed a former Minister of the Republic and concealed his death from his family for five days while calling it a lie,” Mr Mwamba wrote.

He said the Law Association of Zambia and the Human Rights Commission of Zambia had called for an independent investigation, while the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights had urged authorities to stop arbitrary arrests.

Mr Mwamba further told the AU that Mr Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, had taken refuge at the premises of a United Nations agency in Lusaka on August 17, fearing for their lives. He said the UN had formally notified the Zambian Government of their presence, but that police subsequently issued a call-out for the two men on allegations of treason and insurrection.

Mr Mwamba said the situation was unacceptable, particularly because the candidates had millions of votes according to the declared results and were now unable to leave the UN compound for fear of arrest or harm.

He also raised concerns over the approaching constitutional deadline for challenging the presidential result. Mr Mwamba said Article 101 of the Constitution required an election petition to be filed in the Constitutional Court within seven days of the declaration, placing the deadline on August 25.

He said the detention of lead counsel, State Counsel George Chisanga, the arrest or detention of other lawyers, the seizure of campaign funds from counsel’s chambers, and warnings against petitioning had obstructed preparations for the legal challenge.

“The evident object of these measures is that the constitutional window should expire with no petition filed, so that it may afterwards be said that no Zambian challenged the result,” he said.

Mr Mwamba cited Kenya’s 2017 presidential election and Malawi’s 2020 presidential election as examples of African courts overturning disputed electoral processes and ordering fresh polls. He said Zambia’s courts should similarly be given the opportunity to determine any challenge to the election through the constitutional process.

Mr Mwamba asked the AU to seek guarantees for the safety of Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu and to ensure that the inviolability of UN premises was respected. He also urged the continental body to demand the release or court production of detained lawyers, an end to obstruction of the election petition, and recognition that a constitutional remedy prevented by State action should not be treated as having been voluntarily abandoned.

He also asked the AU to support an independent investigation into Mr Kafwaya’s death, including independent forensic pathology with the participation of the family.

Mr Mwamba also called on the AU to withhold any additional step normalising the declared election outcome until the final reports of the AU-COMESA, SADC and EU observation missions had been issued and any lawfully filed petition adjudicated. He urged the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights to consider the allegations, including issues concerning the right to life, arbitrary detention and citizens’ right to participate freely in the government of their country.

Mr Mwamba said the alliance had continued urging its supporters to remain calm and had chosen evidence, courts and African and international institutions as its avenues of recourse.

“I know this Union. It was not built to watch such machinations succeed,” he said.

World.title: Zimba proposes unity government framework for UPND and NRPUP after 2026 election
World.content:
By Dr. Chris Zumani Zimba

…..This political letter is addressed to both Republican President, Mr. Hakainde Hichilema of the ruling UPND and our NRPUP Tonse Alliance Presidential Candidate, Hon. Brian Mundubile…..

Yes, petitioning presidential results in Zambia is a constitutional right and everyone is free to do so. But the painful legacy of post election conflicts of this nature following the death of former minister of transport and Lunte former lawmaker, Hon. Mutotwe Kafwaya are horrific and tragic for anyone to continue with any form of hard politics, divisive tensions, antagonistic rhetoric and hostile confrontations.

Hence, wiser, patriotic and sober Zambian politicians in UPND and NRPUP Tonse Alliance must prioritize political ceasefire, stakeholders dialogue and reconciliation through a domestic tailor made unity government than any Western styled legal or political consideration. “A give and take approach” is now more appropriate, desirable and necessary that is premised on mutual understanding and compromise.

Proposed Conditions NRPUP Tonse Alliance’s BM and President UPND’s HH May Consider for a National Unity Government on a Give and Take Basis

1. National Amnesty for Political Detainees

Declare unconditional national amnesty and mutual forgiveness to free and release all NRPUP political detainees arrested and detained before, during and after presidential elections countrywide. More than 60 NRPUP members and leaders such as Chester Morepower, IDC, Patrick Mwansa, Bishop Mwamba, Hon. George Chisanga, etc are all detained for political reasons and need this urgent presidential amnesty from HH for national reconciliation and healing to take off.

2. Drop Charges Against Mundubile and Zulu

Unilaterally drop the political charges against NRPUP Presidential candidate, Hon. Brian Mundubile and his running mate, Hon. Makebi Zulu. Dialogue and reconciliation with UPND is the only practical option if we desire to redeem BM, MZ and many others already arrested from facing multiple malicious political charges and prolonged imprisonment instead of more legal confrontations and political battles.

3. Political Ceasefire Between UPND and NRPUP

Declare political ceasefire between UPND and NRPUP Tonse Alliance members and bloggers both at home and abroad so that both camps denounce and stop attacks, insults, malice, misinformation and cyber warfare against each other. This is very crucial if we want to bring about national healing, true reconciliation and peace in Zambia as political bloggers have become main catalysts of brutal tribalism, regionalism, hostility, tensions, hatred, political divisions and violence.

4. Protect NRPUP’s Elected Seats from Petitions

Openly commit not to maliciously petition and replace NRPUP parliamentary, mayoral and council seats in order to respect the will of the people and sustain multiparty democracy. By seeking to dialogue for peace and reconciliation with the ruling UPND, NRPUP Tonse Alliance must aim to protect and safeguard more than 300 seats of our victorious NRPUP candidates at various levels from possible malicious petitions and nullifications.

5. Cabinet, Diplomatic and Parastatal Positions for NRPUP

Demand that NRPUP Tonse Alliance is offered 4 cabinet positions, 4 diplomatic positions, 4 permanent secretary positions, 4 CEO positions at parastatal level, 30 DC positions in the national unity government between HH and BM. Once UPND and NRPUP Tonse Alliance secures such an accord, then political healing, reconciliation and peace is practically attained regardless of the election outcome. This is where “give and take” comes in effect!

6. Electoral Reforms for an Autonomous ECZ

Mutually agree to undertake specific electoral reforms in order to ensure that ECZ is autonomous and ready to administer future elections that guarantee stakeholders trust, confidence and accountability. Without such reforms, future elections will only fabricate and repeat the 2026 electoral and political horror episodes. This is the most important issue NRPUP must focus on than any petition in court.

7. NRPUP to Accept the Election Outcome

To benefit from the fruits of a unity government with UPND, NRPUP Tonse Alliance must painfully accept defeat and publicly acknowledge the outcome of the 2026 August elections as declared by ECZ and assure the President Elect of their support, cooperation and partnership than seek legally confrontation through a court petition. This is the hallmark of a meaningful dialogue, political reconciliation, peaceful resolution and national unity.

8. Dialogue Over Western-Styled Court Petitions

Complex, regionally and politically divisive post election conflicts and volatile sectarian disputes of this nature before Zambians today cannot successfully and amicably be resolved in any Western styled court petition unless through culturally sensitive dialogue, political reconciliation and traditional peace building mechanisms.

9. A Dignified Burial for the Late Former President

Zambia now needs healing process than more divisive politics and bitter rivalry so that our late former President, ECL could be buried with dignity soonest. Now that elections are over, Zambia must remember that we have failed to burry our Former President, Dr. Edgar Chagwa Lungu for more than a year. UPND and NRPUP Tonse Alliance unity government can resolve this issue mutually and amicably.

10. A Mutotwe Kafwaya Truth and Reconciliation Commission

Under such bitter circumstances for a grieving nation like Zambia today, everything must point to “a Mutotwe Kafwaya Truth and Reconciliation Commission” than any temptations to sustain political confrontations, provocations, antagonism and tensions at court level. A divided, mourning and sad nation like ours is in need of political reconciliation, unity, healing and peace.

11. The Petition as a Risky Legal Gamble

Moreover, a court petition of this nature is a dangerous gamble like one last bullet in the gun that is more likely to miss the target or desired outcome on any given day. From African perspective, this presidential petition is like to fail as a BID legal project only good at delaying the inauguration ceremony of HH to a future than securing a desired nullification of the results.

12. The Fate of Detainees if the Petition Collapses

So what will become of BM, MZ and many others with heavy political charges after the fall and collapse of the petition? What will become of our more than 60 NRPUP members like Chester Morepower, IDC, Patrick Mwansa, Bishop Mwamba, Hon. George Chisanga, etc detained for political reasons countrywide? What will be future of many people on the run and hiding in Zambia and diaspora for political reasons?

The reason I keep on sharing my personal views on this topic is simple : I am trained in comparative politics with specialization in democracy promotion and public policy analysis. So, l have chosen to be relevant to this debate than shy away or be muted in silence. Hence, l equally respect the views of others who believe and champion the opposite position. Zikomo!

Dr. Chris Zumani Zimba is the founder and Secretary General of Tonse Alliance as well as NRPUP Chief Presidential Advisor. He was Political Advisor to late President Edgar Chagwa Lungu from 2019 to 2025. He is a political scientist with a certificate, bachelors, masters and PhD in political studies.

World.title: Kalumba alleges UPND plot to arrest him for treason as party, police deny knowledge
World.content:
Kalumba alleges UPND plot to arrest him for treason as party, police deny knowledge

Former home affairs minister Katele Kalumba says he has uncovered a scheme by United Party for National Development officials to have him arrested and charged with treason, an allegation both the ruling party and police say they know nothing about.

Kalumba told journalists that he had received information suggesting instructions had already been issued for his arrest, and that his name had been linked, alongside that of former intelligence chief Xavier Chungu, to claims of plotting a coup d’état. He dismissed the suggestion outright, saying it defied both logic and his own political history.

“It is extremely annoying that people want to accuse me and individuals like former intelligence chief Xavier Chungu of plotting a coup d’état,” Kalumba said. “My name has come up that we were trying to plot a coup, which to me is actually nonsense.”

He accused the current administration of running what he described as a witch-hunt aimed at silencing critical voices, and challenged law enforcement agencies to produce evidence for any claims that he had been involved in militia activity. He said investigators should be prepared to prove, rather than simply assert, that offensive weapons had been found or that anything untoward had taken place.

Kalumba pointed to his own record with the ruling party as evidence against the allegations, noting that he had previously supported UPND in Chienge and had contributed financially to the party. He said it was upsetting that his name and Chungu’s were now being associated with illegality after that history of support.

UPND media director Mark Simuuwe, when contacted for comment, said the party had no knowledge of any such plot. He said the investigation and apprehension of lawbreakers fell squarely within the mandate of law enforcement agencies rather than the party itself.

“As UPND, we are not aware of such an activity because, as you are aware, such undertakings are being conducted by law enforcement agencies and not the party,” Simuuwe said.

Zambia Police Service deputy public relations officer Chipo Kaitisha gave a similarly cautious response when asked about Kalumba’s claims, saying her office had no knowledge of any scheme to arrest or detain him, though she said she would look into the matter further.

“I am not aware of any plot to arrest Dr Kalumba. But I will find out,” Kaitisha said.

The allegation surfaces at a moment when concerns over the treatment of opposition and other political figures are already running high. Eleven people arrested in connection with a security operation at opposition leader Brian Mundubile’s Kabulonga residence face treason charges that carry no possibility of bail, while Mundubile and running mate Makebi Zulu remain at United Nations premises in Lusaka after being summoned for questioning rather than formally charged.

Against that backdrop, the Apostles Council of Churches in Zambia has urged government to extend a hand of reconciliation to achieve national unity and healing following the election. Separately, Apostle Zulu has warned that continued arrests and police summonses of opposition-linked figures risk deepening division rather than promoting the national healing political leaders say they want.

Kalumba’s allegation cannot currently be verified independently, and neither UPND nor police have confirmed any arrest plan or investigation targeting him. Whether the claim develops into a formal case, or fades as an unconfirmed rumour, will likely depend on whether either side produces evidence to support their respective positions in the days ahead.

World.title: Commonwealth demands end to arbitrary arrests as it condemns Kabulonga killing
World.content:
Commonwealth demands end to arbitrary arrests as it condemns Kabulonga killing

The Commonwealth has called on President Hakainde Hichilema’s government to halt arbitrary arrests and release all persons detained for political reasons since the 13 August election, in one of the strongest international rebukes Zambia has faced since the disputed vote.

Secretary-General Shirley Botchwey said in a statement issued from London that the Commonwealth was dismayed by the security operation carried out in Kabulonga, Lusaka, in which a police officer was injured and former minister Mutotwe Kafwaya lost his life. She called for a transparent investigation into the incident and urged all parties to exercise restraint.

“The Commonwealth expresses concern at the post-election situation in Zambia and urges full respect for the rights of all persons and for the rule of law, in conformity with the Commonwealth Charter and values,” Botchwey said.

She went further, extending condolences to Kafwaya’s family and wishing the injured officer a swift recovery, while calling for constructive dialogue to de-escalate tensions and safeguard peace and stability in the country.

The intervention places the Commonwealth alongside a growing list of international bodies that have raised concerns over Zambia’s post-election conduct. The United Nations Human Rights Commission, Amnesty International, and observer missions from SADC, the European Union, COMESA and the Great Lakes Region have all condemned aspects of the crackdown that followed the vote.

The security operation at the centre of the criticism took place at the Kabulonga residence of opposition leader Brian Mundubile the day after the election. Government says the raid targeted a suspected militia cell and that officers came under fire from occupants of the property. Kafwaya, a former minister of transport and communications, was shot and killed during the operation.

Mundubile has given a different account, saying he witnessed Kafwaya shot at close range and that the killing has stained Zambia’s democratic credentials. He has also accused the Electoral Commission of Zambia of aiding Hichilema’s victory and has alleged that the military was unleashed on ordinary citizens to help manage the election outcome, allegations government has not directly addressed.

Hichilema, for his part, has accused Mundubile of running a militia together with retired Anglican Bishop Trevor Mwamba, lawyer and former Law Association of Zambia president George Chisanga, Kafwaya, and a Lusaka businessman. Mundubile has dismissed the militia claims as a ruse designed to discredit him ahead of his planned legal challenge.

Eleven people found at the Kabulonga property that night have since been charged with treason-related offences, charges that carry no possibility of bail under Zambian law. Mundubile and running mate Makebi Zulu have not been charged themselves but have been summoned for questioning over alleged links to national security threats, and are currently staying at United Nations premises in Lusaka rather than returning home.

It is against this backdrop that the Commonwealth’s statement lands with particular weight. Unlike earlier expressions of concern from human rights bodies, the Commonwealth speaks for an association of 56 member states with historical and institutional ties to Zambia, and its language, invoking the Commonwealth Charter directly, signals that Lusaka’s handling of the post-election period is now being measured against standards the country has formally signed up to uphold.

Government has not yet issued a detailed public response to Botchwey’s statement. State House has previously rejected broader allegations of arbitrary arrests, with communication specialist Clayson Hamasaka describing the post-election security operations as lawful investigations rather than a campaign against the opposition, and citing reports of high-grade weapons, alleged mercenary-style training and threats against the Head of State as grounds for the crackdown.

Mundubile is expected to file his Constitutional Court challenge to the presidential result within the seven-day window prescribed by the Constitution, a deadline that falls in the coming days. The Commonwealth’s call for dialogue and restraint, rather than confrontation, will now sit alongside that legal process as Zambia works out how to move from a disputed election toward a settled outcome.

For the family of Kafwaya, the immediate concern remains simpler than the wider diplomatic and legal manoeuvring: an independent, transparent account of what happened at Kabulonga, and confirmation that whoever gave the orders that night will be held to answer for them.

World.title: Kasonde drops citizen election petition as Zambia enters decisive post-poll week
World.content:
Kasonde drops citizen election petition as Zambia enters decisive post-poll week

Zambia begins a new week with one proposed challenge to the August general election now abandoned, while the country waits to see whether Brian Mundubile will proceed with his separate presidential petition.

Prominent lawyer and civil society advocate Linda Kasonde, who had been exploring a citizen-led challenge to the election, has told stakeholders that efforts to build the case have ended because sufficient evidence could not be assembled within the required period.

“It appears that we do not have enough evidence to proceed with the petition challenging the just ended general elections as all efforts to get the Petition off the ground have not succeeded,” Kasonde said in a communication circulated among stakeholders.

Her withdrawal matters because concerns over the election have not gone away. The EU Election Observation Mission reported weaknesses in parts of the results tabulation process, while the Christian Churches Monitoring Group has identified statistical discrepancies in 30 constituencies and called for greater transparency from the Electoral Commission of Zambia.

CCMG has been careful to draw a line under how far those findings go. The group has said the discrepancies it identified do not change the overall winner of the presidential election, even as it presses ECZ to release the underlying polling-station records for independent verification.

Kasonde is now redirecting her energy from overturning the election to the framework that governs future ones.

“Going forward, we hope to shift our focus towards electoral reform challenging decisions, measures and laws taken in the run-up to the August 2026 election,” she said.

Attention now returns to Mundubile. He has rejected the presidential result and has previously said his team gathered evidence for a Constitutional Court challenge. His position has increasingly diverged from figures within the political structure that backed his candidature. Ezra Tembo, NRPUP president, has accepted President-elect Hakainde Hichilema’s victory, while Tonse founder and secretary-general Chris Zumani Zimba has said he will not support a petition.

The clock is running regardless of that internal split. Hichilema was declared president-elect on 18 August after securing 2,965,326 votes against Mundubile’s 1,856,217, a margin of 1,109,109. On the constitutional timetable being applied, the seven-day window for challenging the presidential election expires on Tuesday, 25 August.

A separate but related story is playing out away from the courts. Police have summoned Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu for questioning over alleged links to activities authorities say concern national security. Both men have been staying at the premises of an international organisation in Lusaka. Neither has been convicted of any offence, and Mundubile has firmly rejected government claims linking his camp to an alleged militia.

The new week therefore opens with Zambia edging closer to a political and constitutional resolution, even as key questions remain unsettled. Kasonde’s proposed petition is off the table, and her focus has already shifted to longer-term reform. Mundubile’s challenge, by contrast, remains only an intention until it is formally filed, and the security investigation around him continues in parallel.

Tuesday now stands as the date that decides which of two paths Zambia takes next: another court battle over the presidency, or a final, uncontested road toward Hichilema’s inauguration.

World.title: Mundubile accuses state of moving to block election petition as deadline nears
World.content:
Mundubile accuses state of moving to block election petition as deadline nears

Opposition leader Brian Mundubile has accused the Zambian government of working to derail his planned Constitutional Court challenge to President Hakainde Hichilema’s re-election, with the seven-day window to file the petition closing on Monday, 24 August.

The Electoral Commission of Zambia declared Hichilema winner of the 13 August vote on 18 August, with 2,965,326 votes, or 60.49 percent, against 1,856,217, or 37.87 percent, for Mundubile. Under Article 103 of the Constitution, a presidential petition must be filed within seven days of the declaration, after which the Constitutional Court has 14 days to determine it.

Mundubile has rejected the result, saying his campaign documented serious irregularities in the counting, transmission and declaration of results. He has gone further, alleging that soldiers entered some totalling centres and interfered with the count. Government has not addressed that specific claim, and it has not been independently verified.

His legal team is understood to have engaged senior lawyers, among them Chifumu Banda and Bonaventure Mutale, to build the case ahead of the deadline. Reports suggest the effort has come at considerable cost to Mundubile’s campaign, a sign of how far he intends to press the challenge despite the pressure closing in around him.

That pressure, his camp says, now extends to the petition itself. Mundubile’s team alleges the state has moved to disrupt preparations through the arrest of lawyers and officials involved in assembling the case, and points to reports of heightened security around the Constitutional Court grounds as the deadline nears. Neither claim has been confirmed independently, and government has not responded to them directly.

State House has taken a different public line. It says Mundubile remains free to pursue his challenge through the courts. Clayson Hamasaka, State House Communication Specialist, has separately rejected broader claims of arbitrary arrests, describing the government’s post-election operations as lawful investigations rather than a campaign against the opposition.

The petition is also exposing strain within Mundubile’s own alliance. Zumani Zimba, Secretary General of the Tonse Alliance, has distanced himself from the court challenge, warning it risks deepening division rather than resolving it, while other alliance partners have already conceded the presidential result.

To understand why Mundubile believes the petition itself is under threat, the story has to go back eleven days, to the night the count began. On 14 August, the day after the vote, a security operation at Mundubile’s Kabulonga residence turned violent. Government says officers encountered gunfire when they moved on the property; Mundubile says his group was unarmed and fired upon without warning. Former cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya, 49, was shot and killed during the operation, in what Mundubile says happened in his own presence.

Eleven people found at the scene that night were subsequently charged with treason-related offences: Bishop Trevor Mwamba, George Chisanga, Patrick Mwansa, Jackson Mutyoka, Brazil Soko, Bernard Chewe, Simon Phiri, Richard Banda, Francis Mulenga, Emmanuel Mulenga and Darius Mwila. President Hichilema has since accused Mundubile of forming a militia, an allegation Mundubile rejects as an attempt to obscure his claims of a manipulated election. Police have issued a call-out for Mundubile and Zulu to report over treason and insurrection allegations, and Volker Türk, the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, has urged Zambian authorities to halt arbitrary arrests and ensure due process for those held.

It was that raid, and its aftermath, that sent Mundubile and Zulu into shelter at United Nations premises in Lusaka, where they remain. Mundubile now argues the operation and Kafwaya’s killing were the opening move in a broader effort to weaken him before he could get to court, an effort he says has continued through the past eleven days and into the current fight over his petition. Government maintains the raid targeted a suspected militia cell and had nothing to do with the election challenge that followed it.

International observers, including the European Union mission, described the pre-election environment as shaped by legal uncertainty and unequal campaign conditions, but stopped short of alleging manipulation of the count itself. That distinction will matter once the case reaches court, since any evidence Mundubile presents will be weighed on its own merits rather than on the surrounding political noise.

The immediate question is narrower than the wider dispute over who won. It is whether Mundubile can get his petition filed, and his legal team through the courthouse doors, before Monday’s deadline passes. Once that happens, the Constitutional Court’s 14-day clock begins, and Zambia moves from a fight over process into a fight over evidence.

World.title: Africa: The Deadly Bundibugyo Ebola Outbreak Can Be Stopped
World.content:
Dr Mohamed Janabi (WHO Regional Director for Africa -left), Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus (WHO Director-General - center), and Dr Jean Kaseya (Director-General of Africa CDC -right) at a press briefing in Kinshasa during a joint high-level mission to Uganda and DRC on 4 and 5 August 2026.

guest column

Each time we travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), we first go to listen.

In Bunia, we have met dozens of community representatives: survivors, women, young people, local organisations, health workers and leaders from affected areas. Their message is direct: involve us. We know our communities. We know where families seek care, how information moves and why trust is breaking down. Give us the means to help drive the response. They are right.

Ebola spreads through communities, and communities hold the knowledge required to stop it. They can identify illness early, alert health teams, help identify and trace contacts, challenge dangerous rumours and support families through access to treatment and safe, dignified burials. The response always moves faster when communities lead alongside national authorities and health workers.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Communities are not just part of the response. They are at its heart." - Tedros

One hundred days ago, the Government of the DRC declared the country's 17th Ebola outbreak following confirmation of the Bundibugyo virus. WHO subsequently declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, followed by Africa CDC's declaration of a Public Health Emergency of Continental Security.

Priorities are clear: reach every affected area, protect frontline workers and turn commitments into action.

The scale of the emergency is immense. As of 21 August 2026, the DRC has reported 5,290 confirmed cases and 2,516 deaths across 56 health zones. This is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak recorded, and it is moving faster than any previous one. It is being fuelled by insecurity caused by decades of armed conflict that have undermined law, order and social services and displaced more than a million people.

At the centre of the response are the people who show up every day. Health workers care for patients. Laboratory teams identify the virus. Contact tracers follow its path. Community health workers build trust where fear and misinformation have taken hold. Burial teams help families honour their loved ones safely and with dignity.

They are working under extraordinary pressure, often in insecure and hard-to-reach areas. Some have contracted Ebola in the line of duty.

Their service must be met with action: safety, protective equipment, training, sufficient medical supplies, timely payment, psychosocial support and access to rapid diagnosis and high-quality supportive care if they fall ill. The safety of frontline workers is central to stopping transmission.

The response has made progress. Under the leadership of national authorities, Congolese responders, WHO, Africa CDC and partners have expanded surveillance, deployed laboratories, supported treatment centres, reinforced infection prevention and delivered essential supplies.

Uganda has interrupted locally acquired transmission of the virus. Several health zones in northern Ituri province and South Kivu have also interrupted transmission. These experiences prove that the outbreak can be stopped more quickly when rapid detection, decisive national leadership and close cooperation with communities break the chains of transmission. But the continued emergency in Ituri and five other provinces demands urgently scaled up action.

To turn the corner, surveillance teams are being expanded and equipped to detect cases early and rapidly identify contacts. Safe clinical care and infection prevention measures are being increased wherever people seek treatment. More risk communication and community engagement teams are being deployed to reach out to communities to empower them to participate in the response and address barriers to care. More safe and dignified burial teams are working to prevent transmission associated with deaths. Special efforts are being made to reach vulnerable populations and communities in insecure and hard-to-reach areas.

But despite all these efforts, more is needed. We need to scale our response by two to three times current capacities, across all the response pillars.

Front-line workers' safety is essential to stopping Ebola.

Health facilities require urgent protection from infection. As of 20 August 2026, 158 health workers have been infected and 45 have died. Every facility in an affected or high-risk area needs trained staff, protective equipment, clean water, sanitation and functioning infection-prevention systems.

National and local teams need predictable funding for surveillance, laboratories, treatment, logistics, infection prevention and community engagement. Frontline workers must be paid on time. Local organisations need direct support to work consistently with communities. Supplies must arrive before stocks run out.

Delayed financing costs lives. Fragmented financing leaves gaps. Ebola exploits both. On the ground we at WHO and Africa CDC have established tight integration among health and relief organizations working with the government. Donors therefore need to support and enhance that integration, rather than support siloed and disconnected efforts.

Cross-border also coordination must remain strong. People move within and between countries to trade, work, study, seek care and support their families. Borders must serve as bridges for coordinated public health action. This does not require closing borders or imposing blanket travel and trade restrictions. Such measures can disrupt response operations and livelihoods without stopping transmission.

Close 

The priority is coordinated surveillance, rapid information-sharing and prepared health services along movement routes. Find every case. Follow every contact. Break every chain of transmission, protect every health and frontline worker, save lives and ensure that no community is left behind. Bring testing, and treatment closer to every affected community. Bolster cross-border coordination. Scale up international support. Turn every pledge into action.

African leadership and international support are necessary.

WHO and Africa CDC will continue working with the DRC, neighbouring countries, communities and partners to deliver on these priorities. Our responsibility is to bring the full strength of international and continental cooperation behind the nationally led response.

Uganda and areas in DRC have shown how the course of the outbreak can be turned, through rapid detection, decisive action and close cooperation with communities. But these measures must be delivered at scale. Success depends on sustained national leadership, continental solidarity and international support. We must rise to this challenge, together.

Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus is Director-General of the World Health Organization. Mohamed Yakub Janabi is Regional Director of the World Health Organization African Region. Jean Kaseya is Director-General of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.

World.title: Togo: Togo Says It Has 'Serious' Evidence Against Detained French Journalists
World.content:
Togo's government says it has "serious and consistent evidence" against two French documentary filmmakers detained since July on charges of making false statements. Gaël Mocaër and Sebastian Perez Pezzani were arrested along with their Togolese fixer, Fred Vedomey, and have denied wrongdoing.

In their first official statement on the case, released on Saturday, Togo's ministries of justice and security accused the team of not having the proper permits to film.

The three men were arrested on 27 July while shooting a travel documentary in northern Togo for French television.

The government says their paperwork was only in Vedomey's name and did not authorise them to film in locations they visited in the Savanes region and Bimah prefecture, where they were detained.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

They are also accused of using a drone "whose specifications had not been declared in advance".

A lawyer for the journalists, Martial Akakpo, told French news agency AFP his clients denied all the allegations.

Rights group calls for release of two French journalists held in Togo

Press freedom concerns

According to Reporters Without Borders (RSF), Mocaër and Vedomey remain in pre-trial detention in Togo's capital, Lomé, while Perez Pezzani was moved to house arrest earlier this week.

He is suffering from serious health problems and required urgent care, the media rights group said.

RSF has called the men's detention "unjustified and disproportionate", while the Togolese Press Association demanded their immediate release, saying the case risked damaging Togo's international reputation.

The government's statement said the case was not connected to the editorial nature of what the team was filming, nor an attempt to restrict press freedom, but represented simply the enforcement of administrative procedures.

Togolese authorities consider the areas where they were shooting sensitive due to the threat of jihadist attacks. Parts of the north are subject to a state of emergency due to incursions by Islamic militant groups over the past five years, particularly from neighbouring Burkina Faso.

French media has also faced pressure from Togo's government in recent years.

RFI and fellow public broadcaster France 24 remain off the air after being suspended in June 2025 over an alleged lack of impartiality.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Joint Statement Between DR Congo and the Alliance Fleuve Congo/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23) on the Doha Process
World.content:
Signing of the Doha Framework for Peace between the Government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Congo River Alliance (M23 Movement) on November 15, 2025 in Qatar.

document

The following statement was released by the representatives of the Government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the representatives of the Alliance Fleuve Congo/March 23 Movement, as well as the State of Qatar, the United States of America, the Republic of Togo (as the African Union mediator), Switzerland, and the African Union Commission, on the meetings held August 17 to August 21 in Switzerland, on the implementation of the Doha Framework for a Comprehensive Peace Agreement.

Begin text:

From August 17 to August 21, 2026, representatives from the Government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and representatives from the Alliance Fleuve Congo/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23), along with the State of Qatar, United States of America, the Republic of Togo (as the African Union mediator), the African Union Commission, and Switzerland, convened in Switzerland to assess progress made and challenges encountered to date in the framework of the Doha Process. They also discussed the path forward for the implementation of existing obligations and commitments and the negotiation of remaining protocols under the Doha Framework for a Comprehensive Peace Agreement between the Government of the DRC and AFC/M23, signed in Doha on November 15, 2025.

The Parties welcomed continued progress on the operationalization of the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus (EJVM+), including the establishment of its Secretariat, and the EJVM+ reconnaissance mission, with the logistical support of MONUSCO, conducted on August 20 in advance of the first EJVM+ ceasefire verification mission, scheduled for August 24 in Minembwe. The Parties agreed on the importance of a standardized method for reporting allegations of ceasefire violations.



The Parties agreed to establish a mechanism tasked with reviewing progress and addressing challenges in implementation of obligations and commitments under the Doha Framework Agreement.

Following this evaluation, the Parties developed a roadmap setting out sequenced steps and timelines for negotiations under the Doha Framework Agreement and committed to flexibility and creativity within the existing structure provided by the

Framework Agreement. The Parties agreed that the order of negotiation of the protocols does not dictate the order of implementation of the protocols. They reaffirmed their commitment to pursue negotiations towards comprehensive peace and conflict resolution through the implementation of the Framework Agreement.

The Parties shared recommendations with the facilitation regarding the path forward for constructive negotiations and to promote implementation of commitments undertaken by both Parties.

The representatives of the Government of the DRC and the representatives of the AFC/M23 expressed their gratitude to the State of Qatar, the United States of America, the Republic of Togo as the AU Mediator, Switzerland, and the AU Commission for their steadfast support in advancing peace and stability in eastern DRC and the broader Great Lakes region.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: DR Congo Ebola Outbreak Spreading Exponentially, UN Responders Warn
World.content:
Health workers gather at an Ebola treatment centre in Bunia, in the eastern DR Congo.

As the deadliest Ebola outbreak in DR Congo's history continued spreading on Friday, UN responders renewed their urgent appeal for immediate international support, with existing funding for lifesaving work critically low.

Key points

Ebola deaths reach 2,516 in DRC

Response funding could run out within weeks

Dozens of frontline healthcare workers among dead

"We're only covered for the next weeks, and very soon funding will run out," said Julien Harneis, UN Senior Ebola Coordinator. "Every delay in funding and implementation makes this epidemic more deadly, more difficult to stop and more expensive. So, we need that international support immediately."

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Since the outbreak was declared on 15 May, 5,290 people have been infected 2,516 have died, according to latest health authority data published on Friday.

Of the total confirmed number of cases, 1,152 people have recovered and nearly 840 people remain in isolation or hospitalized. The fatality rate is 47.6 per cent and contact follow-up is 82.9 per cent.

Deadly progression

Briefing journalists from the Ebola epicentre in Bunia, Ituri province, Mr. Harneis warned that the disease is "growing exponentially", with half of all deaths occurring in just the last 20 days.

"The epidemic is spreading to an area that is bigger than France. And the outbreak is growing faster and wider than the Ebola response," he stressed, as "brutal" operating conditions continue to impede the progress of frontline workers.

Three months into the outbreak, 160 healthcare workers have contracted Ebola and 43 of them have died. "And then when we do respond, apart from the threat from the virus, healthcare workers and frontline workers have been attacked by youths, ambulances have been burned and stoned and the healthcare facilities have been attacked," Mr. Harneis explained.

"Conditions on the ground are extremely difficult, but we will continue deploying all the humanitarian and medical assistance needed until the job is done," the veteran aid official said.

"Last week, I was trying to get into an Ebola hotspot, and it took three hours to drive 60 kilometres (37 miles)," he added.

Another key obstacle to the response is the lack of basic social services in the six eastern, provinces where the virus is spreading (Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, and Bas-Uélé), a direct result of decades of violence in the resource-rich area.

Gaps in government-run, coordinated healthcare services and a limited number of banks have created further problems.

"In this area, the banking system barely functions," Mr. Harneis explained. "We're unable to bring in the amount of money that is required to pay the workers, which has led to great unhappiness amongst frontline workers."

Close 

US aid boost

And although the United States has contributed $80 million to the DRC Government to boost bed capacity and safe burial practices, among other support, cuts to aid work - especially in the last two years - have reduced the capacity of humanitarian organizations by more than 30 per cent, he added.

Despite these challenges, multiple specialist UN agencies continue to work alongside the DRC authorities to push back Ebola. They include the World Health Organization, the World Food Programme, the UN Children's Fund (UNICEF), the UN migration agency (IOM) and partners including Médecins Sans Frontières.

"It's a disease, it's an invisible threat which comes into your community and suddenly people start falling sick around you and your loved ones die," Mr. Harneis said. "And that generates a lot of fear in any community."

World.title: Louisiana girl, 8, dies after contracting suspected brain-eating amoeba linked to lake swim
World.content:

Lillian Smart, an 8-year-old girl who health officials believe contracted a brain-eating amoeba while swimming in a northern Louisiana lake, died Saturday at a Ruston hospital from an infection linked to the pathogen.

Lillian died one day after celebrating her eighth birthday.

"The injuries to her brain were too severe for her little body to recover from," the Smart family said in a statement posted Sunday morning on Facebook. "Everyone did everything they could to keep her here. We are heartbroken and honestly do not know what to do next. How do we put one foot in front of the other without our girl?"

MICHIGAN REPORTS 2 DEATHS IN RARE PARASITE OUTBREAK THAT HAS SICKENED MORE THAN 11,000

The Louisiana Department of Health announced Wednesday that a state resident had been hospitalized after becoming infected with Naegleria fowleri, a microscopic amoeba that can cause a rare and often deadly brain infection.

State health officials have not publicly identified Lillian as the patient referenced in the announcement. Her family, however, said on social media that she had been admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit at a Ruston hospital and identified Naegleria fowleri as the cause of her illness.

The health department said the infection in the case it announced was most likely acquired while the patient was swimming in Lake Claiborne shortly before becoming ill.

BEACHGOERS WARNED AFTER DEADLY 'FLESH-EATING' BACTERIA KILLS 5 IN SOUTHERN STATE

A representative for the Louisiana Department of Health did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Louisiana Department of Health records identify three previous deaths associated with Naegleria fowleri in the state since 2011.

Two happened in 2011. A 20-year-old man in St. Bernard Parish died after using tap water to rinse his sinuses, while a 51-year-old woman in DeSoto Parish died after using tap water for a similar purpose.

In 2013, a 4-year-old boy contracted the amoeba while visiting a home in St. Bernard Parish, where he had played on a slip-and-slide. State officials later reported that CDC testing detected Naegleria fowleri in the parish water system.

DEADLY BACTERIA FOUND IN WATERS NEAR LUXURY VACATION DESTINATION AHEAD OF SUMMER

Naegleria fowleri causes primary amoebic meningoencephalitis, or PAM, an extremely rare brain infection that can develop when contaminated water enters the nose and the amoeba travels to the brain. People cannot become infected by swallowing contaminated water.

The amoeba is not found in saltwater or properly chlorinated swimming pools.

Symptoms typically begin with headache, fever, nausea and vomiting before progressing to a stiff neck, seizures and coma. Symptoms generally appear about five days after infection, and the disease can lead to death within about one to two weeks.

A tree-trimming employee has been charged with manslaughter after allegedly crushing his coworker’s head with a hydraulic grapple while the pair were reportedly "f—ing around" on the job, according to Minnesota authorities.

The incident happened in Apple Valley on Thursday when Christopher Boone Crimmins, 34, was operating machinery on the back of a truck while his coworker, Tyler Anthony Lynch, 26, was on the ground cleaning up branches, according to a criminal complaint filed by Dakota County.

Responding to reports of an incident, police discovered Lynch lying on the ground with "a significant amount of blood around him and significant trauma to his head," the complaint said.

Lynch was pronounced dead at the scene, according to the county.

WORKERS WARNED OHIO TRENCH WAS TOO DEEP BUT WERE TOLD TO ENTER MINUTES BEFORE FATAL CAVE-IN: REPORT

While looking at the shadows, Crimmins allegedly maneuvered the grapple so that its shadow appeared to grab Lynch’s shadow.

However, he did not realize that the grapple itself was moving toward Lynch’s head.

TWO WORKERS KILLED, SEVERAL INJURED AFTER EXPLOSIONS TEAR THROUGH OHIO RECYCLING FACILITY

WORKERS KILLED AND MANY TREATED AFTER REFINERY CHEMICAL RELEASE AS INVESTIGATORS PROBE CAUSE

Officers observed blood on the grapple, which was directly above Lynch, according to the complaint.

Crimmins has been charged with one felony count of second-degree manslaughter. If convicted, he faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison and a $20,000 fine.
