"We need to cancel these contracts," Hawk said.

Flock has been the target of much of the public's ire, but its rivals have largely avoided it. Now, some of those competitors are trying to cash in on Flock's fall from grace.

More than 130,000 automated license-plate readers, or ALPR's, can be found in cities and towns across the country, according to the crowdsourced database DeFlock.org . The cameras take images of the backs of cars. Law enforcement has increasingly turned to this tool to help solve crime.

"The Flock ALPR technology has captured the public's attention" and spurred a realization that "maybe we don't want to be surveilled all the time," said Andrew Ferguson, a law professor at George Washington University.

But now, he said, Flock is the one that has "the target put on its back."

Why is Flock facing so much heat?

Flock CEO Garrett Langley regularly posts on social media extolling the benefits of his company's tech , often noting that communities are safer because of it. Flock was credited with helping to track the suspect in last year's Brown University shooting, which killed two students and injured nine other people.

"On a very personal level, I go to bed every night very proud of the impact we have in the world," Langley told NPR.

Sponsor Message

Many automated license plate readers, including Flock's, use AI to capture information such as a vehicle's make, model and color. Police can search Flock's shared national database of these images — including vehicles outside of their own jurisdiction.

That national database is a core point of contention for Flock opponents.

"People got really mad at Flock because they realized that it was a window into a whole network of surveillance," said Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a digital privacy advocacy group. He strongly opposes the technology broadly, not just Flock's version of it.

With this network "suddenly your cameras are being used to enforce things that you don't agree with or that are not illegal in your town," he said.

In Texas, for instance, deputies used Flock data to help investigate a woman suspected of traveling to have an abortion.

Hits against Flock keep coming. Police officers have been found to use this technology to stalk women. And while Flock allows customers to control the information they share on its network, there are some cases where information was unknowingly shared more widely, including with federal immigration agencies.

In response, the company last week announced a host of changes , including reducing its data retention period and emphasizing safeguards around local data searches.

The ACLU said the changes were largely unsatisfying.

Competitors step in

License plate readers are only one piece of a growing police surveillance industry.

Many law enforcement agencies use integrated tools such as facial recognition , gunshot detectors , predictive policing , drones and real-time crime centers that pull all this information into one central hub used by investigators.

Ferguson, who is also the author of Your Data Will Be Used Against You: Policing in the Age of Self-Surveillance, says in his view, those integrated systems raise far more red flags for privacy than license plate readers alone. Yet, they've drawn almost no large-scale public protest.

toggle caption PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images





Guariglia believes Flock is at the center of the license plate reader firestorm, in part, because of its cameras' visibility.

Sponsor Message

"Once you know what they look like, you become aware of how ubiquitous they are," he said.

Dozens of communities have turned against Flock amid widespread public backlash. About 100 cities have deactivated cameras, rejected deals or cancelled contracts, according to DeFlock's database . Some, such as Denver and Longmont, Colo. , signed contracts with Flock competitors this year, including Axon, a trend reported by 404 Media .

Axon, a multibillion dollar company that provides tech and weapons to law enforcement and the military, says it's positioned to step in amid the "deFlock movement." During Axon's most recent earnings call, CEO Rick Smith told investors that law enforcement agencies are making the switch.

"We're seeing a significant number of agencies want to come over to Axon and convert from existing license plate readers to us." He credited the company's "controls and privacy work."

Axon declined to say how much business the company has gained from cancelled Flock contracts.

When asked how Flock is responding to other providers swooping in on their departing business, Langley said he is unconcerned.

"We will have added seven times the number of new customers that have left us this year," he said.

Langley said he was especially surprised about Denver's move to sign a one-year deal with Axon, after residents voiced concerns over data sharing for immigration enforcement.

"I guess in some ways I scratch my head because that company works with ICE," he said. "They lack the accountability and transparency we have, and so I don't know why they made that choice."

Axon holds several multimillion dollar contracts with the Department of Homeland Security for its products, including body cameras and Tasers.

"For more than 30 years, we've built products to protect life," Axon spokesperson Kate MacKinnon said in an email to NPR. "As new technologies emerge, we know that our customers require solutions that protect data and privacy."

But privacy experts warn the switch to other police surveillance technologies isn't a fix.

"You're just replacing one color of camera for another," Guariglia said. "Those dangers you were concerned about are still going to be there."

World.title: Soccer fans boo U.S. anthem as Canadians react to breakdown in trade negotiations
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Soccer fans booed the U.S. national anthem on the weekend as Canadians reacted to news that trade talks between the two countries had broken down again.

The Canadian Press reported jeers echoing through Vancouver's B.C. Place ahead of a Major League Soccer game between the Whitecaps and FC Dallas on Saturday, following booing at Stade Saputo, where CF Montréal hosted the L.A. Galaxy earlier in the day.

This came hours after Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended talks with the United States and recalled his negotiators, saying the U.S. made unreasonable demands at the last minute after previously agreeing to a tentative framework.

The U.S. followed through on its threat to impose 50 per cent tariffs on a wide swath of Canadian goods, and Canada promised to match the U.S. tariffs dollar for dollar by Sept. 8, a move that was largely backed by premiers across the country.

Many Canadians who spoke with CBC News over the weekend seemed to echo the sentiments from those inside the stadiums.

'We've got to stand up'

Niiamaa Laryea in Vancouver said the tariff news is "horrible" but that it's important for Canada to stand up to the U.S. "We're in a tough situation, but I think Carney is doing the right thing," he told CBC Vancouver. "We've got to stand up eventually. We can't let the U.S. bully us into submission."

In Ottawa, Lesley Combden said the economic pain will get worse before it gets better, and she would like to see Canada continue to diversify its trade away from the U.S.

Niiamaa Laryea in Vancouver, left, and Lesley Combden in Ottawa were among the Canadians reacting to news that trade talks between Canada and the U.S. had broken down again. (CBC)

"I think that Carney made the right decision in walking away," she told CBC Ottawa. "Why would we want to deal with the U.S. when they won't take away tariffs, they want us to make concessions?"

The sweeping tariffs will cover about $28 billion worth of Canadian exports, or about five per cent of products sent to the U.S.

Ontario, B.C. and Quebec are expected to feel the biggest impacts, with some of the most affected industries including agriculture, textile, electronics, furniture and plastics manufacturing.

University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe estimates some 87,000 jobs could be lost across the country as a result of the new duties.

WATCH | Layoffs in Canada on the horizon: Canada could lose tens of thousands of jobs due to Trump’s 50% tariffs | Duration 2:32 After Canada-U.S. trade talks broke down, U.S. President Donald Trump hit Canada with 50 per cent tariffs on various items. Analysis from economist Trevor Tombe indicates that if the tariffs last, Canada would shed tens of thousands of jobs.

Retaliatory tariffs questioned

Some callers to CBC's Cross Country Checkup on Sunday were more critical of Carney.

While few criticized the prime minister for ending negotiations, some questioned the wisdom of retaliatory tariffs.

Peter Arndt in Pickering, Ont., said Carney "100 per cent" had to walk away based on what he's heard about the U.S. demands, but he said retaliatory tariffs are not the right way to go off the bat because they'll also hurt Canadians.

"Tariffs are just a bad plan all around," Arndt said.

Economists have also told CBC News that retaliatory tariffs will further hurt Canadians financially.

Kathy Woudzia in Vancouver said it's hard to know what to make of the prime minister's decision without having more details about what exactly was on the table in the negotiations.

"I really think that before Sept. 8, it would be nice to have some transparency about the deal that was rejected," she said.

"Without really knowing what was offered and why it was rejected, we can't meaningfully compare that option with the economic consequences of the current 50 per cent tariff environment."

WATCH | PM outlines last-minute changes U.S. made to trade deal: Carney outlines the last-minute changes U.S. tacked onto trade deal terms | Duration 2:44 Asked for specifics of the Americans' last-minute changes to terms of a trade deal, Prime Minister Mark Carney outlined three examples. He said Americans looked to change the scope of tariffs on Canadian auto content, made efforts to restrict Canada's ability to have other trade deals around the world and made efforts to restrict Canada's protections of language, culture 'and in effect, our sovereignty.'

Officials have not released many specifics about what was on the table, but Carney said the U.S. made unacceptable demands at the last minute on culture, autos and sovereignty — and ultimately "asked too much and offered too little."

Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette said the Americans had proposed negotiating matters around the province's French-language legislation, such as the requirement that French be included on consumer devices like electronics or household appliances and user manuals.

Trump, writing on his Truth Social platform early Sunday in his first public comment since the talks broke down, did not mention the negotiations specifically but said Canada "wants the benefits" of being a U.S. state "without being one" and accused Canada of imposing "massive amounts of Tariffs" on American farmers for years.

Canadians feeling 'betrayed': pollster

Matt Ambida in Markham, Ont., said he thinks the Canadian government is doing a "great" job in its negotiations and needs to take a more serious approach to trade with other countries. "At the end of the day, we have to hold firm on our stance," he said. "We're not dealing with the same America that we were dealing with before, and that means that we have to make tougher calls."

An Angus Reid Institute poll conducted online Saturday and Sunday found that 76 per cent of Canadians support the Carney government's decision to walk away from negotiations.

Angus Reid president Shachi Kurl said the findings are a "snapshot in time" but fall in line with a long-expressed resolve from Canadians to see officials take a hard line with Washington.

"It's unusual for a majority of Canadians, especially coast to coast to coast, in every province and territory, to agree on something," Kurl told CBC News.

The poll found Canadians are still bracing for the impacts of the new tariffs, with 89 per cent expressing concern about the costs of goods and services and 38 per cent saying they have some level of anxiety about losing their job.

The randomized sample of 1,468 Canadians polled was weighted to represent adults nationwide according to region, gender, age, household income and education, Angus Reid says. A sample of this size would carry a margin of error of plus or minus two percentage points, 19 times out of 20, according to the non-profit foundation.

David Coletto, founder and CEO of Abacus Data, said his polling firm has found most Canadians feel "deeply betrayed" by the U.S. and are willing to endure short-term economic pain for a better deal in the future.

"I get a sense from my polling that the majority of Canadians have decided that deeper integration with the United States, continuing to be reliant on them, is not going to do Canada well in the long term," Coletto told CBC News Network on Sunday.

World.title: Why are there suddenly so many data centres planned in Canada? Your questions answered
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This story idea came from audience members, like you, who got in touch with us. Send us all of your questions about data centres and the environment. We are listening: ask@cbc.ca

In 2026, AI seems to be everywhere — and some Canadians are questioning whether they want the massive buildings that power it humming away in their backyards.

Canada has bet big on AI, and part of that push is a boom in planned or proposed AI data centres, which require vast amounts of water and energy.

Proponents say the facilities could help secure Canada's future as an AI leader. But the rapid pace of development has some communities hitting pause. In Ontario, Oakville voted in August to impose a one-year moratorium on data centre construction, while Mississauga is set to vote in September on a similar moratorium. Councillors there brought forward the motion after a data centre the size of three football fields was proposed.

On Thursday and Friday, hundreds of people turned up at town halls to demand answers from Alberta's technology minister over the province's plans for AI data centres.

People rally before participating in a march to protest the opening of AI data centres, in Vancouver in June. Telus is moving forward with two new AI data centres in Vancouver and the expansion of an existing facility in Kamloops. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

Many CBC readers have also reached out with questions about the sudden spike in data centres being built in Canada.

Here's what we know.

What are data centres?

A data centre is a facility that houses and powers computer servers, networking equipment and other technology needed for computing and storing data. Any time we visit a website or watch a movie online, a physical server processes that request for us.

But the AI data centres making headlines today are much larger and more energy-intensive than traditional data centres. They use more powerful computer chips — graphic processing units, or GPUs — driving up energy consumption and requiring more intensive cooling systems to manage the resulting heat.

"For an older-style conventional cloud facility, we might have a couple of megawatts moving into that building, but for AI facilities, it's much more common to see hundreds of megawatts," Anne Pasek, Canada Research Chair in Media, Culture and the Environment at Trent University, told CBC News.

These facilities can span thousands of square feet, with "hyperscale" data centres becoming more common. Definitions of hyperscale vary: Some place the threshold at 50 megawatts, others at 100. Just 50 megawatts is enough electricity to power 37,500 homes.

Aerial images show construction of the TOR1X0 Data Centre at SteelesTech Campus in Toronto. The three-storey data centre and office building, designed by WZMH for Yondr Group, is southwest of the intersection of Steeles and Victoria Park avenues. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

"The facilities we're building for AI are just bigger and bigger, both in terms of the footprint that they have in the lands they occupy, in terms of the energy bills and water impacts that potentially come with them," Pasek said.

Why are so many being built in Canada suddenly?

Demand for AI has skyrocketed in recent years, and Canada is looking to establish itself as a leader in the field, hoping to attract investors and give the economy a boost.

In 2024, up to $700 million was dedicated specifically to leveraging investments in new or expanded data centres.

Prime Minister Mark Carney unveiled Canada's national AI strategy in June , dubbed "AI for All," promising at least $2 billion in new investments. One stated goal is to increase AI adoption among Canadian businesses from 12 per cent today to 60 per cent by 2034.

WATCH | Carney unveils national AI strategy: Carney's AI strategy big on jobs and training promises, light on details | Duration 1:57 Prime Minister Mark Carney unveiled the government's long-delayed strategy on artificial intelligence, pledging 250,000 AI-related jobs and billions for training programs, but little in the way of privacy and safety details.

Supporters say wider AI adoption is inevitable and that Canada is better off staying ahead than being left behind.

"It's a facet of modern life," Martin Karsten, a professor of computer science at the University of Waterloo, told CBC News Kitchener-Waterloo on Aug. 18. "As long as we are all very interested in using these [AI] services, I think we have to accept the fact that these data centres keep coming."

But many communities are pushing back, citing concerns about water, energy and health. Critics also question whether data centres bring enough local economic benefits to offset those concerns, saying they provide a temporary boost in construction jobs but do little to spur secondary industries.

Some experts have warned that the rush to fund AI could be a bubble that could burst, potentially leaving AI data centres as stranded assets. Some companies that embraced AI are now pulling back in the face of rising costs , raising questions about the technology's return on investment.

Canada currently has only five hyperscale data centres with a capacity of at least 50 megawatts, but 159 facilities were proposed or under construction across the country as of July, according to a recent York University study . Of those, 116 are expected to have a capacity of more than 100 megawatt capacity — a first in Canada.

The study found the scale of the industry is ramping up rapidly. Over 200 new projects have been announced, with an average capacity of 122 megawatts — more than 10 times the average capacity of Canada's 194 active sites.

While most active data centres are in Ontario, followed by Quebec and British Columbia respectively, the majority of proposed projects are in Alberta. If all are built, Alberta's share of total data centre capacity in Canada would rise from three per cent to 93 per cent.

"If you look at the location of the data centres, we can see that the amount of electricity that the average new data centre would use is as much as some of the communities where they're going to be located in," Alexander Carlo, a postdoctoral researcher at York University's Schulich School of Business and one of the study's authors, told CBC News.

Data centres accounted for 4.4 per cent of U.S. electricity demand in 2023, according to the U.S. Department of Energy, which predicts this share could rise as high as 12 per cent by 2028.

During a heat wave or snowstorm, electrical grids may struggle to handle the added load from a data centre, Pasek said, increasing the risk of brownouts. There are also concerns that the additional strain could increase consumers' power bills .

WATCH | Digging into the hyperscale data boom in Canada: A hyperscale AI data centre boom is coming | Duration 6:21 A boom in hyperscale AI data centres in Canada is coming, promising economic opportunity and tech sovereignty, but as CBC’s Nora Young explains, there’s a growing resistance to the impact the massive, power-hungry facilities have on local communities.

How do data centres affect water sources?

Computing equipment generates a lot of heat, so facilities use water to cool it. Many cooling systems then evaporate that water to expel the heat, meaning it may not return to the water cycle in the same place.

"They can pull water from a watershed, that water can evaporate off, become a cloud, that cloud will float away and will become rain in a totally different region where that water doesn't get returned to the [original region's] watershed," Pasek said.

Smaller-scale operations can draw tens of thousands of litres a day, while hyperscale operations can draw more than a million.

A 2025 report by the U.K. Government Digital Sustainability Alliance found that a single 100-megawatt hyperscale facility could consume about 2.5 billion litres of water annually — enough to serve 80,000 people.

Some areas can absorb that demand, but in drought-stricken regions, it could pose a problem.

"We are already water bankrupt in many places around the world. So adding an extra pressure on the system, even if it's small, can have significant impacts," Kaveh Madani, director of the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health, told CBC News in August.

WATCH | Why data centre communities worry about water: Why data centre communities worry about water | Duration 6:02 As resistance to AI data centres grows, industry leaders say there are ways to build more community-friendly facilities. For Radio-Canada, Anaïs Elboujdaïni examines the water concerns and explores the arguments for a more sustainable approach in Canada.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said in August that the province's data centre framework would prioritize closed-loop cooling systems, which reuse water and cut down on intake compared to evaporative systems.

Are there health risks living near data centres?

Experts say there can be, but the risks vary depending on the data centre's size, design and power source, meaning that different data centres can carry vastly different risks.

Air pollution

Data centres can draw electricity from local grids, but it can take years to fully connect them. As a result, many are now being designed with on-site power plants fuelled by natural gas or methane gas. When powered by fossil fuels, data centres produce emissions that contribute to climate change, as well as a type of air pollution called fine particulate matter, also known as PM2.5.

Wildfire smoke is one of the main sources of PM2.5, a dangerous type of air pollution. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

"We do know that exposure to fine particulate matter increases the risk of all kinds of [negative] health outcomes, from respiratory, cardiovascular and neurocognitive," Francesca Dominici, a professor of biostatistics at Harvard Chan School of Public Health, told CBC News. She added that chronic exposure to air pollution can also increase annual hospital visits and worsen asthma.

An independent analysis she worked on with EmPower Analytics Group examined a specific AI data centre steps from a residential area in northern Virginia and found its eight natural gas turbines and 51 diesel generators could result in $53 million to $99 million US a year in health-related damages.

Studies have suggested that chronic exposure to PM2.5 may also be linked to a higher risk of lung cancer.

Noise pollution

Like other industrial buildings, data centres produce noise around the clock from fans and backup diesel generators. They can also emit a low-frequency hum, and chronic exposure can cause stress, sleep problems and long-term health complications, Dominici said.

According to NBC News, residents have filed at least 15 lawsuits in 12 U.S. states over constant data centre noise in the past three years.

WATCH | Toronto residents pushing back on data centres: Why these Toronto councillors, residents are pushing back against data centres | Duration 2:13 Some Toronto councillors and residents are pushing back against two proposed data centre projects in Etobicoke and Scarborough. As CBC's Naama Weingarten explains, they are concerned about potential noise, electricity demand and water use.

Concerns have also been raised that closed-loop cooling systems could affect water quality if wastewater is mismanaged. Much remains unknown about the overall risks, Dominici said, which is why she believes development should be paused to give researchers more time.

"There has been a race to build these AI hyperscalers without really thinking through about what could potentially be the negative health impact on the surrounding community," Dominici said.

Are there alternatives to traditional big-box data centres?

Experts say it's a question of trade-offs. One option is to make data centres more sustainable.

The health risks associated with air pollution, for example, can be mitigated if a data centre and its backup power systems use wind and solar instead of fossil fuels.

"If you could make the facilities optimally efficient and power them with renewable energy, either in the moment or stored in batteries or other types of storage, we'd be making some real progress there," Daniel Bresette, president of the U.S.-based Environmental and Energy Study Institute, told CBC News.

But that approach is more expensive, meaning developers may have little incentive to adopt it without regulations or community pressure. Most new projects in Alberta are set to use natural gas, including a $13-billion AI data centre project announced by Meta last month.

The facility, shown in this rendering, will be a one-gigawatt, nearly 270,000-square-metre data centre powered by a natural gas-fired plant. Meta, the tech giant behind Facebook and Instagram, says it's building a new AI date centre in Sturgeon County, Alta. (Handout - Sturgeon Data Centre/The Canadian Press)

Reducing noise pollution through design can also be costly. Some regions in the U.S. are introducing zoning restrictions based on noise pollution and requiring developers to conduct noise studies before construction.

Locating AI data centres in more remote areas can also reduce risks to the general population, but it could shift those impacts onto rural and Indigenous communities.

A proposed $70-billion gas-powered data centre in northern Alberta is currently being challenged by nearby Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation, which says it was not properly consulted about a water licence.

WATCH | UN report investigates environmental risk of AI data centres: UN report highlights environmental impacts of AI data centres | Duration 1:39 The United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health has released a report that examines the environmental impacts of AI data centres. It comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney unveiled his new AI strategy that includes plans for 'large-scale' data centres throughout the country.

Another option is to spread AI computing capacity more broadly rather than hyperscaling it, Pasek said, in order to "break up the burden" on communities.

The third option is to "rethink fundamentally what we want AI to be," she said. This could mean a return to smaller, open-source development rather than massive AI projects that, in her view, are profitable only if the technology is pushed onto businesses and Canadians.

World.title: More grizzly bears killed in 2024 than any other year on record in Alberta
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

More grizzly bears were killed by people in 2024 than any other year on record in Alberta, according to data from the provincial government.

The province publishes human-caused grizzly bear mortality rates on its website, with data from 2005 to 2025 publicly available.

In 2024, a total of 40 known grizzly deaths were reported, with a list of causes including poaching, vehicle collisions and lethal removal by law enforcement.

That data indicates 21 grizzlies were killed through "agency removals" — meaning they were killed by Alberta Fish and Wildlife Enforcement Services, conservation officers or other law enforcement officials.

Those are the highest numbers of any year on record, and the only year in which more than half of the total grizzly bear deaths were agency removals.

Before that, the highest number of known human-caused grizzly bear deaths was 29, reported in 2016. Most deaths that year were vehicle strikes.

And the previous highest number of lethal removals by law enforcement was recorded in 2023, when 12 out of 26 known grizzly deaths were listed as agency removals.

'A hit list on male bears'

Retired Fish and Wildlife officer John Clarke says he believes the 2024 increase could be attributed to the province's grizzly bear response guide, which was updated in 2023.

Under that framework, bears are classified based on factors such as age, whether they have cubs, and their specific problematic behaviour — whether that's becoming habituated to the presence of humans, learning to associate humans with food, or preying on livestock, pets or humans.

He says t he changes gave officers more authority to make decisions regarding what to do with a bear , while lowering the bar for male grizzlies to be killed.

"They've kind of put a hit list on male bears," he said.

Fourteen of the 21 grizzlies killed by law enforcement in 2024 were male.

John Clarke, pictured with a tranquilized grizzly bear during his time working with Alberta Fish and Wildlife Enforcement Services, now operates the Canadian Bear Safety Authority. (LinkedIn)

Under the latest response framework, a male grizzly can be killed the first time it's reported as habituated or food-conditioned, if the bear is outside designated recovery areas under the province's Grizzly Bear Recovery Plan.

If the bear is in neither a designated recovery nor support zone, it can be killed regardless of sex — unless it has cubs, in which case it gets what Clarke calls "one get-out-of-jail-free card," meaning it is relocated the first time, but killed if an incident happens again.

"When you look at a population, females are more important than the males because they're breeders," Clarke said.

Grizzly bears have low reproductive rates. Adults typically begin breeding when they’re five to eight, and sows only have one litter every three to five years after that.

Grizzly bears have been a threatened species in Alberta since 2010.

Two grizzly bear cubs cross Highway 40 in Kananaskis Country. (Amir Said/CBC)

Under the new changes, an officer still has to justify their actions if they kill a grizzly bear. Clarke says they are still expected to consult with others to determine the outcome. The guide also says "preventative action" — which can include hazing (non-lethal attempts to move a bear) closing the area to the public, or removing food attractants — is expected to be the initial response before the decision is made to capture or kill a bear.

In a statement sent to CBC News, the provincial ministry of Forestry and Parks said "there is no one-size-fits-all solution to human-grizzly conflicts."

"The higher number of human-caused grizzly bear mortalities and agency removals in 2024 reflects annual variability in conflict incidents rather than a single, province-wide cause. In some areas, bears were more likely to come into conflict with people, livestock, and other attractants," the province said.

The mortality data covers multiple parts of the province, rather than being attributed to any specific areas.

Many black bears have brown fur, which can lead to the two species being mistaken for one another. The province's data indicates 17 grizzly bears were killed after being mistaken for black bears from 2006 to 2021. (Amir Said/CBC)

In 2025, the number of total deaths dropped to 18, with six of those being agency removals.

"Conflicts between grizzlies and Albertans can fluctuate from year to year and are influenced by a range of factors, including local bear populations, food availability, environmental conditions, and the presence of human attractants such as livestock, grain, garbage and other food sources," the province said.

Clarke says the drop in 2025 could be attributed to a variety of factors, including the possibility that specific bears causing problems for people and livestock were killed the year before.

The province says 2024 saw two attacks involving humans and 92 involving livestock. In 2025, there were three attacks on humans and 80 that involved livestock.

Those numbers, provided by Public Safety and Emergency Services, don't include incidents in parks and protected areas.

The Alberta government hasn't recorded any grizzly bear attacks on humans this year — though a grizzly attack did take place in Jasper National Park earlier this summer — and there have been 57 attacks involving livestock so far this year.

To address grizzly conflict with humans and livestock, the Rural Municipalities of Alberta has called for the provincial government to legalize grizzly bear hunting.

Grizzly bear sport hunting was banned in 2006. The year before — the only year on record in which grizzly hunting numbers were included in the total death count — saw 73 hunting licenses allocated and 10 grizzlies killed in the hunt. A total of 23 human-caused grizzly deaths were recorded that year.

The Alberta government estimates there are about 1,000 grizzly bears in the province today, though there hasn't been a provincial population count since 2018.

World.title: 'I didn't think I could do it': A 13-year-old N.S. girl fought a 711-pound tuna and won
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Five hours off the west coast of Nova Scotia, a 13-year-old girl broke a world tuna-fishing record during the 22nd annual Wedgeport Tuna Tournament and Festival.

Délynn Jacquard was aboard the Pelagic Predator when she reeled in the 711-pound (323-kilogram) catch Wednesday. If ratified, it will mark a new International Game Fish Association female junior world record.

The former record of 618 pounds was set 12 years ago by Nova Scotian Jenna Gavin in Ballantynes Cove, meaning Jacquard beat the record by nearly 100 pounds.

"I was thinking to myself, 'I don't think ... I might not be able to do this,'" Jacquard said in an interview Saturday. "But then I did it and I was just proud of myself."

Jacquard says it took just over an hour to reel the tuna in.

"It's a lot of work," she said. "You're hooked on to the rod and to the chair. Once you see the tip of the rod start coming closer to you, that's when you start twisting the line and pulling it in."

Jacquard’s father, Camille Jacquard, captains the Pelagic Predator. He has participated in the tournament for roughly 20 years. But this year was Délynn's first outing as a relative newcomer to the world of big-game fishing.

Délynn said she's not sure if she'll be back for next year's tournament.

WATCH | 13-year-old N.S. girl reels in record-breaking 711-pound tuna: 13-year-old N.S. girl reels in record-breaking 711-pound tuna | Duration 1:33 Délynn Jacquard smashed the junior female world record by nearly 100 pounds during Nova Scotia's Wedgeport Tuna Tournament. The CBC's Ben Dornan reports.

Brandon Doucette, a board member for the tournament, said it could take up to six months for the record to be official, though he is confident it will be confirmed.

Doucette said that IGFA records are based on the weight of a fish before it is gutted, whereas the Wedgeport tournament counts the weight after partial gutting. Jacquard’s tuna weighed 711 pounds fresh out of the water and 635 pounds after being partially gutted.

Doucette said that "2026 is going to be known as the year of records," as another vessel reeled in the heaviest tuna in tournament history. Capt. Brent Pothier caught an 801-pound bluefin aboard the Lucas & Noah, a vessel named for his two sons, who were also on board for the catch.

It is the first fish to clear the 800-pound mark in the tournament’s 22-year history, breaking the previous record of 796 pounds set in 2014 — the same year Gavin made her record-setting catch.

"When they started yelling the weight out, the excitement was unbelievable," Doucette said. "We were just so excited to have not just one world record, but also a Wedgeport Tuna Tournament record."

Doucette said the annual tournament is as much about community history as it is about records. Between the 1930s and 1960s, Wedgeport hosted anglers from around the world for its International Tuna Cup Match, earning a reputation as the sport tuna fishing capital of the world.

"We’re able to come out, celebrate our culture, and it's really such an incredible event for our community," Doucette said.

As for the thousands of pounds of tuna landed during the event, Doucette said that all catches fall within the region’s commercial quota.

"It's going to end up either in a restaurant or on somebody's plate in their house," he said.

World.title: Conservative MP calls for 'full details' of failed Canada-U.S. trade deal to be released
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Conservative Party is urging Prime Minister Mark Carney's government to release "the full details" of the proposed Canada-U.S. trade deal that was on the table before negotiations collapsed late on Friday.

Conservative MP Shuvaloy Majumdar, the party's shadow minister for Canada-U.S. relations, said in a letter to Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc on Sunday that the Conservatives aren't asking for "negotiating secrets."

But the party is seeking information that Ottawa and Washington already know, Majumdar said. "This information will allow Canadians to debate and discuss the way forward as a country."

Fifty per cent U.S. tariffs on about $28 billion worth of Canadian goods came into effect early on Saturday after extended trade negotiations between the two countries fell apart.

Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters on Saturday that Canadian negotiators decided to walk away from the talks after the United States had made what he said were unacceptable demands.

That included " efforts to restrict our ability to have other trade deals ," Carney said.

"We were not prepared to compromise Canada's sovereignty or to undermine our key industries," he said, adding that his government would impose "dollar-for-dollar" tariffs on U.S. goods, starting Sept. 8.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the talks failed after "new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada."

The U.S. "offer would have led to supply chain co-ordination on aerospace, complementary actions to address unfair trade practices, critical minerals co-operation, increased enforcement against imports produced with forced labour and the announcement of formal U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement negotiations," he said in a statement early Saturday.

Greer also told the New York Times in an interview on Saturday that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration offered, in part, to cut 10 per cent tariffs on softwood lumber and lower steel tariffs from 50 to 25 per cent.

WATCH | Canada could lose tens of thousands of jobs: Canada could lose tens of thousands of jobs due to Trump's 50% tariffs | Duration 5:40 After Canada-U.S. trade talks broke down, U.S. President Donald Trump hits Canada with 50 per cent tariffs. CBC’s David Common says this could result in the loss of thousands of Canadian jobs.

Exact details not yet released

But neither government has released the exact details of the deal that was being negotiated.

Despite that, Carney's decision to walk away from the talks appears to have garnered widespread support in Canada, including from provincial leaders like Ontario Premier Doug Ford and B.C. Premier David Eby.

Many also have backed Carney's plans to impose reciprocal tariffs on the U.S. next month.

There is "anxiety" among Canadians for what the escalating trade dispute means for the economy and their daily lives, said David Coletto, founder and CEO of the Abacus Data polling firm.

But there is also a sense that "we're not going to let Donald Trump bully us," Coletto told CBC News in an interview Sunday. "And I think most Canadians still feel good about what the prime minister said yesterday and now are going to wait to see what comes next."

After Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed, Conservative Party leader Pierre Poilievre said Canada 'cannot accept one-sided tariffs that will deindustrialize our country' or 'a bad deal.' (Christopher Drost/The Canadian Press)

Opposition party leaders have also said Canada should remain united in the face of Trump's tariffs.

" Canada cannot accept one-sided tariffs that will deindustrialize our country. Nor can we accept a bad deal. Instead, we must continue the fight for tariff-free trade," Conservative Party Leader Pierre Poilievre said in a social media post Saturday morning.

Poilievre said he would seek a call with Carney "to discuss what we can do to fight for our workers, businesses and economy."

Asked by reporters on Saturday if he would brief opposition leaders on the trade situation, Carney said that would likely happen Monday afternoon or Tuesday morning.

World.title: Trump says Canada 'wants the benefits' of being a U.S. state 'without being one' as trade dispute deepens
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump makes his first comment since U.S.-Canada trade talks broke down and new tariffs came into effect.

‘Canada wants the benefits of being a state, without being one’: Trump’s response to Canada’s no deal

U.S. President Donald Trump says Canada "wants the benefits" of being a U.S. state "without being one."

Trump's comments, in a brief post on his Truth Social platform early Sunday, are his first since trade talks between the two countries broke down and come after a slate of new U.S. tariffs came into effect.

Trump also accused Canada of imposing "massive amounts of Tariffs" on American farmers for years. "No more!!!" he wrote in the post.

There was no immediate reaction from the Canadian government to the remarks from Trump, who has repeatedly said since entering his second term in office in 2025 that he wants Canada to become the 51st U.S. state.

Fifty per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian goods were ushered in early Saturday after extended negotiations aimed at reaching a trade deal fell apart.

WATCH | U.S. tariffs designed to 'hurt and divide,' Carney says: Carney says U.S. tariffs designed to ‘hurt and divide us’ | Duration 0:38 Prime Minister Mark Carney called U.S. President Donald Trump's new 50 per cent tariffs a 'miscalculation' because Canadians are united and 'masters of our destiny.'

Carney says U.S. made 'unacceptable' demands

Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters that Canadian negotiators walked away from the talks after the Trump administration made "unacceptable" demands, including restrictions on Canada's ability to make trade deals with other countries.

"We cannot accept what they've offered, and we will not give what they've asked," said Carney, adding that the U.S. "asked too much and offered too little."

Carney also announced that his government would impose reciprocal, "dollar for dollar" tariffs on U.S. goods, starting Sept. 8.

Under the Trump administration's new policy, tariffs of 50 per cent will apply to hundreds of products worth more than $28 billion — from plywood and cement to wine and hockey sticks.

Cross Country Checkup wants your reaction to Canada's trade dispute with the U.S. Leave your comment here and our team may get in touch or read your comment on air

The trade deal was also expected to lower existing U.S. tariffs on the Canadian aluminum, steel and automobile sectors, sources told CBC.

On Sunday morning, Conservative MP Shuvaloy Majumdar urged the federal government to release "the full details of the proposed deal."

Majumdar, the party's shadow minister for Canada-U.S. relations, said Conservatives aren't asking for "negotiating secrets," but are seeking information that Ottawa and Washington already knows.

"This information will allow Canadians to debate and discuss the way forward as a country," Majumdar wrote in a letter addressed to Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and shared on X.

Premiers back decision not to back the pact

Provincial and territorial premiers have largely backed Carney's decision to walk away from the negotiations.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, for instance, said Saturday that he was "glad" the prime minister didn't sign the pact "because it was a bad deal."

"We need to fight these tariffs, tariff to tariff, dollar to dollar," Ford told reporters.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Saturday there were no plans for new talks with Canada.

"Our interest is in protecting American workers and protecting American supply chains," Greer said in an interview with Fox News.

He said the Trump administration had offered to cut tariffs on steel, automobiles and lumber.

"They've always had the best deal, and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn't want that," Greer said, referring to Canada.

WATCH | B.C. premier weighs in on the Canada-U.S. trade situation: B.C. premier says U.S. alcohol won't return to provincial shelves amid tariffs | Duration 0:59 B.C. Premier David Eby says that U.S. booze won't be seen on provincial liquor store shelves until the softwood lumber sector is treated fairly. Eby says even Russian forest products have better access to the U.S. economy than Canadian forest products

'Canadians do not want to be bullied'

Jamie Gillies, co-ordinator of the communications and public policy program at St. Thomas University in New Brunswick, said there was an expectation that Canada "would match" U.S. tariffs "dollar for dollar."

"Polling has shown that Canadians do not want to be bullied by the U.S. administration," Gillies told CBC News.

Despite the escalating dispute, he said, there is "some wiggle room" to get back to the negotiating table because Canada's retaliatory tariffs aren't expected to come into effect until Sept. 8.

Gillies also said the Trump administration is looking for a trade win as the cost of living in the U.S. is rising and could become a major issue for Republicans ahead of midterm elections in November.

"There might be some pressure on Greer to salvage parts of what they were trying to negotiate; maybe [there is] something that Canada and the U.S. can agree to, where we can climb down from just this set of tariffs."

World.title: 'Super' El Niño didn't cause this year's fires and heat waves, but it's about to take us on a 'wild ride'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Whether you call it a "super" El Niño or a "Godzilla" El Niño, the Pacific Ocean warming event that disrupts global weather patterns is back and packing a punch, at a time when many parts of the planet are already overheated.

This July was the hottest on record for North America and Europe, where successive heat waves have led to thousands of heat-related deaths, dried up rivers and fire-scorched landscapes. That includes Canada, which has already seen more than 4.1 million hectares of woodland go up in flames and produce thick smoke that blanketed much of the eastern half of the country and parts of the northern U.S.

Although this scorching summer aligned with the arrival of an El Niño and climate scientists say it's not to blame for those devastating extreme weather events. However, they note we may only be starting to see how this naturally occurring phenomenon could amplify extreme weather already super-charged by fossil-fuel driven climate change.

"El Niño's impacts are going to be large and broad across a huge area," said Josh Willis, a climate scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

"Get ready, because it's going to be a wild ride."

WATCH | What might happen when El Niño mixes with human-caused climate change: El Niño expected to add fuel to climate disasters | Duration 2:06 The UN's weather agency is warning that the return of El Niño will make temperatures even higher this summer, which they also warn will exacerbate climate disasters, including drought and wildfires.

Flipping the weather upside down

El Niños occur naturally every three to seven years, usually beginning in spring and enduring well into the following year, as the water surface temperature in the area of the Pacific where they form along the equator, rises at least 0.5 C above the average.

Willis says that warming heats up the air above the water and "rearranges the atmosphere."

"It flips the weather upside down," he said, causing drier places to get heavier rainfall and wetter regions to dry up.

A satellite map from the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration shows sea surface temperature anomalies recorded on Aug. 20, with hotter than average temperatures stretching across the El Niño region toward the west coast of South America. (NOAA)

Although this El Niño may have begun forming in May and June just as successive heat waves and fires began to scorch the northern hemisphere, Willis says they usually don't start to impact northern places like Canada until they peak in the late fall and winter.

But Muhammad Azhar Ehsan, a scientist at the Center for Climate Systems Research (CCSR) at New York's Columbia University, says this El Niño is so unprecedented that while he can't directly link it to current heat and wildfire conditions, he does wonder if the "exceptional" temperatures associated with it could be contributing to these disasters.

At the very least, he thinks it's grounds for more research

Ehsen says this El Niño is on track to rival those experienced in 2015-16 and 1997-98, the strongest El Niños since official records began in 1950.

WATCH | How a very strong El Niño will affect the planet in 2026 and into next year: What exactly is a ‘super’ El Niño? And what does it mean for you? | Duration 3:25 Some climate models predict 2026 will be an El Niño year — and that it'll be a particularly strong one. CBC’s Nick Logan breaks down what that means, and what Canadians can expect.

What to expect when you're expecting El Niño

Models suggest much of Canada and the northern U.S. can expect a warmer winter than usual due to this El Niño, with British Columbia's normally wet south coast potentially seeing far less precipitation and a much lower snowpack.

The southern U.S., meanwhile, is likely to experience a much wetter winter.

There are also noticeable effects happening right now in the tropics that Willis says are likely associated with El Niño. He says the phenomenon "sort of juices up" conditions that may already be occuring.

Peru and Ecuador sit at the eastern edge of the El Niño region, where Willis says a lot of warm water has "smashed up" against the coast, posing a threat to fisheries.

Peru is also bracing for heavy rains and flooding in some areas and drought in many inland regions.

"But we're also beginning to see a lot of drought away from the equator," Willis said, highlighting a prolonged lack of rainfall in Panama, which is already affecting water levels in the lake that supplies the Panama Canal.

At the opposite end of the El Niño region are countries like Indonesia, which is already experiencing a much longer and more active wildfire season.

16-year-old Rudiyansah wears a Superman costume while extinguishing a fire at a wildfire-affected area in Indonesia's Central Kalimantan province on Aug. 14. (Ajeng Dinar Ulfiana/Reuters)

One thing people in North America can see happening now, Willis says, is the change to the hurricane season. In an El Niño year, there are fewer tropical storms and hurricanes in the Atlantic Ocean.

"The jet stream, which is migrating a little bit farther south, tends to shear off the top of the hurricanes in the Atlantic," he said.

"And because we have all this warm water in the Eastern Pacific, it fuels storm generation there and tropical storms and depressions, which might not have been hurricanes otherwise."

The Eastern Pacific season has already recorded nine named storms ahead of peak season — including Category 5 Hurricane Genevieve in late July and Lala, which caused significant damage as a tropical storm on Hawaii's Big Island last week.

WATCH | Hawaii's Big Island spared direct hit from Lala but suffers widespread damage: Tropical Storm Lala leaves destruction across Hawaii | Duration 1:40 Despite not making a direct hit, Tropical Storm Lala left widespread destruction on Hawaii's Big Island. Lala was downgraded from hurricane status on Sunday morning, but forecasters warned it remained powerful and dangerous

An El Niño born into a much warmer world

The record heat and wildfires this summer were the result of human-caused climate change, which has already been attributed for the past four years being the hottest on record, says Zachary Labe, climate scientist at U.S.-based nonprofit organization Climate Central.

"El Niño is just sort of a temporary boost on top of this long-term trend," Labe said.

But such a significant warming event happening in a world that's even hotter due to climate change could, he says, defy expectations climate scientists have based on previous data.

Authorities in Panama have begun restricting shipping through the Panama Canal, seen in this March 13 file photo, as the country copes with drought conditions exacerbated by El Niño. (Enea Lebrun/Reuters)

Labe says what's more certain is that we'll be dealing with the effects of this El Niño well into 2027.

"Because it takes time for that El Niño to have all that heat that's building up in the ocean to transfer into the atmosphere," he said.

"So, this will be around with us for at least the next six to 12 months."

World.title: Rare thunderstorm with lightning strikes wows southern B.C., causing havoc at Vancouver airport
World.content: The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Lightning strikes lit up the skies across B.C.'s South Coast overnight in a rare display as a severe thunderstorm passed over the region, snarling traffic at Vancouver International Airport and causing flight issues in the process. "This was quite the system, hundreds of cloud to ground strikes ... mainly in Vancouver/Richmond," CBC meteorologist Johanna Wagstaffe said. Wagstaffe said the centre of a low-pressure system pushed onshore near Richmond after travelling from the equator, loaded with moisture. A preliminary count from Environment Canada reported more than 1,800 incidences of lightning over the Lower Mainland on Saturday night and Sunday morning, while the B.C. Wildfire Service said it recorded more than 7,000 strikes provincewide. B.C. Hydro reported numerous outages overnight. As of Sunday morning, over 3,800 customers were without power in the Lower Mainland and Sunshine Coast regions. Ian Crook took this image of lightning strikes hitting over Stanley Park and downtown Vancouver on Saturday night. (Submitted by Ian Crook) Cancellations, delays at Vancouver airport The storm created havoc at Vancouver International Airport (YVR), causing multiple overnight delays and cancellations between about 9 p.m. Saturday and 3 a.m. PT on Sunday. That left hundreds of passengers like Simone McCallum stranded at the airport terminal overnight. Several lightning strikes were observed from the University of British Columbia's Vancouver campus. (Submitted by Parsa Nourian/@parsanourian5) McCallum said passengers were directed to head back to the check-in area for new boarding passes, but were not allowed back through security again — leaving them to sit or sleep on the ground. "It was horrible, there was no place to stretch out at all, almost every surface where you could put yourself down was hard as rock," she said. "I can't even imagine what that would have been like with children, or if you had some kind of physical disability. It would have been just a complete nightmare." the scene at #YVR at 4am today. pandemonium! pic.twitter.com/OZbU9EdhPB —finalcutgod YVR spokesperson Stephen Smart apologized to travellers who were inconvenienced, and said the airport called in extra staff as quickly as it could to help deal with the situation. Smart said the storm delivered lightning for more than five hours and dumped 64 millimetres of rain on the airport, more than double the precipitation the facility usually gets in the entire month of August. Videos posted to social media also appeared to show flooding in parts of the airport. "Normally when we see something like that, it lasts for 20-30 minutes, operations get back to normal. Last night our operations were effectively paused," Smart said. "We can land aircraft during a storm like that, that's not a problem. But we can't have employees out on the airfield, we can't have aircraft taking off." Overnight thunderstorms impacted operations at YVR. Today, flights are arriving and departing with some continued impacts to schedules. Travellers are encouraged to check flight status before coming to the airport. See latest here: https://t.co/kCum4EzB5D pic.twitter.com/bgYSPJVuaF —yvrairport The airport said some flights are also being impacted Sunday as the airport works with airlines to get back to normal operations. YVR's website showed multiple delays and cancellations Sunday. People are urged to check their flights before going to the terminal. WATCH | Lightning snarls traffic at Vancouver airport: Lightning snarls traffic at YVR as rare thunderstorm strikes Metro Vancouver | Duration 3:17 A series of lightning strikes lit up the skies across B.C.'s South Coast in a rare display Saturday night. Environment Canada reported nearly 2,000 strikes between Saturday night and Sunday morning, as the storm also disrupted operations at Vancouver International Airport. Wildfire crews on alert B.C. Wildfire Service (BCWS) information officer Sarah Budd said it recorded about 2,000 lightning strikes in the Coastal Fire Centre, with another 5,000 in the B.C. Interior, mostly in the Kamloops and Cariboo fire centres. Budd said lightning was responsible for at least 48 wildfires in the last 48 hours, though 60 per cent of them were already being held. "In anticipation of this pattern coming through, we had pre-positioned our crews and resources, just allowing for an efficient initial response to any new starts because we knew this was coming," she said. Budd said the storm also brought a "generous amount of precipitation," which helped firefighters — both by dampening fire activity and reducing the likelihood that lightning would start new fires. But she said the rain wasn't enough to offset months of drought, and that new fires could yet pop up from lightning strikes that cause fuel to smoulder for days before flames break out. Thunderstorm watch moves east Environment Canada issued severe thunderstorm watches on Sunday for most of southeast B.C., including the Kootenays, Boundary and East Columbia regions, Arrow Lakes and Yoho Park. The storm system also triggered a high streamflow advisory for the Central Interior, including the Pemberton area and its upstream watersheds, the Chilcotin River, the Bridge River and the Cariboo River. Lightning strikes and loud thunder wowed people in Metro Vancouver on Saturday night, in a region not used to getting widespread thunderstorm activity. (Renée Lukacs/CBC) Environment Canada says the storm dumped significant rainfall across southern B.C., including a whopping 43.4 millimetres at Horseshoe Bay. Forecasters measured 37.4 millimetres at the Coquihalla Summit, 25.4 millimetres in North Cowichan, nearly 23.8 millimetres in Merritt, and 20.6 millimetres in Lillooet. A travel advisory issued for most of the stretch of Highway 99 between Pemberton and Lillooet due to heavy rains near Pemberton also warned that the road could close on short notice.

World.title: Colombia expands disaster region in 2nd emergency decree
World.content:
Colombia’s government drastically expanded the region affected by the August 10 earthquake in a second decree declaring an economic emergency.

According to the decree, President Abelardo de la Espriella declared the emergency in 15 of the country’s 32 provinces “for a period of thirty (30) calendar days, in order to conjure the crisis and prevent the spread of the disaster’s effects.”

“The territorial scope includes all municipalities listed in UNGRD Situational Report No. 36 and any additional municipalities where direct damage from the August 10, 2026 earthquake is specifically demonstrated,” said the decree.

The emergency decree declared a State of Exception, which allows the government to “adopt, through legislative decrees, all additional necessary measures and budgetary/credit operations to address the crisis” in the emergency region.

According to the decree, the government is considering the following extraordinary measures to respond to the disaster that left more than $9.5 billion in damages.

Tax, credit, and budgetary flexibility to direct new resources to disaster recovery.

Expedited public credit operations bypassing lengthy CONPES/DNP approvals.

Use of the Royalty Savings and Stabilization Fund (FAE) resources as repayable loans.

Expanding the “Works for Taxes” (Obras por Impuestos) mechanism to affected municipalities.

Direct management and monetization of seized assets administered by SAE/FRISCO to fund emergency shelters and humanitarian relief.

Authorizing financial cooperatives to temporarily extend credit and savings services to non-members affected by the disaster.

Streamlining judicial operations, education delivery (remote/alternative spaces), school feeding programs (PAE), housing subsidies, telecommunications repairs, and labor support transfers.

Previously, De la Espriella announced a “Miracle Fund,” which would be used to channel donations from the private sector and international partners.

Since then, Colombia’s elite donated COP1.6 trillion ($526 million) of the $30 billion the government believes it needs for reconstruction.

World.title: Colombia’s government publishes “white paper” on corruption by Petro
World.content:
The government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella gave Prosecutor General Luz Adriana Camargo a white paper with more than 80 complaints over alleged corruption by the previous government.

The 135-page “Book of Truth that was presented by De la Espriella, contained “the result of the work carried out under the coordination of Vice President José Manuel Restrepo during the transition weeks between the presidential election and August 7” when he took office.

De la Espriella suspended the transition process on July 7 after Petro said he refused to recognize the president as his legitimate successor.

Consequently, the book contains mainly political criticisms of the previous “regime” and no evidence of misdeeds that hadn’t been picked by the Comptroller General’s Office, which monitors public spending.

This white paper, my fellow Colombians, does not intend to replace, far less anticipate, judicial investigations or the outcome of actions taken by prosecutors, inspectors, and comptrollers. The book actually represents something simpler and, at the same time, more serious, monumental, and decisive: the fulfillment of my duty as Head of State. I am fulfilling the responsibility that falls upon me by gathering available information and not allowing the facts recorded here in the book I have just delivered to be buried by silence and impunity. The duty of a leader is to bring the truth to the doorstep of justice and stop there, scrupulously respecting the independence and majesty of the judicial system. That moment has arrived. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president blamed the budget deficit on the “sacking” of the Petro administration rather than Congress’s failure to approve the legislation that allowed the previous government to carry out its 2026 budget.

De la Espriella previously said he would extradite Petro if the US Government asked him to.

World.title: Colombia says 377 still missing three days after 7.4M earthquake
World.content:
The director of Colombia’s disaster management agency UNGRD said Thursday that at least 273 people died and that 377 were missing from the region that was struck by a 7.4M earthquake on Monday.

According to UNGRD director David Tamayo, the earthquake affected a total of 97,515 people.

So far, rescue workers and neighbors were able to rescue 348 people from the rubble alive and 3,826 people were injured.

The earthquake, which was the strongest in a decade, destroyed 12,563 homes and damaged another 75,654.

At least 172 apartment buildings collapsed, said Tamayo.

Damaged public infrastructure

217 health centers and hospitals

2,206 educational facilities

825 community centers

226 roads

71 aqueducts

24 vehicular bridges

8 pedestrian bridges

5 airports

The disaster triggered President Abelardo de la Espriella to declare an economic emergency in the disaster area, and in the southern Putumayo and the eastern Norte de Santander province where no damages were reported.

This State of Exception allows the president to govern by decree when it comes to matters related to disaster relief and reconstruction in the affected area.

The State of Exception will last three months and can be extended by another three with congressional approval.

World.title: Colombia declares economic emergency to rebuild after earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said he would declare an economic emergency and create a reconstruction fund for homes and small businesses that were destroyed in Monday’s earthquake.

In a press statement, De la Espriella said that the government would initially support victims with temporary relief and will declare an economic emergency to find the funds for reconstruction.

Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said the government was not yet considering raising taxes to find the approximately COP20 trillion ($6.4 billion) that would at least be needed for reconstruction.

The president said his government would initially prioritize relief for the estimated 24,000 families from the west of the country who have lost their homes or businesses.

The temporary relief measures would include:

The payment of public services for affected families by the government.

Housing rent subsidies for those who lost their homes.

Tax and financial relief measures.

Economic support for the most vulnerable families.

Support mechanisms for merchants and small business owners who have been affected by the earthquake.

As part of the emergency, De la Espriella announced the creation of a “Miracle Fund, an entity that will channel national and international contributions destined for the reconstruction of hospitals, educational centers, properties, roads, and airports that suffered damage from the earthquake.”

“The state of emergency must encompass economic reactivation measures that stimulate investment, reduce obstacles to project development, and generate more jobs in the affected areas,” said the president.

An economic emergency gives the president three months to issue decrees related to the cause of the emergency without having to go through Congress.

The legal validity of the decree declaring an emergency and those that follow will only be tested by the Constitutional Court.

At the time of publication the President’s Office had yet to issue its first decree.

World.title: Colombia asked US to carry out joint military operations: Hegseth
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the US Government for joint military operations “to destroy terrorists and terror networks,” said US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Wednesday.

At an event of the so-called Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC) in Panama, Hegseth said that “Colombia will join the ACCC, becoming the 19th member.”

Through the newly inaugurated president, as our president likes to say “President El Tigre,” Colombia has already requested that our department of war join Colombia in its fight against narcoterrorism. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

Hegseth’s announcement was rejected by leftist opposition party Historic Pact, whose Senate chief Ivan Cepeda said that “the US citizen Abelardo de la Espriella wants to surrender our government, our territory and our sovereignty to the strategic interests of the United States.

Cepeda stressed that Colombia’s constitution allows only the Senate to permit the entry of foreign troops to the country.

Colombia’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation, it is not to be surrendered, and it cannot be subordinated to the military interests of any foreign power. To defend it is to defend the dignity of the nation, the independence of the Republic, and the right of the Colombian people to freely decide on their territory and their destiny. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Ahead of taking office on Friday, De la Espriella said that he would join US-led alliances that allegedly seek to combat drug trafficking.

In his inaugural speech, the president said he intends to “defeat, without truce, narco-terrorism and all criminal organizations that threaten the freedom of Colombia.”

The State Department last week announced that it would seek to send a $1 billion military aid package to Colombia to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

World.title: Controversy in Colombia over refusal to allow foreign search and rescue teams
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella has been criticized over its refusal to accept foreign search and rescue workers in the crucial hours after Monday’s earthquake.

One of the first to raise the alarm was China’s ambassador to Bogota, Zhu Jingyang, who called on the government on Tuesday to “release the name of the official and his or her designated contact person to coordinate international aid for the earthquake victims.”

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele said that he was told that Colombia’s “rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency responders are on the scene and handling the situation” and “they do not require personnel support.”

Mexico’s President Caudia Sheinbaum said that her government was waiting for approval to send a team of 225 rescue workers to look for survivors, but was waiting for a “formal invitation” from Bogota.

In a response to growing pressure, newspaper El Tiempo said Colombia didn’t need foreign search and rescue teams because “the country has 23 teams with personnel that is part of the global elite.”

The Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday evening that it had “called on the international community to provide support in addressing the emergency, in order to tackle the most severely affected areas and mitigate the disaster.”

But social leader Leonard Renteria from Buenaventura said Wednesday that “as of yesterday, we still didn’t know anything about the arrival of rescue workers” in the partially destroyed port city.

“On the streets, we’ve seen people from the neighborhoods with the firefighters and civil defense personnel,” Renteria posted on social media platform X.

Fifty hours after Monday’s disaster, the US Department of State said it had “mobilized urban search-and-rescue (USAR) technical teams from Fairfax County, Virginia, and Los Angeles County, California to support Colombia’s search and rescue efforts.”

With chances of finding people alive rapidly decreasing, pressure on the government to respond increased online.

“I would really like to know the technical reason for rejecting assistance from teams that specialize in this type of disaster. There are many affected areas and plenty of evidence of technical inadequacies,” said civil engineer Gina Villalobos on X.

According to opposition congresswoman Maria Fernanda Carrascal, “it was an ideological decision, they only wanted rescue workers from Israel and the United States to enter while the Mexicans have been ready since Monday.”

On Wednesday afternoon, newly appointed disaster response chief David Tamayo said the government would also allow search and rescue workers from Ecuador and El Salvador “that can guarantee the provision of search and rescue teams and that are recognized by their own governments as meeting international search and rescue standards.”

These teams would come to search for hundreds of people who are feared to be under the rubble of buildings that collapsed in the worst earthquake in 10 years.

World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”
