World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018914/What Happens When Chinese Dreamcore Meets the Real World?
World.title: What Happens When Chinese Dreamcore Meets the Real World?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018914/What Happens When Chinese Dreamcore Meets the Real World?
World.content:
What if the zombie apocalypse was already here?

In the late 2010s, Chinese indie band Hardcore Raver in Tears imagined just such a world in “Take Her to Wanda Plaza,” a jagged, synth-heavy sendup of the country’s mindless consumer culture. Over pounding beats, singer Lu Yan sang of zombified shoppers and took aim at Wang Sicong, the scion of the Wanda real estate empire and one of the most infamous of China’s “second-generation rich.”

The joke landed because Wanda Plaza is more than a shopping mall; by the 2010s, it had become shorthand for a particular vision of urban life. In the 2000s, local governments across the country saw real estate and urbanization as key engines of economic growth as well as fiscal revenue. Teaming with developers like Wanda, they built vast new tracts of standardized residential districts across the country. These new neighborhoods needed new stores and restaurants, a niche that Wanda also filled by building over 500 Wanda Plaza malls in more than 200 cities nationwide.

At the time, this was all taken for granted as modernization in action. China was urbanizing at a staggering speed, and clean, convenient, and air-conditioned shopping malls like Wanda Plaza were welcomed by both the country’s rising middle class and brands hungry to tap an emerging market.

But for the generation that came of age during this transformation, the convenience and prosperity of the new urban landscape is increasingly tinged with a sense of sameness. Rapid urban expansion did not just change how Chinese cities looked, they argue; it also displaced what anthropologist Xiang Biao calls the “nearby”: the small-scale places and relationships immediately around us through which everyday life acquires meaning.

That longing has since found an outlet online. From obsessively documenting faded Y2K architecture to creating virtual cities and nostalgic video games, young Chinese are attempting to recreate an idealized virtual version of the turn-of-the-millennium city: chaotic but colorful, and full of corner shops, wet markets, arcades, street stalls, and other places to hang out.

The most obvious example of this trend is Chinese dreamcore, which blends aspects of the global dreamcore subculture with elements drawn from China’s own millennial moment. The walking simulator “There Exists Nobody,” for example, invites players to revisit China’s bustling millennium-era towns, where neighborhoods were filled with unpolished mom-and-pop shops rather than sleek shopping malls.

A more sophisticated case is artist Huang Heshan’s digital metropolis “Too Rich City,” which he dubbed a work of “socialist cyberpunk.” Drawing on Huang’s experiences growing up in the southern province of Guangdong, the virtual city mixes modern LED screens with nostalgic elephant slides and swan-shaped boats — both recurring motifs in Chinese dreamcore.

Similarly, Liu Yujia, a photographer better known by his social media handle, “Tiehe West Street,” has built a large following for his dreamcore-style documentation of China’s long-maligned Y2K architecture.

When asked why his work resonates with so many, Huang commented that China’s millennial buildings — many of which have been allowed to fall into disrepair — nevertheless remain vibrant in ways the newer, more uniform apartment blocks aren’t. They’re “a little chaotic, but also more human,” he explained.

Indeed, a key motive of Chinese dreamcore is a desire for more human-scale spaces. Cookie-cutter blocks of shopping malls, chain stores, and gated residential communities have smoothed the rough edges of many Chinese cities, yet their lack of texture — places with which people can establish organic connections — has also led to widespread disorientation and disillusionment.

It is in this context that the “nearby,” the academic term popularized by Xiang, has entered public discourse in recent years. Rather than accepting the numbing comfort offered by places like Wanda Plaza, China’s younger generation is searching for informal spaces and trying to rebuild tight-knit communities.

Standardized urban planning, alongside an increasingly digital economy, has also reshaped people’s sense of time. In 2000, an ordinary Chinese person might experience time through walking to a grocery store, a school, or a park. Nowadays, such embodied experience has been replaced by the “estimated time of arrival” displayed in food delivery and car-hailing apps. This abstraction has rendered interpersonal relationships likewise abstract and fragile, contributing to the desire to return to a slower, less hectic era.

It’s worth noting that Chinese dreamcore is not the only space where the younger generation is seeking shelter and trying to build a digital “nearby.” The anime and fandom subcultures, for example, offer a similar sense of belonging.

Much of this can be traced back to worldwide trends like the loss of “third places” where young people can hang out away from parents and teachers, forcing them into online spaces increasingly divorced from their physical surroundings and leading to what the scholar Keith Hayward calls a culture of “self-infantilization” — such as the global social media craze for kitsch toys like Labubu.

It’s not hard to see why dreamcore-tinged nostalgia would find such fertile ground in both the West and China, even if one romanticizes malls while the other rejects them. These online trends have limits, however. Loosely organized, they lack the capability to make an impact offline. Meanwhile, some of the very offline spaces dreamcore fans like to criticize have effectively incorporated the subculture, positioning themselves as a new kind of “nearby.” Shopping hubs such as Shanghai’s Bailian mall and Beijing’s Wangfujing street now host regular events for anime fans, while Changsha’s Wenheyou has redecorated its commercial complexes to look like vintage markets and evoke feelings of “old Changsha.”

Ultimately, Y2K nostalgia is not immune to the consumerism it seeks to reject. With mounting financial pressure for commercial real estate developers, the Wanda Plaza model may have passed its heyday. Yet the urban landscape it has imposed upon us seems likely to last. They may complain about monotonous “new districts” and their lack of organic street life, but young Chinese continue to find the convenience that modern cities offer irresistible. Chinese dreamcore provides a temporary relief — sooner or later, though, we’re snapped awake by the buzz of our phones.

(Header image: 500px/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018906/China’s Post-Gaokao Teens Are Spending Big Before College
World.title: China’s Post-Gaokao Teens Are Spending Big Before College
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018906/China’s Post-Gaokao Teens Are Spending Big Before College
World.content:
When Wang Yijun walked out of the gaokao examination room on June 8, she immediately started thinking about what she’d do that summer. After three years of putting aside her hobbies and personal interests to study for China’s national college entrance exam, the 18-year-old from the eastern city of Wuxi finally had a summer of her own.

But the summer’s freedom came with a price tag. After the exam, Wang’s parents bought her a laptop costing over 10,000 yuan ($1,400), both as a reward for her years of effort and a tool for her future studies. She also traveled to Beijing and its neighboring city Tianjin, dined out with friends, and enrolled in an audio mixing course.

“I’ve spent around 20,000 yuan in total since the exam,” she told Sixth Tone in August.

Wang’s experience reflects a broader shift taking place across China. This summer — from the end of the exam to early September — students fresh out of the gaokao are splurging on electronics, graduation trips, and new hobbies before they have to buckle down at university.

For many, the spending can reach upwards of 40,000 yuan. For comparison, China’s per capita disposable income last year was 43,377 yuan.

This year, approximately 12.9 million students sat for the gaokao. A report jointly released by XKB Data Research Center and iiMedia Research estimated that incoming first-year students would spend an average of 18,600 yuan this summer, more than double compared with 2020. Spending by family members, such as on accompanying students on trips and celebratory meals, also ranged from 30,000 to 40,000 yuan. Together, the sector — termed the “post-gaokao economy” — is expected to surpass 387 billion yuan this year.

Merchants are moving quickly to seize the opportunity. Electronics sellers have launched promotions that give students special discounts when they present their gaokao admission tickets, while 327 top-rated scenic attractions across the country have rolled out concessions targeting the group. Cosmetic surgery clinics introduced student packages priced below 1,000 yuan, along with interest-free installment plans for customers who show their exam credentials.

But although the trend has provided a much-welcomed boost to the domestic economy, it has also sparked a growing generational debate over where celebration ends and excessive consumption begins. Posts by other young Chinese showing off their purchases, and sometimes sharing tricks to get their parents to buy things for them after the gaokao, soon began to spread online. And parents, facing financial pressure from their 18-year-olds, have now taken their complaints online.

A new coming-of-age ritual

The debate has fueled a popular online meme: “After all, you only finished the gaokao — you didn’t suddenly become rich,” capturing parental concerns over the post-exam consumption fever.

A screenshot of a mother’s chat messages reacting to her daughter’s post-exam shopping list — with items totaling more than 30,000 yuan — has also made the rounds on social media. In it, she says to her child, “How about you be my mom?”

For Chinese students, the summer after the gaokao carries a special significance. Longer than other school-time summers, it is widely considered the last extended break before adulthood brings a new set of pressures — from grad school applications and civil service exams to career choices.

“That makes it feel like a milestone worth celebrating,” Wang said.

On the last day of the gaokao, images of parents waiting outside examination halls with gifts for their children routinely flood domestic short-video platforms.

In one widely circulated video this year, students walked out of an exam room to find their parents holding stacks of laptops, smartphones, tablets, smartwatches, and earphones, jokingly referred to as quanjiatong, or a “bucket meal,” a reference to KFC’s all-in-one spread. Many such gift packages feature high-end brands such as Apple, with a full set costing north of 30,000 yuan.

Wang said her social media feed is now filled with posts by peers sharing graduation trips, unboxing new devices, and making plans to transform themselves during the break.

Seeing others mark the transition with new phones, designer products, and overseas travel, she added, has left many her age who have taken the gaokao but haven’t received or purchased such gifts feeling as though they are falling behind.

Coming from a working-class family, Wang said she tries to balance enjoyment with practicality. For instance, she decided to continue using her old phone because it still worked well.

“Families inevitably differ widely in their financial circumstances, and that’s a reality we cannot avoid,” she said. “If there is something we want, working for it ourselves is a sign of maturity.”

Before the gaokao, Wang added, grades provide a clear standard of achievement. “But once you walk out of that exam room, you’re suddenly surrounded by a world where people are judged by their material possessions. You start to believe that spending, having the latest gadgets, and traveling can fill the ‘void’ that comes with a major shift in identity.”

But, she added, “We’re not just ‘consumers.’ We can create, contribute, and slowly grow as people, which defines us far more than what we own.”

Greater costs

Qiu Jiqing, a professor of women’s studies and family relations at Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s Lifelong Education College, told Sixth Tone that when she took the gaokao in 1996, her experience was vastly different.

“My parents didn’t buy me any special gifts,” she said. “They simply prepared the necessities I would need for college. When I left for university, I basically took only my bedding and daily essentials with me.”

Qiu said she believes that spending within a family’s means after their child takes the gaokao is justified, especially in an era where electronic devices have become an essential part of education. However, she cautioned that social media and marketing campaigns could overly boost spending and desire for material goods among young people who are still developing their understanding of how and when to save and spend money.

“Learning to distinguish between what we truly need and what we simply want is part of growing up,” she said.

Regardless of whether or not they partake in gaokao celebratory splurging, for many families, the end of the exam marks the beginning of a new stage of spending.

Zhang Chunxing, a mother from the eastern Shandong province whose son took the gaokao this June, has already started calculating the costs of her son’s higher education.

She said that her son’s living costs will amount to around 18,000 yuan a year and tuition will add another 6,000 yuan annually. Transportation, accommodation, and other daily expenses will require additional investment.

“After the gaokao, many children want new phones, trips or other rewards,” she said. “But parents also have to think about the next four years.”

For Zhang, preparing for university is not only about covering costs, but also about teaching her son — who will be leaving home for the first time — how to manage his own expenses.

Qiu, the professor from Jiao Tong University, said that because students spend all their time and energy studying before the gaokao, other skills such as financial literacy, self-management, and independent living are often lacking.

She added that the transition is a challenge for the entire family, as most families are used to a dynamic where parents decide and children follow. After the gaokao, both must learn a new way of relating to each other.

“Students need to learn independence and parents also need to adjust to start seeing their children as individuals who can make their own decisions,” she said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A teenager (right) receives a Nintendo Switch 2 from his older sister outside an exam site after the gaokao in Hefei, Anhui province, June 9, 2026. Han Suyuan/CNS/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018913/After Nolan Interview Fame, Chinese Scholar Accused of Plagiarism
World.title: After Nolan Interview Fame, Chinese Scholar Accused of Plagiarism
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018913/After Nolan Interview Fame, Chinese Scholar Accused of Plagiarism
World.content:
Chinese social media influencer Zhuge Yiyang, also known by her online alias Zhong Shu, has been accused of plagiarizing content across multiple podcast episodes and a Chinese article.

The allegations, which emerged last weekend on domestic social media, come just two weeks after she went viral for an interview with British-American director Christopher Nolan about his recent blockbuster “The Odyssey.”

The 29-year-old from eastern China’s Zhejiang province is currently a Ph.D. candidate in political philosophy at Boston College in the U.S. She also hosts the Chinese podcast “Monologues of a Committed Observer,” which has over 970,000 subscribers on domestic podcast platform Xiaoyuzhou.

Her July 31 interview with Nolan in Beijing was viewed over 18 million times in an X post by video game journalist Geoff Keighley, the son of Nolan’s friend David Keighley.

Subsequent overseas media coverage of the interview — praised for Zhuge’s deeper philosophical questioning — brought her wider recognition on the Chinese internet, where many admired her prolific output, including podcast episodes released roughly every three days alongside her academic, translation, and writing work.

But that acclaim has been overshadowed by recent allegations that Zhuge used translated material from overseas podcasts, books, and magazines without attribution.

Among the allegations, her 310th podcast episode, released in March discussing Iran’s Islamic regime, was accused of plagiarizing an episode of the English-language podcast “Breaking History” released last August.

In the original episode, a guest mentions the establishment of both a health and literacy “corps,” which an AI-generated transcript on Apple Podcasts incorrectly renders as “court.” In her podcast, Zhuge similarly refers to them as “courts” in Chinese.

Social media users also pointed out that, beyond the use of “court,” the surrounding passages also closely overlap with the original podcast in both content and phrasing.

Users also accused Zhuge of plagiarizing a May article in The Atlantic on university students’ use of AI in a similar column she wrote in August for Chinese business news outlet Caixin.

Among the similarities, the first paragraphs of both articles cite the same line from Princeton University’s student newspaper. Zhuge’s second paragraph also describes the university’s honor code as having “lasted through two world wars, the upheaval of the 1960s, the disillusionment of Watergate, and even the rise of search engines” — a line from the third paragraph of the Atlantic article.

In an interview with domestic media outlet Southern Metropolis Daily published on Monday, Zhuge responded to the allegations only by saying, “We live in an age that demands apologies from greatness,” a line she had used in her interview with Nolan. She did not elaborate on how the remark related to the allegations.

In her 364th podcast episode, released the same day, Zhuge said that when she first began podcasting, her life in the U.S. was “a mess” while people in China had been “quite friendly.”

“Now the situation has completely reversed,” she said without elaborating.

Zhuge also said in the episode that she had plans to appear on “a whole bunch of podcasts by Western intellectuals.” She added that American intellectuals also routinely face intense criticism online, citing American political scientist Francis Fukuyama as an example.

The same day, three August book talks Zhuge was scheduled to attend in Shanghai and the central Hubei and Hunan provinces to promote her recent translations of works by German-American philosopher Hannah Arendt were also canceled, with the organizer citing “changes to (Zhuge’s) personal schedule.”

Sixth Tone contacted Zhuge multiple times for comment on the controversy through her publicly listed personal email address, but received no response.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG and Bilibili, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018905/Cash Cow: China’s Most Mocked Cartoon Is Suddenly a Viral Hit
World.title: Cash Cow: China’s Most Mocked Cartoon Is Suddenly a Viral Hit
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018905/Cash Cow: China’s Most Mocked Cartoon Is Suddenly a Viral Hit
World.content:
Poorly animated yellow cows walking on two legs, raw voice acting, and extremely slow pace — these are characteristics of China’s most recent box office hit and viral phenomenon.

Released Aug. 5 after virtually no promotion, the movie, “Niu Lai,” or “Cow Comes,” is named for its titular character: a calf who struggles to stand. The film follows Niu Lai and his herd as they overcome a number of difficulties while migrating, eventually growing up into an able-bodied adult cow unfazed in the face of danger. Except, Niu Lai awakens, realizing that he is still a calf — but he is finally able to support his own weight.

The movie, reported to have no financial backing, earned just 5,500 yuan ($815) at the box office in its first week. But after multiple viewers posted images of the film on social media criticizing it, that number suddenly surged to over 710,000 yuan on Aug. 15, according to ticketing platform Maoyan. As of Tuesday afternoon, it has taken in 20 million yuan, a figure projected to grow to 135 million yuan by the time it leaves screens.

The reason for its explosive popularity? Its absurdist visuals and overall crude production design have turned it into a word-of-mouth viral phenomenon. The characters’ legs rarely move in sync, making them appear like they’re sliding. Close-ups of their heads are overblown and blurry. Transitions between scenes are jarring and illogical, and the characters’ voices are poorly recorded and overly stilted.

The effect has led to highly polarized ratings on domestic review platform Douban, with many giving it either one or five stars. As one highly upvoted comment on Maoyan reads, “You don’t have to watch bad movies, but when a movie is bad enough, you have to.”

Wang Yunfei, the founder of a cartoon studio and an acting animated film judge at various film festivals, told Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper, “Professional animators couldn’t produce something this poorly even if they made mistakes. So from a professional standpoint, there’s really nothing to critique. It’s just spectacle-watching.”

The movie’s unexpectedly raw, homemade production has also been regarded by critics and viewers alike as a rebuke to high-investment but poorly reviewed films.

“Niu Lai” was produced by Jingyuan Culture Film and Television Media, based in the northeastern city of Dalian, which was converted from a one-person renovation company, according to corporate data platform Qichacha.

The renovator in question is the film’s creator, 34-year-old Xin Yumeng, who made it alongside his mother, Sun Lifang. The pair reportedly had no background in animation and made the film over five years, without the help of AI. They also provided the voices for the characters, while Sun composed and sang the film’s theme song.

On a domestic radio show, Xin said that he made the film out of a love for animated films, and chose a cow as the protagonist because his father was born in the Year of the Ox.

As for the quality of the film, Xin added that much of the equipment he bought secondhand for the film’s production eventually broke down. “Even the computer motherboards burned out ... The final result has a lot to do with the equipment used.”

Le Fumin, a 35-year-old security worker from Shanghai, told domestic media that he liked that “Niu Lai” was made by two ordinary people, rather than having large film-industry backing. “It shows a bit of rebellion against the assembly-line formula of mainstream filmmaking,” he said. “Why should I only be allowed to watch what the industry feeds me? The kind of happiness I choose for myself is worth the ticket price, too.”

Le said the atmosphere in the theater was particularly relaxed. “Over the course of two hours, the pressure of meeting KPIs at work, the exhaustion of commuting, and all the troubles of everyday life just melted away with the laughter of the whole theater,” he said. “It felt like returning to something simple and genuine — like the carefree feeling of watching random films in a video rental shop as a kid.”

As “Niu Lai” has risen in popularity, fan-made tributes to it have spread online and offline, with some placing Niu Lai into posters for recent international box office hits such as “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “The Odyssey.” Cinema staff have also put up rudimentary, hand-drawn posters advertising the film — and paying homage to its crude animation — outside theaters.

Even stocks of three companies with “niu” in their names — Jinniu Chemical Industry, Goneo Group, and Tongniu Information — shot into the top five trending list on domestic finance data platform Tonghuashun over the weekend, as the film’s title can be interpreted as “the bull market is coming,” domestic media reported.

Other entities are also capitalizing on the film’s virality, creating their own animal-based animated shorts to promote products. On Monday, local authorities for Dongguan City in the southern Guangdong province produced a video titled “E Lai,” or “Goose Comes,” to promote the city’s local specialty — roast goose — garnering more than 26,000 likes on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok.

For most, however, the movie is simply about having fun. Mak SzeNing, a 27-year-old pet care worker from Hong Kong, watched the film in the eastern city of Hangzhou at a nearly sold-out screening. “I don’t think the movie’s value lies in its production quality,” she told Sixth Tone. “Its value is that it brings a group of strangers into the same theater, and suddenly everyone feels like they’ve found their kindred spirits and laughs together.”

“If a movie can make people laugh, then I think it’s a good movie,” she said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A still from “Niu Lai.” From Douban)

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

World.title: Tens of thousands evacuate in Nevada as fire threatens Reno
World.content:
FIRE. Smoke and flames rise from the Hawk fire in Reno, Nevada, USA, August 22, 2026, in this screengrab from a video obtained from social media.

The fire burns over 5,261 hectares and is currently under investigation for being human-caused, with several injuries reported among civilians and first responders

NEW YORK, USA – Tens of thousands of people have been evacuated this weekend from the area of Reno, Nevada, and many others were under orders to leave on Sunday, August 23, as a wildfire reached the outskirts of the state’s third-most-populous city.

About 42,000 residents have been displaced or are in active evacuations with an additional 45,000 in “be prepared to evacuate” status as the Hawk Fire threatened northern Reno, local officials said late Sunday morning.

Local TV footage showed flames approaching roads. In eyewitness video verified by Reuters, smoke from the hills billowed over nearby residential neighborhoods.

Fire-tracking websites showed evacuation zones extending from the Sierra Nevada hills to the University of Nevada in northwest Reno.

The fire has burned 5,261 hectares so far, officials said at a press conference on Sunday. The fire was human-caused and remains under investigation, they said.

Three civilians and three first responders have been injured, said Shane Akerson, a commander leading fire and rescue operations.

Officials first received reports of a fire off Hawk Meadow Trail at about 11:15 am PDT (1815 GMT) on Saturday, August 22, said Richard Edwards, chief of Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District. Firefighters on Saturday worked amid “extreme red flag conditions,” he said.

Red flag conditions are a combination of warm temperatures, very low humidity and strong winds that raise the risk of wildfires.

“We expect those same strong conditions to come back this afternoon,” Edwards said on Sunday.

Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency late Saturday in Washoe County, which includes Reno and parts of Lake Tahoe.

“This is an active and rapidly evolving situation, and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials,” Lombardo said in a statement.

Lombardo authorized the deployment of two National Guard helicopters to help fight fires and 60 National Guard personnel to support operations with the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office, officials said.

The Reno-Tahoe International Airport remained outside the evacuation area, and commercial flights were operating normally on Sunday. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kieffer Alas stars as Ateneo storms back to beat Benilde
World.content:
STAR. Kieffer Alas in action for the Ateneo Blue Eagles in the 2026 Pinoyliga Cup.

Kieffer Alas leads all scorers as the Ateneo Blue Eagles erase a 13-point deficit against the St. Benilde Blazers to advance to the Elite Eight of the Pinoyliga Cup

MANILA, Philippines – Kieffer Alas delivered the big hits and lifted Ateneo to a come-from-behind 81-78 win over St. Benilde in the Sweet 16 of the Pinoyliga Cup at the Blue Eagle Gym on Sunday, August 23.

Alas finished with 26 points, 3 rebounds, and 3 assists as the Blue Eagles stormed back from 13 points down to advance to the Elite Eight.

The Blazers led 48-35 before Ateneo rode on a 21-7 run bridging the second and third quarters to seize the upper hand, with Alas scoring 9 points during that stretch.

Alas capped that rally with a three-pointer to give the Blue Eagles a 56-55 lead.

It was also Alas who secured the victory for Ateneo as he sank the layup that determined the final score with 1.2 seconds left, leaving Benilde insufficient time for a counter attack.

Down 78-79, the Blazers still had a crack at the win, but Jhomel Ancheta coughed up a costly turnover, with Jared Bahay picking up the ball and dishing off the assist to Alas for the win-sealing bucket.

Travis Roberts also shone for the Blue Eagles with 16 points, while Bahay supplied 8 points, 6 assists, and 5 rebounds.

Matthew Jucom and John Mowell Morales paced Benilde with 19 and 17 points, respectively.

The Blue Eagles will face the winner between the Adamson Soaring Falcons and the Mapua Cardinals in the Elite Eight. – Rappler.com

World.title: For poet-singer Toni Panagu, art begins as ideas you gamble on
World.content:
Panagu often finds himself contending with a blank page to write his next poem or next song, and it's his sheer curiosity that allows him to keep things moving

Multi-disciplinary creative Toni Panagu approaches art with a trusty guitar and a way with words that translates beautifully in rhythm and rhyme.

Poetry had been in Panagu’s life for as long as he could remember. In school, whenever the lectures were starting to get boring, he would busy himself with writing poems at the back of his notebook instead of drifting off to sleep. For a time, these lines would never really escape these bound sheets of paper, until a friend suggested that he start posting them on Facebook.

Eventually, he would join an organization, Linangan sa Imahen, Retorik, at Anyo (LIRA), where he would learn the conventions of traditional poetry. Soon after, he would start pursuing his craft on his own terms, and before long, would start writing his own lyrics, too.

“’Yung tatay ko, binilhan ako ng murang gitara sa Surplus (My father bought me a cheap guitar from Surplus),” he said as he pointed out his father seated a few rows away from us in the auditorium where he had just finished performing.

With his own guitar and a pirated CD of The Beatles’ greatest hits, Panagu would then teach himself how to play these songs strum by strum, and chord by chord.

“[May] gitara tapos ang dami kong mga words. Pinagsama ko na. Ginawa ko nang kanta ‘yung tula,” he shared.

(I had a guitar and a lot of words to say. I just put them together. I turned my poems into songs.)

While all this was happening, though, Panagu shared he didn’t know how to sing yet. “I’m serious!” he said in Filipino when I told him I found that hard to believe.

Panagu would cringe at the sound of his own voice before he finally found the confidence to start releasing his original music in 2022. But he attests that the cringe was absolutely necessary for him to test the bounds of his vocals — and define his own sonic profile as we know it today.

But it’s Panagu’s range as a songwriter that’s most fascinating. The one thing that drives it all? Curiosity.

Curiosity fuels the artist

Inspiration is everywhere if you just know how to look. For Panagu, much of it comes from other mediums of art — in the films he watches, the music he listens to, and the paintings he comes across. He is a firm believer in the literary concept of ekphrasis, where an artist is compelled to produce their own art in response to an already existing piece of art. He had once even written a poem inspired by Clairo’s song “Juna” from her 2024 record Charm.

But it’s the human condition that often shapes the music Panagu makes. He has a whole catalogue of love songs on Spotify, but also has several political anthems under his belt.

“Ideas come to me as often as I wake up,” Panagu said when asked how his best ideas come to him. “Hindi naman lahat ng idea nagiging art pero araw-araw may naiisip tayo. So kailangan lang natin isugal ‘yung idea na ‘yun para maging art siya.”

(Not all ideas become art but we think of things every day. We just need to gamble on that idea to turn it into art.)

What may be Panagu’s most noteworthy piece of work yet, however, is the song he performed at the 2026 FILSCAP Songwriters’ Night Select.

When it came time for the poet-singer to finally do his big number, he had almost immediately strode around from one part of the stage to the next as he sang a fast-paced track about attachment issues and the ills of modern dating. It’s upbeat, and its lyrics come to you faster than you can realize that he’s basically trying to say that sometimes, you’re not actually in love. You’re just attached.

Play Video

The song is entitled “Breadcrumbs,” and it plays around with the buzzwords “love bomb” and “trauma dump” to get the point across. Panagu had finished his big number by fake collapsing on the wooden stage as the lights dimmed — earning loud cheers and several standing ovations from the audience.

Yet the process for creating “Breadcrumbs” wasn’t as glamorous as you might think. We often picture the conception of art as this sacred ritual where the singer has to shut themselves into a quiet room to harness the crucial details that will make up the whole song. While it may be true for some artists, things happened a little differently for Panagu.

“Akala natin na sobrang entertaining process ‘yung paggawa pero minsan boring lang siya na nakaupo ka, may gitara ka, tapos talagang kukutkutin mo lang. Bagay ba tong salita na ‘to? Bagay ba ‘tong chord na ‘to? Uupuan mo talaga siya. Minsan kapag hindi mo pa madugtungan, hayaan mo muna. Medyo ganun ‘yung nangyari sa akin sa ‘Breadcrumbs,’” Panagu shared.

(We think creation is such an entertaining process but sometimes it’s boring. You’re just seated, you have a guitar, and you’re there to pick the song apart. Does this word fit? Does this chord fit? You really have to sit on it. Sometimes when you can’t complete the song, you just have to let it be. That’s kind of what happened to me with “Breadcrumbs.”)

The initial puzzle pieces of “Breadcrumbs” emerged while Panagu was in line to pay off the next installment for his motorcycle. He was able to finish the first part of the chorus right then and there, but these waves of creativity can sometimes go as quickly as they come.

It had taken him another week to complete the first verse, and two weeks later, he had the second verse. A little bit later, he thought of adding the bridge, too. All it took was a little patience for everything to slowly come together — until it finally reached the FILSCAP stage.

Blank pages

Panagu is an artist through and through. Nobody is in tune with his own craft more than he is, and it allows him to create a distinction between the many forms of art he puts out into the world.

But they all start the same way. Whether you’re writing poetry or songs, it’s always the blank page you have to contend with first.

“Kapag nagsusulat ka, iba ‘yung approach mo sa language. Kasi ‘pag poetry, oo syempre, hahabulin mo ‘yung cadence, hahabulin mo ‘yung rhymes. Depende rin anong form ng poetry. Pero somehow ‘yung songs, may element siya ng pitch. So kailangan mong mag-assign ng mga nota doon sa mga salita. Ibang klaseng pag-iisip di siya.” he explained.

(When you write, you have a different approach to language. Because when it comes to poetry, of course, you’re after the cadence and rhymes. It depends on the form of poetry, too. But somehow, with songs, there’s an element of pitch. So you need to assign specific notes to specific words. It requires a different kind of thinking.)

Panagu’s almost relentless urge to keep creating has brought him to the right set of readers and the right set of listeners, and he couldn’t be happier.

Even then, he remains as grounded as ever. He’s made it clear that he doesn’t do what he does for public approval. Art requires a different kind of motivation to keep doing, and for Panagu, it’s life in general that sustains his craft.

For as long as he lives, then, Panagu will continue to create. – Rappler.com

World.title: Saudel may enter PAR as super typhoon on August 24
World.content:
FORECAST. PAGASA Weather Specialist Charmagne Varilla explains the bureau's 4 pm forecast for the three tropical cyclones outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility on August 23, 2026.

Typhoon Saudel is located 1,950 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon at 3 pm on Sunday, August 23, still outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility

MANILA, Philippines – The tropical cyclone with the international name Saudel could enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) as a super typhoon on Monday, August 24.

As of Sunday afternoon, August 23, Saudel remains a typhoon outside PAR. It was located 1,950 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon at 3 pm, moving northwest at a relatively fast 30 kilometers per hour (km/h).

So far, Saudel has maximum sustained winds of 165 km/h and gustiness of up to 205 km/h. But it could strengthen into a super typhoon before its possible entry into the northeastern corner of PAR, which may happen either Monday morning or afternoon.

Saudel is likely to remain far from Philippine landmass, and may already exit PAR on Tuesday, August 25. But PAGASA added that the tropical cyclone might stay inside PAR beyond Tuesday — just along the northern boundary — if its track shifts westward. It could also be downgraded back to a typhoon around this time.

Although Saudel is not expected to directly affect weather and sea conditions in the country, it is seen to eventually enhance the southwest monsoon or habagat, which has been weak since Thursday, August 20, but is still affecting Luzon.

Due to the southwest monsoon, PAGASA warned of moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters) in the country’s northernmost province of Batanes from Sunday afternoon to Monday afternoon.

On Sunday evening, the southwest monsoon is also bringing scattered rain and thunderstorms to the rest of Cagayan Valley, Metro Manila, the Ilocos Region, the Cordillera Administrative Region, Central Luzon, Rizal, Cavite, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro, as well as isolated rain showers or thunderstorms to the rest of Luzon.

PAGASA Weather Specialist Charmagne Varilla said the expected enhancement of the southwest monsoon may trigger significant rainfall starting Wednesday, August 26.

Meanwhile, Saudel’s local name would depend on the movement of another tropical cyclone — the tropical depression right outside the PAR eastern boundary.

This tropical depression was last spotted 1,265 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon at 3 pm on Sunday. It is currently moving east northeast or away from PAR at 15 km/h, but if it ends up heading toward PAR, it could enter before Saudel.

The next tropical cyclone that enters PAR would be given the local name Obet. After Obet, the next name on PAGASA’s list is Pilandok.

At the moment, the tropical depression has maximum sustained winds of 55 km/h and gustiness of up to 70 km/h.

There is also another tropical depression with the same maximum sustained winds and gustiness outside PAR — the former Neneng, which had weakened into a low pressure area last Thursday, then redeveloped into a tropical depression on Saturday, August 22.

Neneng, which was given the international name Gaenari, was located 520 kilometers north of Itbayat, Batanes, as of 3 pm on Sunday. It is moving southwest toward China at 25 km/h, and still has no impact on the Philippines.

Even when Neneng was inside PAR, it did not directly affect the country and only enhanced the southwest monsoon for a couple of days.

PAGASA previously estimated that up to four tropical cyclones may develop within or enter PAR in August. So far, there have been three during the month: Tropical Depression Luis, Tropical Storm Maymay (Kujira), and Neneng. – Rappler.com

World.title: Exit Polls Put Adilet Party Near 72% in Kazakhstan’s First Kurultai Election
World.content:
ASTANA – The Adilet party was projected to receive around 72% of the vote in Kazakhstan’s inaugural election to the Kurultai on Aug. 23, according to three exit polls released at midnight on Aug. 24. Exit polls, which were announced during a live election night broadcast, also showed four other parties narrowly clearing the threshold for representation in the country’s new unicameral Parliament.

The seven parties contesting the election were Adilet, Respublica, the Auyl People’s Democratic Patriotic Party, the People’s Party of Kazakhstan, the Aq Jol Democratic Party, the Baytaq Green Party and the Nationwide Social Democratic Party.

The three surveys put Adilet’s support between 70.7% and 72.3%, positioning the party for a commanding majority in the new 145-member unicameral Parliament. The figures are preliminary and do not constitute official election results.

According to the Institute of Public Policy, Adilet is expected to get 72.3% of the vote, followed by the Auyl party with 6.2%, Respublica with 5.2%, the Aq Jol Democratic Party with 5.1% and the Nationwide Social Democratic Party (NSDP) with 5%.

The People’s Party of Kazakhstan received 2.8%, while the Baytaq Green Party received 0.9%. Another 2.5% of respondents selected the “against all” option.

A separate exit poll by the Institute of Eurasian Integration put Adilet at 71.8%, Auyl at 6.4%, Respublica at 5.4%, NSDP at 5.2% and Aq Jol at 5.1%. The People’s Party received 3%, Baytaq 1% and “against all” 2.1%.

The Institute for Comprehensive Social Research-Astana, known as SOCIS-A, projected 70.7% for Adilet, 6.4% for Auyl, 5.5% for Respublica, 5.4% for Aq Jol and 5% for NSDP. It put the People’s Party at 3.2%, Baytaq at 1.2% and “against all” at 2.6%.

All three exit polls suggested that five of the seven competing parties had reached the 5% electoral threshold. The People’s Party and Baytaq remained below the threshold in all three polls.

The Central Election Commission (CEC) is expected to announce preliminary results after ballots have been counted. Exit polls survey voters after they leave polling stations and serve only as an early indication of the outcome.

Preliminary CEC figures showed voter turnout at 74.19% when polling stations across Kazakhstan closed at 8 p.m. Sunday. More than 12.6 million citizens were registered to vote at more than 10,000 polling stations nationwide and abroad. The final overseas voting process will conclude at the polling station at Kazakhstan’s Consulate General in San Francisco at 8 a.m. Astana time on Aug. 24.

Sunday’s vote was the first parliamentary election held under the new constitutional system. The election determines the composition of the 145-member Kurultai, which replaced Kazakhstan’s former bicameral Parliament under the new Constitution that took effect July 1. All seats are allocated proportionally through party lists in a single nationwide constituency. Parties must receive at least 5% of the vote to qualify for seats. A total of 545 candidates representing seven political parties contested the election.

Overall, 777 foreign observers from 42 countries and 13 international organizations have been accredited to monitor Kazakhstan’s election.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s First Kurultai Election Concludes With Preliminary Voter Turnout at 74.19%
World.content:
ASTANA – Voting in Kazakhstan’s first elections to the Kurultai concluded at all polling stations across the country at 8 p.m. on Aug. 23, with 9,352,151 voters, or 74.19% of those registered, having received ballots, according to preliminary voter turnout data from the Central Election Commission (CEC).

Polling stations have now closed nationwide, and precinct election commissions have begun counting the ballots. Under Kazakhstan’s election legislation, the vote-counting process may not exceed 12 hours from the start of counting. Territorial election commissions will transmit preliminary voting and counting results to the CEC through electronic channels.

The highest turnout was recorded in the Turkistan Region at 92.16%, followed by the Zhetisu Region at 91.19% and the Kyzylorda Region at 90.75%. Turnout in the Aktobe Region reached 88.30%, while the East Kazakhstan Region recorded 87.50% and the Zhambyl Region 85.18%.

Turnout stood at 82.69% in the Akmola Region, 81.41% in the Abai Region, 77.31% in the North Kazakhstan Region, 76.47% in the Kostanai Region and 76.28% in the Karagandy Region.

Among the cities of national significance, Shymkent recorded 75.42% turnout, Astana 51.67% and Almaty 43.23%.

Other regional figures included 73.38% in West Kazakhstan, 71.38% in the Mangystau Region, 71.20% in the Pavlodar Region, 71.17% in the Almaty Region, 70.74% in the Atyrau Region and 70.72% in the Ulytau Region.

Voting continues at overseas polling stations

Voting abroad is continuing in accordance with local time zones. As of 7 p.m. Astana time, all 79 polling stations established at Kazakhstan’s diplomatic missions and consular offices in 61 countries had opened. Voting had concluded in 11 countries, with 6,007 of the 11,402 registered voters abroad having cast their ballots.

Polling stations in Washington, New York, San Francisco, Ottawa and Brasilia continued operating as of the latest update. Seventy-four overseas polling stations were expected to complete voting by midnight Astana time.

The final overseas voting process will conclude at the polling station at Kazakhstan’s Consulate General in San Francisco at 8 a.m. Astana time on Aug. 24.

Protocols from overseas precinct election commissions will be transmitted to the CEC for inclusion in the overall election results.

Observers assess new parliamentary system

International observers said the election represents more than a change in the structure of Kazakhstan’s legislature. They noted that the new political system, established under the Constitution adopted in 2026, will ultimately be assessed by its ability to strengthen accountability, ensure institutional stability and create a predictable environment for citizens and investors.

The election marks the first vote for Kazakhstan’s new unicameral Kurultai, which will comprise 145 deputies elected through proportional representation in a single nationwide constituency.

The CEC will announce preliminary election results at a dedicated briefing, with the time to be communicated separately.

World.title: Observers See Unicameral Parliament as Boost for Stability and Investment
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s transition to a unicameral parliament and the implementation of its new constitutional framework were among the key issues raised by foreign observers during the parliamentary vote taking place on Aug. 23. The country’s prospects for attracting international investment were also a major focus of their discussions.

For international observers, the election to Kurultai, a new unicameral parliament, established under the Constitution adopted in 2026, represents more than a change in the structure of Kazakhstan’s legislature. They said the new political system will ultimately be judged by its ability to strengthen accountability, ensure institutional stability and create a predictable environment for citizens and investors.

Indonesian Ambassador to Kazakhstan Rachman Mohamad Fadjroel said the country’s Constitution provides the foundation for its ongoing political reforms.

“I believe the most important point in Kazakhstan is its Constitution, because this is the vision for the future of the country. Article 1 defines Kazakhstan as a democratic, secular, social and law-based state,” Fadjroel told The Astana Times.

He said the reforms underway are guided by these constitutional principles and demonstrate Kazakhstan’s commitment to democratic development.

“Today’s Kurultai election is an opportunity to demonstrate how democracy works in Kazakhstan in practice,” he said, adding that the country’s election has sent a positive message to the international community.

Unicameral parliament as a new political chapter

Domenico Palmieri, secretary general of the Italian Institute of Asia, described the election as a milestone for Kazakhstan, calling it the first major step in implementing the country’s new constitutional framework.

In an interview with The Astana Times, he said the transition to a unicameral parliament could streamline the legislative process and facilitate political reforms.

“From my point of view, a unicameral system is better. It is easier to work smartly and efficiently,” Palmieri said, adding that its effectiveness will ultimately depend on the performance of the new parliament and government.

“Only the future, starting from today, with the new parliament and government, can show whether this was the right decision taken by the Kazakh people,” he said.

He also noted that five Italian parliamentarians were observing the election in the Almaty Region.

“This shows the interest and attention of Italy toward the Kazakh nation,” Palmieri said.

He added that the new constitutional arrangements should now be translated into practical policies that contribute to social stability and economic development.

Clearer institutions could support investment

Nicolas Butylin, head of geopolitics at Berliner Zeitung, Germany’s daily newspaper, spoke about the implications of the new political system for foreign investors. He said a streamlined institutional structure could make it easier to understand where decisions are made and how checks and balances operate.

He described the Kurultai as another step in the country’s institutional development, stressing that the country should be assessed against its own progress rather than measured solely against Western democracies.

“I would not compare Kazakhstan to Western European democracies. I don’t think this is the benchmark. The more useful question, from my perspective, is to compare Kazakhstan with the state of Kazakhstan 10 years ago. To see if, with the new Kurultai, the system is more open, more accountable and more competitive,” Butylin said.

He noted that for Western businesses considering investment in Kazakhstan, institutional evolution and predictability would remain key factors.

Butylin also emphasized Kazakhstan’s growing importance to Germany and Europe through the Middle Corridor, particularly amid disruptions to established trade routes.

“From this perspective, especially in the economic part with natural resources, Kazakhstan will play a crucial role for the future of Germany as well,” he said.

Glenn Agung Hole, professor at the University of Southeast Norway and an expert in economics and international relations, noted that the parliament’s ability to provide legislative stability would be critical for business.

“From an economic perspective, the new Kurultai is important because they need to make stable laws. And business, finance and the stock exchange need to see that taxes and laws are followed through,” Hole said.

He emphasized that international investors need confidence that the rules governing their investments will remain predictable over time.

“We have to see stability over time. At least three to five years, international investors need to see that they can put their investment here and that it will be safe for the next three to five years and longer,” he said.

Kazakhstan’s strategic role in China-West trade

Ken Moriyasu, a senior researcher at the Washington D.C.-based Hudson Institute, placed Kazakhstan’s political reforms within a broader geopolitical and investment context.

“When it comes to investment, it’s important to understand the players involved here. China clearly is the biggest investor,” Moriyasu said.

He described Kazakhstan as a key partner for China as Beijing is seeking to reduce its reliance on maritime routes and expand overland connections.

“Political stability is very important,” he said, noting that Kazakhstan’s vast territory and strategic location make it an important component of these routes.

Moriyasu also emphasized that the development of overland corridors through Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Türkiye does not necessarily conflict with U.S. interests.

“It is very beneficial for the United States that China creates these land transport corridors, but the countries that these corridors pass through remain friends with America,” he said.

The Kurultai vote continues in Kazakhstan with 10,423 polling stations operating across the country. The Kurultai will have 145 seats elected for five-year term. A total of 777 foreign observers from 42 countries and 13 international organizations have been accredited to monitor Kazakhstan’s election.

World.title: Tokayev Says Vice President Appointment Expected Within 10 Days
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said the new Vice President is expected to be appointed within the next week or 10 days, speaking to media representatives after casting his ballot in the country’s first elections to the Kurultai on Aug. 23.

Responding to questions about the reforms and the changes expected after the Kurultai and the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi (People’s Council) begin their work, Tokayev described the newly established Vice President position as a significant and necessary institutional change.

“We deliberately established this new position in the Constitution. I would not be mistaken in saying that it is extremely necessary. In the current difficult times, such a position is particularly needed by our country,” Tokayev said.

He said the name of the person who will take the position is expected to become known within the next seven to 10 days, adding that it would be premature to disclose the candidate’s name during the voting process.

“I think this will be a well-known person whom you all know very well,” he said.

Tokayev also highlighted the planned launch of the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi, a new state body that he said would build on the work previously carried out by the Assembly of the People of Kazakhstan. According to him, the new institution will serve as a multifunctional political mechanism as part of the country’s broader reforms.

Tokayev on 2029 presidential election

Asked whether he intends to use his constitutional right to seek another presidential term in 2029, Tokayev said the Constitutional Court’s recent decision confirming his eligibility is lawful, but that discussing his future candidacy would be premature.

“The Constitutional Court made this decision. It is lawful, and I have the legal right to be re-elected. But as for the upcoming elections or, as you put it, whether I will run or not, and in which year, it is premature to speculate on this,” he said.

Tokayev said the government has many tasks to complete before it can address such questions. He also said the government’s composition would change, while stressing that there are currently no grounds for concern about its work.

“Personnel changes are always inevitable because they give the government new strength,” Tokayev said, adding that such changes should be aimed at providing a serious impetus to the government’s work rather than dismissals for their own sake.

Voter turnout exceeds 65.37%

Meanwhile, voter turnout in Kazakhstan’s first elections to the Kurultai reached 65.37% by 4 p.m. on Aug. 23, with 8,240,336 voters having received ballots, according to the Central Election Commission (CEC).

The Kyzylorda Region recorded the highest turnout at 81.38%, followed by East Kazakhstan at 79.33%, Zhetisu Region at 77.03%, and Turkistan Region at 76.73%.

Turnout in the Aktobe Region stood at 75.63%, Akmola Region at 73.69%, Abai Region at 71.18%, Karagandy Region at 70.91% and Kostanai Region at 70.09%.

Among the cities of national significance, turnout reached 67.92% in Shymkent, 46.38% in Astana and 36.65% in Almaty.

Other regional figures were 67.23% in the Almaty Region, 67.06% in Pavlodar Region, 65.86% in Mangystau Region, 64.29% in Ulytau Region, 63.94% in North Kazakhstan, 63.37% in Atyrau Region, 61.81% in West Kazakhstan and 69.11% in the Zhambyl Region.

The CEC will provide the next update on voter turnout at 6 p.m.

World.title: International Observers Deliver Assessment of Kazakhstan’s First Kurultai Vote
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s transition to a single-chamber legislature entered a new stage Aug. 23 as voters went to the polls to elect the country’s first Kurultai, with international observers monitoring the process.

The election is part of a broader effort to modernize Kazakhstan’s political institutions and strengthen their ability to respond to the country’s changing social and economic landscape, Deputy Foreign Minister Arman Issetov said during an Aug. 22 briefing with foreign media.

He noted that Kazakhstan is pursuing political reform not because it is facing a crisis, but because the country is developing and its institutions should be prepared for the next stage of that development.

“We expect that the new political system will help maintain stability and continuity while ensuring the further development of state institutions. It should also provide more effective representation of public interests and improve the quality of decision-making,” Issetov said.

He also linked the reforms to the country’s economic development, saying a more complex economy requires more effective state institutions, predictable legislation and high-quality public administration.

“The more diverse society becomes, the more important it is to have mechanisms that allow for the various public interests to be taken into account. This is one of the main reasons behind the current constitutional reform,” Issetov said.

“It is not aimed at changing for the sake of change. Its objective is to bring political institutions in line with modern Kazakhstan and prepare them for the next stage of the country’s development,” he said.

The election has drawn international attention, with observers from foreign countries and organizations monitoring the electoral process, visiting polling stations and meeting with election officials and political parties. Their assessments offer an international perspective on how the new political system is taking shape in practice.

Shanghai Cooperation Organization

According to SCO Deputy Secretary-General T.R. Midhun, voting was well organized and polling stations were fully prepared.

“We went to the polling stations when they opened. We saw the procedures and the queues of people who were willing to participate in the election. It was early morning, and people were still very keen to start as early as possible,” he said.

Midhun noted that the mission’s task was to observe all stages of the electoral process and form an objective assessment based on direct observation and factual information. The mission will also monitor the closing of polling stations and procedures required under Kazakhstan’s legislation.

The SCO’s final assessment will be presented at a press conference on Aug. 24, he said.

In an interview with The Astana Times, Midhun said Kazakhstan’s political and economic reforms marked a profound transformation for the country.

“I think and hope that after these reforms Kazakhstan will strengthen its position and potential in the international arena. This, of course, will contribute to the SCO,” he said.

Midhun highlighted Kazakhstan’s role as a founding member of the SCO and praised its contributions in transport, logistics, political relations and cultural cooperation.

He also pointed to the country’s initiative to convene a meeting of heads of ports and logistics centers, calling it a “very constructive” contribution to the organization.

According to Midhun, SCO member states and dialogue partners account for around 40% of the world’s population and approximately one-quarter of global GDP.

“As one of the largest regional organizations, we have always paid special attention to the development of relations between countries in the fields of security, political relations, energy, and transport. When the world is changing, the role of the SCO is, of course, growing,” he said.

Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic Speaking Countries (TURKPA)

Osman Mesten, a Turkish lawmaker who chairs TURKPA’s Commission on Legal Affairs and International Relations, called the election a historic milestone.

“Following the referendum and the transition to a single-chamber legislature, the elections are the first held under the new system,” Mesten said.

Parliamentarians from Azerbaijan, the Kyrgyz Republic and Türkiye are participating in election observation missions.

Mesten noted that the delegation had met with the Central Election Commission chairman and representatives of political parties participating in the election.

“We observed that each party had been able to prepare for the elections and conduct outreach among voters to encourage participation and the exercise of their democratic rights,” he said.

He also highlighted women’s representation among candidates, noting that women account for around 43% of all candidates.

Mesten said Kazakhstan’s transition to a unicameral parliament could streamline the legislative process and improve its efficiency.

“A single-chamber legislature is certainly important from the perspective of democratic representation and for ensuring that the legislative process functions in a more orderly, efficient and effective manner,” he told The Astana Times.

Mesten noted that Türkiye had previously a bicameral legislature but transitioned to a unicameral parliamentary system following constitutional reforms.

“I believe that a single chamber enables decisions to be made more effectively, more quickly and more efficiently. It also eliminates some of the disadvantages associated with a dual-chamber system,” he said.

He also welcomed Kazakhstan’s decision to name the new legislature the Kurultai, describing the term as a reference to the country’s historical roots and shared heritage across the Turkic world.

“By choosing this name, Kazakhstan is referring to its deep historical roots. It also conveys the message that the country seeks to build a strong nation and a strong state by drawing strength from its heritage,” Mesten said.

“The name Kurultai is meaningful not only for Kazakhstan. It reflects our shared history and common roots. For this reason, it has inspired pride and enthusiasm throughout the Turkic world, including in Türkiye,” he said.

A total of 777 foreign observers from 42 countries and 13 international organizations have been accredited to monitor Kazakhstan’s Kurultai election.

World.title: Kazakhstan Records 37.05% Voter Turnout by Noon in Kurultai Election
World.content:
ALMATY – Voter turnout in Kazakhstan’s first elections to the Kurultai reached 37.05% as of noon on Aug. 23, with 4,670,816 voters having received ballots, according to the Central Election Commission (CEC).

The Kyzylorda Region recorded the highest turnout at 47.59%, followed by the Zhetisu Region at 47.29% and the Turkistan Region at 43.14%. Turnout in the Aktobe Region stood at 42.5%, East Kazakhstan at 41.89%, Shymkent at 41.6% and the Karagandy Region at 40.56%.

The lowest turnout was recorded in Almaty at 17.87%. Other regions with turnout below 35% included the Mangystau Region at 34.68% and the Kostanai Region at 34.72%. Turnout in Astana reached 35.28%, while the Almaty Region recorded 39.05% and the Abai Region 38.51%.

Kazakhstan’s leadership votes

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev cast his ballot at polling station No. 520, located at the Palace of Independence in Astana. After voting, Tokayev briefed representatives of the media and described the election as a significant milestone for Kazakhstan, reported Akorda.

“Today is truly a historic day for our country. For the first time, we are holding elections to a unicameral Kurultai. This is an important historical event,” Tokayev said.

He noted that Kazakhstan has carried out large-scale reforms and achieved significant results, while emphasizing that substantial work remains.

Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov also cast his ballot in the first elections to the unicameral Kurultai, while Minister of Foreign Affairs Yermek Kosherbayev voted at polling station No. 514.

First Deputy Head of the Presidential Administration Erlan Karin voted at a polling station in Astana, describing the first Kurultai elections as a historic event for Kazakhstan.

Voting continues abroad

Polling stations for the Kurultai elections are operating now in more than 40 countries, allowing Kazakhstan citizens abroad to participate in the vote.

The election will elect 145 members of Kazakhstan’s new unicameral Parliament. Seven political parties are contesting the election under a proportional representation system in a single nationwide constituency, with a 5% threshold for entering the legislature.

The CEC will continue publishing voter turnout data every two hours throughout election day.

World.title: Kazakhstan Opens More Than 10,000 Polling Stations for First Kurultai Election
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan opened 10,363 polling stations across the country on Aug. 23 for Kazakhstan’s first elections to the Kurultai, according to the Central Election Commission (CEC).

Polling stations began operating at 7 a.m. Astana time, while 107 of them opened earlier at 6 a.m. based on decisions by territorial election commissions. In total, 12,605,788 citizens are included in the voter lists. Authorities also issued 17,132 absentee certificates, allowing voters to cast ballots outside their registered localities.

A total of 10,423 polling stations have been established for the election, including 79 stations in 61 foreign countries.

Voting abroad

Voting has also begun at polling stations abroad. Kazakhstan established 79 polling stations at diplomatic missions and consular offices in 61 countries to ensure citizens living abroad can exercise their constitutional right to vote. A total of 11,402 voters are registered at these stations.

According to Deputy Foreign Minister Arman Issetov, 26 polling stations abroad had opened by 8 a.m. Astana time. Kazakh citizens in Tokyo and Seoul were the first to begin voting, at 3 a.m. Astana time.

As of 8 a.m., 228 citizens had cast their ballots at polling stations abroad.

Election rules

CEC member Lazzat Suyindik reminded voters and media representatives on Aug. 21. of restrictions on the publication of election-related opinion polls and forecasts. Under Kazakhstan’s election legislation, results of public opinion polls, forecasts of election results and other election-related research cannot be published during the five days preceding election day or on election day itself.

According to her, exit polls may be conducted on election day only outside polling station premises and by organizations that have notified the CEC in advance. Photographing or video recording a completed ballot and distributing such material is also prohibited on election day.

At the same time, voters are allowed to take photographs at polling stations, including near ballot boxes or while casting their ballots, provided that the photograph does not reveal which party they voted for. The restriction on distributing such images applies specifically to election day.

First Kurultai election

The election marks a new stage in Kazakhstan’s parliamentary system. Citizens will elect 145 members of the Kurultai, the country’s new unicameral Parliament, through proportional representation in a single nationwide constituency.

Seven political parties are contesting the election, with parties required to secure at least 5% of the vote to enter the legislature. A total of 777 foreign observers from 42 countries and 13 international organizations have been accredited to monitor the election..

Starting at 10 a.m., the CEC will provide updates on voter turnout every two hours throughout election day.

World.title: S&P Upgrade Highlights Kazakhstan’s Economic Resilience and Investment Potential
World.content:
ASTANA – S&P Global Ratings raised Kazakhstan’s long- and short-term sovereign credit ratings on Aug. 21 to BBB/A-2 from BBB-/A-3, while maintaining a stable outlook. The agency also raised its transfer and convertibility assessment to BBB+ and affirmed Kazakhstan’s national scale rating at kzAAA.

The upgrade strengthens Kazakhstan’s position among investment-grade sovereigns and could improve investor confidence, according to the QZ Economy analytical Telegram channel.

“A higher sovereign rating is also an increase in confidence,” the experts said on Aug. 22, noting its potential to improve financing conditions for the economy, support Kazakh companies working with foreign creditors and investors, and strengthen Kazakhstan’s overall investment attractiveness.

Growth remains a key strength

The upgrade reflects what S&P describes as Kazakhstan’s “resilient GDP growth outlook as well as its ample external and fiscal buffers that could cushion future shocks.”

Preliminary data show GDP expanded 4.1% in January-June despite a sharp slowdown in the first quarter linked to disruptions in oil exports and production. S&P forecasts growth of 5.1% in 2026, moderating to 4-4.5% in 2027-2029.

The agency expects non-oil activity to partly offset the impact of fiscal consolidation and lower global oil prices. Construction and manufacturing have already provided additional momentum.

Buffers support fiscal consolidation

Kazakhstan’s government liquid assets are forecast to stabilize at around 21% of GDP over the next four years. The National Bank and government’s external assets exceed the country’s gross external debt, giving policymakers room to maneuver during external shocks.

Fiscal performance is also improving. The national budget deficit was 1.2% of GDP in the first half this year, on track toward the 2.5% full-year target. S&P expects the general government deficit to average 1.2-1.3% of GDP in 2026-2029, compared with 3.7% in 2025.

Tax revenue increased 17% year on year in the first half, including a 42% increase in VAT collection. Efforts to broaden the tax base and control spending are expected to support further consolidation.

Political analyst Gaziz Abishev linked the upgrade to the government’s fiscal and economic policy, including tax reform, expenditure controls and a stronger focus on developing processing industries.

“Financial discipline is what international experts like. The country is rationalizing spending and supporting accumulation, protecting the National Fund from being spent down,” Abishev said.

He also highlighted the government’s work with foreign investors and President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s economic pragmatism, which he said aims to maximize the benefits of cooperation with relevant partners while minimizing geopolitical risks.

Investment could become the key benefit

S&P expects investment to remain high at approximately 30% of GDP, driven by infrastructure, raw-material processing and energy projects. The investment program is central to Kazakhstan’s efforts to diversify its resource-driven economy.

The QZ Economy experts said the rating upgrade could strengthen confidence among foreign investors and international financial institutions, potentially “lower the cost of attracting financing for the economy” and improve conditions for Kazakh companies working with foreign creditors and investors.

The significance therefore extends beyond the sovereign balance sheet. A stronger rating can reduce perceived country risk, but its economic impact will depend on whether investment programs generate new production, infrastructure and long-term productivity.

Oil remains the main vulnerability

Kazakhstan remains exposed to commodity-price volatility and disruptions to oil exports. Nearly 80% of oil flows through the CPC pipeline via Russia, while oil accounts for more than half of exports.

S&P’s stable outlook assumes that possible CPC disruptions will be short-lived. A prolonged fall in global oil prices or extended pipeline disruptions could result in negative rating action. Conversely, stronger fiscal performance and a reduction in the government interest bill could support a positive rating action.

The upgrade is therefore both recognition and a benchmark for Kazakhstan. S&P’s stable outlook suggests that the country’s strong buffers will help it manage possible external shocks, while continued fiscal consolidation and diversification will remain important.

“S&P raised Kazakhstan’s rating even amid uncertainty in the global economy and volatility in commodity markets. This once again confirms that our economy can remain resilient in the face of external challenges. Reforms and hard work are already bearing fruit,” the QZ Economy analytical Telegram channel said.

The next test will be whether stronger sovereign credibility translates into lower financing costs, sustained investment and broader economic diversification.

World.title: Armenia’s new parliament: balance of power, tools of government and opposition’s dead end
World.content:
Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

The parliamentary election results in Armenia have confirmed the continuity of the country’s political system while exposing deep structural contradictions. Political competition has shifted decisively towards intense polarisation. The National Assembly risks turning into little more than a platform for mutual accusations resembling a television talk show, rather than the country’s highest legislative body.

Political analyst Alexander Iskandaryan’s assessment

Continuity of the system, limits of influence and a fragmented opposition

“The new National Assembly has retained the key feature of its predecessor. The Constitution allows the ruling Civil Contract party to make almost any decision on its own, except on issues that require a constitutional majority. The two opposition factions — former president Robert Kocharyan’s Armenia Alliance and businessman Samvel Karapetyan’s Strong Armenia — have access to the media and the parliamentary platform, and can openly express their views and criticise the government. However, they have no real leverage over current policy.

The opposition forces have undergone a reshuffle. In the eighth National Assembly, Kocharyan’s faction held the largest number of seats. In the new parliament, however, it is the smaller of the two opposition factions. They are also unlikely to build a stable coalition or an “umbrella” structure. Because of their different origins and the lack of a practical basis for cooperation, even if they unite, they will not secure 50% of the seats needed to take the initiative. A long-term alliance is impossible. In 35 years of the Third Republic, the opposition has never managed to produce a successful example of unity. The minority is therefore left with little more than keeping the protest movement alive.”

Legitimacy, voters and the government’s narratives

“The ruling party has significant external legitimacy. This includes recognition of the election results by the US, EU, Turkey and Azerbaijan, as well as Russia’s refusal to withhold recognition from Nikol Pashinyan. The ruling force also relies on support from the bureaucracy. In fact, bureaucratic legitimacy has grown stronger. Civil servants clearly understand their ties to the political leadership and recognise the risks that a change of elites could bring.

At the same time, the government’s social legitimacy remains low. Kocharyan won 10% despite his high negative rating, while Karapetyan’s party, hastily assembled over six months with its leader under arrest, won a quarter of the vote despite high turnout. This is a serious signal of the level of public dissatisfaction.

Realising that its support will not grow, the government abandoned any real ideology. Political strategists pragmatically discarded the “high-minded Yerevan intelligentsia”, which would not have voted for the government anyway and would not have gone to the polls. Instead, they focused on their target audience: residents of small towns and villages with lower levels of education, young people and older generations.

To maintain control, the government uses several narratives:

“Peace versus war” — portraying opponents as the “party of war” and frightening voters with the prospect that an opposition victory would lead to a new war in September.

“Democrats versus oligarchs” — selectively labelling businesses. Wealthy entrepreneurs who support the government are simply called “businessmen”, while any affluent opponents are automatically branded “oligarchs”.

“Europe versus Russia” — systematically linking the entire opposition to Moscow. Karapetyan is portrayed this way because he came from Russia, Gagik Tsarukyan because of his ties to Belarus, and Kocharyan as Putin’s personal friend.

Accusing voters of supporting the opposition solely for money. This new level of polarisation has emerged in official statements by the authorities.”

The government’s geopolitical narrative and the opposition’s dead end

“The government’s anti-Russian discourse found fertile ground. These sentiments had been developing for years, and the events of 2020 and 2023 — the war in Karabakh, followed by the exodus of the entire Armenian population from Nagorno-Karabakh — only strengthened them.

At the same time, people across the post-Soviet space have traditionally associated the word “European” with quality and development: European healthcare, European education, European cars and so on. The government has effectively exploited this perception. Direct public support for Pashinyan from senior US officials, up to and including the US president, also played an important role.

The opposition has found itself in a strategic dead end. It cannot openly say “we are pro-Russian” or “we are not pro-Russian”.
