Unable to reject the geopolitical trend that enjoys broad public support, opposition parties have had to adapt and repeat that they are “also in favour of cooperation with Europe, but for a more carefully calibrated policy”.

Personal attacks instead of alternative programmes

“Instead of substantive work, the opposition is sliding into negative rhetoric and personal attacks: who is corrupt, who got their wife a job, who owns which flat and who once “didn’t even have a washing machine”. Armenian society knows perfectly well how the bureaucratic hierarchy works, so such “exposés” do not work. All these scandals only play into the government’s hands, allowing it to say: “Look who we have to work with in parliament.”

A constructive alternative would be to develop concrete programmes in different areas — healthcare, pensions, the economy, the army and so on. Even if the ruling majority rejects, say, 15 such professional programmes in a row, a systematic effort to offer solutions will eventually resonate with society. For now, trolling has replaced politics.”

Real state priorities: security, energy and meritocracy

“While parliament is busy trolling, the country’s key problems remain unresolved. One of them is security.

It is wrong to call the situation with Azerbaijan peace. You can see what real peace looks like on the border with Georgia, for example: people can cross freely using an ID card, while there are no transport corridors, European observers, military guards or concrete walls, even though 30% of the border remains undelimited. With Baku, however, there is only a state of “no war”. That is far from peace. At the same time, Azerbaijan is rapidly expanding its military capabilities in every sphere, including its air force.

Armenia needs to make foreign policy decisions and find ways to overcome the energy crisis.

Relations with all four neighbours — Russia, Turkey, Azerbaijan and Iran — are in crisis. Meanwhile, the Armenian-American TRIPP “Trump Route” project — a transit route through Armenia — remains little more than a political narrative. At the same time, launching new facilities, such as an AI data centre in Hrazdan, could create an acute electricity shortage that talk of American small modular nuclear reactors alone cannot solve.

In the Armenian city of Hrazdan, Firebird AI’s artificial intelligence factory has begun operations. The facility is the largest AI data centre in the region. The first phase of the project, worth more than $500 million, uses advanced NVIDIA accelerators and server equipment from leading global manufacturers. Some experts believe the factory’s launch could put additional pressure on the country’s energy system. (firebird.ai)

The state needs a competent administration to overcome these challenges.

The country needs to embrace meritocracy, appointing people based on competence rather than loyalty.

Finally, the country’s leadership needs to reconsider its attitude towards citizens.

Nikol Pashinyan is the prime minister of all Armenians, not just the voters of Civil Contract. The claim that people could only have voted against the government in exchange for money is false and toxic. The government now faces a vast array of real problems. Its first task is to recognise the scale of those challenges and start addressing them.

Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

World.title: Anea the raccoon’s favourite activity at Tbilisi Zoo – video
World.content:
Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

Raccoons love water. You can often see them swimming, wetting their fur or carefully washing their paws. Anea, a resident of Tbilisi Zoo, is no exception.

On hot days, Anea particularly enjoys dipping her paws in water and having a cool shower. So her keepers set up an improvised shower in her enclosure, which, as you can see in the video below, delighted her.

There is a metal container in her enclosure for drinking water, but who says she cannot take a bath in it too? Despite its small size, Anea fits perfectly inside, happily splashes around in the water and uses it to escape the summer heat. After noticing the raccoon’s love of bathing, her keepers have already ordered a bigger “bath”.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status.



The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo.



We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Opinion: ‘Moscow’s main fear is that Armenia will choose European Union’
World.content:
Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

In recent days, Russia‘s demand for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether the country should remain in the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) or choose the European Union has increasingly been seen as a threat. Experts from the “Armenian Council” think tank made the assessment in an article.

Russia has long demanded such a referendum, including at the highest level. But there are now threats to initiate proceedings concerning Armenia’s membership of the EAEU. Decisions within the bloc require consensus, and Yerevan has the right to veto them.

“Russia’s main phobia is that the situation will deteriorate over time, leading the Armenian people to choose the European Union,” the authors argue.

They stress that this is not only Russia’s “main phobia”, but also its “main misconception”. The analysts believe that even the “economic pressure and blackmail” that Russia began applying to Armenia in May, during the pre-election period, have not changed Armenian public opinion. They cite the results of the parliamentary election on 7 June as evidence: Armenia’s ruling party won, rather than pro-Russian forces.

Ahead of Armenia’s parliamentary election, Russia imposed restrictions on imports of Armenian agricultural products. It also banned imports of flowers, Jermuk mineral water, certain alcoholic drinks and fish products. The authorities justified the measures by citing failures to meet required quality standards. However, Armenian experts and officials viewed the issue in the context of the election campaign. They therefore expected the pressure to end after the election. But that did not happen. Moreover, Russia introduced new restrictions after the election. At the same time, in early June, four EAEU member states called on Armenian authorities to hold a referendum as soon as possible on choosing between the Eurasian bloc and the EU. Yerevan responded that there were currently no grounds for such a vote because Armenia’s European integration process had not yet reached the stage at which citizens could make a choice. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has repeatedly said that Armenia should first obtain EU candidate status or, at the very least, put the issue on the agenda. However, Moscow continues to insist. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin said the EAEU expects Armenia to hold a referendum by December. Otherwise, the bloc’s leaders would “take this fact into account when determining appropriate further joint steps”. He said a report on the possible consequences of suspending the EAEU Treaty in relation to Armenia would be discussed at the December meeting of the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council.

Armenia’s prime minister spoke about a referendum on EU membership

“No one in Armenia has ever talked about holding a referendum on EAEU membership or an alternative in the form of the EU.

On 9 January 2025, when the Armenian government discussed and approved a bill to launch the EU accession process, Prime Minister Pashinyan said:

“Armenia can begin the process of joining the EU only if a certain number of referendum participants vote ‘yes’ in accordance with the procedure established by the Constitution.”

Senior Armenian officials later repeated this point on various occasions.

The key point is that Armenia will hold a referendum on joining the European Union, not on whether to remain in or leave the EAEU.

This fundamental difference significantly changes the forecasts for the expected outcome. However, if Armenia votes to join the EU, it will inevitably leave the EAEU at some stage of the subsequent process.”

Russia is pushing for a referendum on a different question

“Armenia’s willingness to hold a referendum on EU membership is fundamentally different from what Moscow wants to impose.

Russia is clearly manipulating the situation by demanding a referendum on the EAEU now, when Armenia is at least a decade away from joining the EU.

We need to understand the real reason for this urgency.

The Kremlin understands that if EU membership becomes a genuine possibility, no rational society could vote against it.

Therefore, to keep Armenia in the EAEU and have a chance of stopping its move towards the EU, a referendum must take place as soon as possible, while the prospect of EU membership remains unclear and uncertain.”

Moscow is trying to “beat” Europe by exploiting Armenian businesses’ dependence

“The EAEU mechanisms currently work in favour of Armenian businesses, creating influence and dependence.

At the same time, Armenia is steadily diversifying its economy, reducing that influence and dependence.

The question of whether to remain in the EAEU directly affects many companies with specific interests in Russia. By contrast, EU membership remains a more abstract issue for them for now.

Moscow does not expect to “beat” Europe in economic competition over the next few years or even decades and offer Armenia more attractive conditions. It therefore believes it still has an opportunity to influence the situation now. That is why it is in such a hurry.”

Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

World.title: Armenia-Azerbaijan exports could begin ‘soon’: Pledges, figures and remaining barriers
World.content:
Exports from Armenia to Azerbaijan

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan told journalists that “exports from Armenia to Azerbaijan could begin in the near future”. He also said that bilateral trade was already on the agenda. According to Pashinyan, Azerbaijani specialists visited Armenia in September 2025 and January 2026 to discuss infrastructure issues, including power lines, railways and pipelines.

The statement comes against the backdrop of tangible but still highly asymmetrical trade relations between the two countries, which began to take shape following the signing of the declaration in Washington in August 2025.

Official data and figures

According to Azerbaijan’s State Customs Committee, Azerbaijan exported around $17.4m worth of goods to Armenia between January and July 2026. The shipments consisted mainly of petroleum products, particularly diesel and petrol. Over the same period, Azerbaijan’s indirect imports from Armenia amounted to just $960. This figure was recorded in March, with imports falling to zero in subsequent months.

Following the lifting of transit restrictions in October 2025 and the start of the first fuel deliveries in December, Azerbaijan has facilitated both direct exports to Armenia and the transit of goods from Russia and Kazakhstan, including grain, fertilisers and other products. Volumes remain small, but the direction of travel has changed: borders that had been closed for decades have effectively begun to open.

There has yet to be any official commercial export from Armenia. In January 2026, Armenian Economy Minister Gevorg Papoyan said the two sides had exchanged lists of potential goods for bilateral trade. These included aluminium foil and raw materials for its production, ferromolybdenum, textiles, flowers, greenhouse produce including tomatoes and peppers, raw materials for brandy production, and other goods.

The specific contents of the lists and the expected volumes of shipments have not yet been officially published. Further development of trade will depend on agreements between companies.

What could be traded, and why?

Azerbaijani experts note that, at the initial stage, developing trade in industrial goods and raw materials appears more realistic than focusing primarily on food products. Vugar Bayramov, an MP and member of the Milli Majlis Committee on Economic Policy, citing preliminary estimates, puts the potential annual trade turnover for 38 categories of goods at up to $300m. These include food and industrial products as well as raw materials. In his view, mutual supplies of goods other than fuel could begin between the two countries in the near future.

Economist Natig Jafarli says the process is developing gradually. According to him, Azerbaijan has an advantage in energy resources, while potential Armenian exports could include agricultural products, fish, fruit and iron ore. However, Azerbaijan is not yet importing goods from Armenia, while the necessary infrastructure, including bank transfers, insurance and contractual mechanisms, has yet to be fully established.

Akif Nasirli, chairman of the Centre for Liberal Economists, believes food products could also be viable export candidates, including fruit and vegetables such as apricots, peaches, cherries, tomatoes and peppers, as well as fish, mineral water and wine. In his view, restrictions on the Russian market are forcing Yerevan to seek alternative export markets.

Former Finance Minister Fikret Yusifov has previously argued that, if trade relations are restored, a trade deficit for Armenia would be inevitable, but that these economic ties should nevertheless be developed for the sake of peace.

There is also a widespread view among experts that food and beverages are psychologically more sensitive categories of goods. Construction materials, cable and electrical products, industrial raw materials, chemicals and light-industry goods, by contrast, may be perceived considerably more favourably.

Psychological barrier

This is one of the deepest and most sensitive aspects of the issue. Expert assessments published by Caliber note that memories of the 44-day war remain fresh. The appearance of products labelled Made in Armenia on shop shelves could initially provoke mixed reactions, ranging from curiosity to social media campaigns. Trust in food and beverages, including wine and brandy, is particularly important, as some consumers may have irrational concerns about their safety. With industrial goods and construction materials, by contrast, the country of origin is less visible to consumers and purchasing decisions tend to be more pragmatic.

During a transitional period, neutral packaging in English or Russian, or rebranding, could potentially be used. The appearance of Azerbaijani fuel on the Armenian market has already created a precedent for a kind of “economic truce”. A similarly pragmatic approach could work in the opposite direction, although this will not happen automatically.

In both societies, support for peace does not yet necessarily translate into an equally positive attitude towards goods from the neighbouring country. Traders from border areas who wished to remain anonymous, as well as entrepreneurs with experience of informal “re-exports” through Georgia using channels that have existed since the 1990s, say that price and quality could eventually become the decisive factors. However, this process could take years.

Practical obstacles and possible timeframes

Issues surrounding certification, phytosanitary controls, customs procedures, bank transfers and insurance have yet to be fully resolved.

Logistics currently operate mainly through Georgia. Direct rail links and the TRIPP corridor are still at the infrastructure development stage. Competition also remains high, with suppliers from Turkey, Russia and Iran already present in the market alongside domestic producers. The competitiveness of Armenian goods will therefore depend on their price, quality and logistics costs.

Under an optimistic scenario, small-scale shipments of industrial goods and raw materials could begin within several months to a year. A more realistic scenario would see trade gradually expand over one to three years, while under a pessimistic scenario, political fluctuations and public reaction could delay the process considerably.

What to watch next

Key indicators could include the first genuine commercial shipments from Armenia appearing in customs statistics, the introduction of banking mechanisms for cross-border payments, official approval of a list of potential goods for trade, and changes in the procurement policies of retailers such as Bravo, Araz and others.

Independent polling and sociological research in both countries will also be needed to assess public attitudes towards goods labelled “Made in …”. Without such data, statements about future trade will remain largely expressions of intent.

World.title: ‘From crisis management to stability’: Pashinyan unveils new government programme
World.content:
Armenia’s 2026–2031 government programme

The Armenian government has approved its programme for 2026-2031. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said it marked a shift from crisis management to stability. Looking back on his eight years as prime minister, he said the coronavirus pandemic, followed by the war and the post-war situation, had forced the government to operate in crisis-management mode. Now that Armenia and Azerbaijan have established peace, the government can “return to the unfinished part of the agenda of the 2018 Velvet Revolution”.

The new programme focuses on stability, he said. Pashinyan stressed that it rests entirely on the concept of “Real Armenia” and the principles underpinning the establishment of the Fourth Republic.

In 2025, the ruling Civil Contract party announced a new strategic goal: establishing the Fourth Republic of Armenia. The party congress unanimously adopted a declaration to this effect. According to the document, the Fourth Republic “will be based on the concept of preserving the internationally recognised sovereign territory of the Republic of Armenia, covering 29,743 sq km, in accordance with the 1991 Alma-Ata Declaration”. The declaration says the party reached this decision after analysing the history of the Third Republic. The Third Republic refers to the present-day Republic of Armenia, which declared independence following a nationwide referendum in 1991. The First Republic refers to the republic proclaimed on 28 May 1918. Accordingly, Soviet Armenia is considered the Second Republic.

“Following the 7 June 2026 election, the ideology of ‘Real Armenia’ won. This means it has become the official ideology. Armenia is therefore entering the stage of its history that we call the Fourth Republic. We must continue and give new momentum to democratic, anti-corruption, economic and public administration reforms,” the prime minister stressed.

Government plans for the next five years

According to the new programme, the Armenian government will pursue the following goals in 2026-2031:

strengthening and further institutionalising the peace established between Armenia and Azerbaijan;

maintaining and further developing a favourable security environment around Armenia, in particular by normalising and developing relations with countries in the region and deepening existing partnerships beyond it;

unblocking Armenia through the Crossroads of Peace project and the “Trump Route” (TRIPP) transit programme;

liberalising the visa regime with the EU for Armenian citizens;

deepening democratic, anti-corruption, economic and public administration reforms.

With whom does Yerevan plan to deepen partnerships under its “balanced foreign policy”?

In 2026-2031, the Armenian government will pursue a “balanced and proportionate” foreign policy.

“It has proved effective in stabilising Armenia’s external environment. Regionalisation plays a key role in foreign policy, whose goal is to ensure conditions in which Armenia can not only live without external support, but do so comfortably,” the document says.

Based on this approach, the government places particular importance on further developing relations with Georgia, Iran, Turkey and Azerbaijan. The government has outlined the following steps for each neighbouring country:

Georgia

Yerevan will continue implementing the measures set out in the Declaration on Establishing a Strategic Partnership between Armenia and Georgia. This will create new mutually beneficial opportunities for political, trade, economic, energy and transport cooperation, as well as regional and joint infrastructure projects.

Iran

Armenia will continue energy cooperation with Iran, develop cross-border infrastructure and expand transport routes through Iran, including North-South and Persian Gulf-Black Sea corridors.

Turkey

The Armenian government will continue efforts to establish diplomatic relations with Turkey, open the Armenian-Turkish border and put at least two modern border crossing points into operation. It also plans to restore and expand transport, energy and digital infrastructure, as well as bilateral and multilateral trade.

Azerbaijan

The government plans to continue efforts to sign and ratify a peace agreement and carry out work on the delimitation and demarcation of the state border. Contacts between civil society and business communities in the two countries will continue, helping to establish bilateral trade.

The foreign policy priorities specifically include deepening strategic partnerships with the European Union, the US, France and China. With Russia, Armenia plans to “transform and deepen its partnership”.

Against the backdrop of tensions over the ban on Armenian food and other exports to Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), which Russia leads, the programme says:

“Work will continue to ensure the full and uninterrupted exercise of the EAEU’s fundamental freedoms — the free movement of labour, services, goods and capital — as well as to develop relations with member and observer states.”

Regarding relations with the European Union, the programme stresses that Armenia will continue working to meet standards in democracy and the rule of law, as well as in the economic, financial and other spheres.

Armenia intends to deepen its partnership with the United States further. Cooperation will continue based on the principles set out in the Strategic Partnership Charter and bilateral memorandums of understanding.

“The TRIPP project, the ‘Trump Route’, will be implemented, at least in terms of operating energy and railway infrastructure, while integrating Armenia into major regional infrastructure projects,” the programme says.

Armenia’s 2026–2031 government programme

World.title: Parrots Rocky and Kiki: Tbilisi Zoo’s brightest residents – video
World.content:
Macaws at Tbilisi Zoo

Tbilisi Zoo is home to two species of macaws: scarlet macaws (Ara macao) named Rocky and Kiki, and blue-and-yellow macaws (Ara ararauna) named Chico and Paco. Their bright plumage catches visitors’ attention at first sight.

The macaws at Tbilisi Zoo are currently in the middle of their breeding season. Chico and Paco are expecting chicks. They usually incubate their eggs for 24–28 days. During this period, both parents actively protect and care for their future offspring.

Rocky and Kiki have become particularly cautious during this period. They often hide from people and rarely leave their enclosure. If you are planning to visit them at the zoo, keep in mind that they may be difficult to spot at the moment.

Macaws are known for their strong bonds. Pairs almost always stay together: they preen each other’s feathers, look for food together and protect each other when danger threatens.

With proper care, macaws can live for 50–60 years, and sometimes even longer — more than 70 years. Rocky’s exact age is unknown, but he is the oldest parrot at Tbilisi Zoo. Despite his advanced age, Rocky still has the same short-tempered and grumpy nature he has always had.

Once, when a keeper was a little late with a treat — a nut — Rocky immediately made his “protest” known by biting him on the finger. Because of their powerful beaks, macaw bites can be very painful and may cause serious injuries.

Macaws are incredibly intelligent birds. They have excellent memories, and some can even imitate human voices and words.

Although macaws are often kept as pets, caring for them is no easy task. They need plenty of space, daily attention, mental stimulation and constant variety in their surroundings.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Macaws at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Opinion from Abkhazia: ‘Nika Gvaramia said nothing new about resolving Georgian-Abkhaz conflict’
World.content:
An interview with Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Georgian opposition, about ways to resolve the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict attracted considerable attention in Georgia. In Abkhazia, however, it attracted almost no attention.

In his blog, Inal Khashig, editor of the Abkhaz newspaper Chegemskaya Pravda, offered his view on why. He believes the lack of interest among Abkhaz people is mainly because Gvaramia said nothing new in the interview and offered none of the things Abkhaz people would want to hear.

Inal Khashig: “From my strictly Abkhaz perspective, Gvaramia did not say anything radically new. If anything, he simply revived the old idea of resolving the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict through Georgia’s integration into the European Union, which would serve as an attractive incentive for Abkhaz people.

Georgian politicians have periodically put forward this idea since the presidency of Mikheil Saakashvili. The most recent was Georgia’s current prime minister, Irakli Kobakhidze, who in 2024 even set a specific deadline for achieving the goal. ‘Georgia will join the European Union together with our Abkhaz and Ossetian brothers by 2030,’ he declared at the time from a high-profile podium. In short, the EU idea has already been discussed many times.”

From Gvaramia’s interview, I also understood that Georgia cannot resolve the conflict through military means at present because it lacks the resources needed to guarantee the desired outcome. In this context, economic development and shared security interests should form the basis for resolving the conflict.

The only “new” idea proposed by the opposition politician is that Georgia needs to overcome the trauma it suffered after the Georgian-Abkhaz war of the 1990s because these memories “prevent it from moving forward and hold back development”. And on this point, I completely agree with Nika Gvaramia.

In my view, Georgia’s constant insistence on the need to regain Abkhazia is actually a heavy burden that prevents the country from achieving its full potential.

It is like a man who devotes all his energy and the rest of his life to trying to win back a wife who left him long ago. You can consider his life wasted.

I am convinced that if Mikheil Saakashvili had not abandoned his reform agenda in favour of “restoring territorial integrity” during his presidency, Georgia would almost certainly have made much greater progress in building its statehood.

I can well imagine that when Nika Gvaramia speaks about the need to overcome the trauma, he actually means giving up once and for all on claims to the lost territories. But as a politician, he understands the consequences of making such an admission openly.

As for the idea of restoring trust between Abkhaz people and Georgians, Gvaramia talks about this as well. But his understanding of “trust” is not very different from that of other Georgian politicians: essentially, “we will open up the world to you and shower you with benefits, but first come back to us”. In other words, it is a kind of bargain, with no guarantee that the other side is not bluffing.

But genuine trust looks very different.

In my view, a tangible step towards beginning the process of rebuilding trust between Abkhaz people and Georgians would be for Tbilisi to abolish the discriminatory Law on Occupied Territories, which does little short of preventing Abkhazia and South Ossetia from breathing freely without Georgia’s permission. But Nika Gvaramia did not mention this law even once. Perhaps that is why his interview went unnoticed in Abkhazia.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.



Nika Gvaramia interview

World.title: Opinion: ‘Removing Kobakhidze would be logical move for Ivanishvili if prime minister does not move against him first’
World.content:
Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze

According to Eka Gigauri, executive director of Transparency International Georgia, removing Prime Minister Kobakhidze could eventually become a logical step for Ivanishvili — provided the prime minister does not manage to seize political power himself.

Eka Gigauri: “The Garibashvili case has once again confirmed what we already knew:”

None of this has anything to do with fighting corruption. Ivanishvili is reshuffling his inner circle, while Kobakhidze — with his approval and Mdinaradze’s assistance — is getting rid of political rivals. In “Georgian Dream”, no one is surprised when people enrich themselves at the public’s expense or engage in corruption: they all steal. The entire system is built on corruption, and Ivanishvili gave them the freedom to do so. So the “fight against corruption” is merely a staged performance designed to conceal a settling of scores. Kobakhidze does not get his hands dirty himself. He has Mdinaradze to do that for him, who has become his loyal executor and servant. It is obvious that the overwhelming majority of “Georgian Dream” supporters genuinely support Garibashvili. The same cannot be said of Kobakhidze and Mdinaradze. Look at the reactions from “Dream” supporters to statements by Garibashvili and his wife. If the authorities imprisoned Mdinaradze and then Kobakhidze, “Dream” supporters would not say a word in their defence. To them, Kobakhidze is still a former NGO worker and employee of international organisations. He is not a churchgoer and has no particular ties to the Church. The same applies to much of his team. There is no friendship, brotherhood or willingness to support one another in the “Georgian Dream” party. Apparently, none of them possesses that quintessential Georgian sense of honour. Out of fear of Bidzina, and now of Kobakhidze as well, they will betray one another, throw each other under the bus and abandon one another in times of trouble. Ivanishvili is deliberately deepening divisions within his own team and turning its members against one another. His goal is to prevent them from uniting against him and to force them to constantly undermine and confront each other. Today, Kobakhidze is clearly Ivanishvili’s favourite. However, he appears to have been carried away by this status. He often talks about his personal achievements, as though he had the power to act even without Ivanishvili. He may not have many genuine supporters within “Georgian Dream”, but today he exercises almost complete control over state institutions. “Georgian Dream” members appear to fear Kobakhidze greatly — perhaps even more than Bidzina. They know that Kobakhidze has direct access to Bidzina and can tell him something about a fellow party member that could ultimately destroy them. Even Garibashvili did not have this kind of influence. Kobakhidze has placed his people almost everywhere, while parliament is under his complete control. He has gradually concentrated enormous power in his hands. If this continues, even Ivanishvili may find it difficult to dismantle the system.

The experience of authoritarian regimes around the world also shows that dictators manage their inner circles according to the principle of “divide and rule”. They periodically replace their favourites and involve everyone in corruption schemes and other crimes, so that they can later use their weaknesses and complicity against them. At the same time, they pit influential groups against one another and keep everyone in a constant state of fear through selective punishment.

Thus, no individual or group can accumulate enough power to pose a real threat to the leader. However, such a system also carries a significant risk: a favourite who has concentrated all the levers of power in their hands may eventually begin building an independent political force. That is why dictators often get rid of their most loyal and influential allies.

At the same time, members of an authoritarian ruler’s inner circle often initiate changes of power. In other words, autocrats and dictators have good reason to fear their own inner circles. Today, if Kobakhidze wanted to, he could even remove Bidzina, and no one in “Georgian Dream” would dare oppose him. Therefore, removing Kobakhidze would eventually become a perfectly logical step — unless he managed to remove Ivanishvili first.

Opinion on Georgian Prime Minister Kobakhidze

World.title: China accounts for nearly 30% of Uzbekistan's foreign-invested firms
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 24. China accounted for nearly 30% of all enterprises with foreign investment operating in Uzbekistan as of August 1, 2026, making it the country's largest source of foreign-invested businesses amid rapidly expanding economic ties between the two countries.

This was reflected in data published by Uzbekistan's National Statistics Committee.

A total of 20,973 enterprises with foreign investment were operating in Uzbekistan as of August 1, including 6,241 with Chinese participation. Of the overall total, 4,685 were joint ventures and 16,288 were foreign-owned enterprises.

Russia ranked second with 3,512 enterprises, followed by Türkiye with 2,327. Kazakhstan accounted for 1,321 enterprises, South Korea for 730 and Afghanistan for 706. Azerbaijan ranked seventh with 492 enterprises.

Kazakhstan accounted for 1,321 enterprises, South Korea for 730 and Afghanistan for 706. Azerbaijan ranked seventh with 492 enterprises, followed by Tajikistan with 467, the UAE with 453 and India with 439.

Trend's analysis shows that Uzbekistan's foreign-invested enterprise base remains concentrated among its largest economic partners. China, Russia and Turkey together accounted for 12,080 enterprises, or about 57.6% of the total.

China alone represented approximately 29.8% of all foreign-invested enterprises in Uzbekistan, meaning that nearly three out of every 10 such companies had Chinese participation.

The scale of Chinese business activity reflects the broader acceleration in economic ties between the two countries. Bilateral trade reached $17.8 billion in 2025, up 34% year on year, while Chinese direct investment in Uzbekistan increased fivefold to $17 billion, according to Uzbekistan's Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade. More than 6,000 enterprises with Chinese capital were operating in the country as of July 2026.

Trend's calculations show that the 6,241 Chinese-invested enterprises recorded by the National Statistics Committee account for about 29.8% of Uzbekistan's entire foreign-invested enterprise base. The figure is also substantially higher than the 4,731 Chinese-invested enterprises reported as of November 2025, indicating continued rapid expansion of Chinese business presence.

The growth extends beyond the number of companies. According to the Eurasian Development Bank, China's FDI stock in Uzbekistan rose from just $284 million in 2016 to $10.7 billion in the first half of 2025. Energy accounted for about 51% of that stock, while manufacturing represented another 31%, pointing to a growing focus on industrial and energy projects rather than purely trade-related activity.

The structure of Chinese investment is particularly relevant to Uzbekistan's industrial development. The concentration of Chinese capital in energy and manufacturing links the bilateral relationship directly to the country's efforts to expand production capacity, modernize infrastructure and develop new industrial value chains.

Recent cooperation has also broadened into green energy, agriculture, technology, logistics and export-oriented manufacturing. At a July 2026 Uzbekistan-China business forum in Tashkent, companies discussed projects in mining, green energy, agriculture, health care, advanced technologies and industrial cooperation. Moreover, the two countries have also been expanding cooperation in digital infrastructure and irrigation modernization. Uzbek and Chinese officials agreed in April to accelerate projects under the "Digital Silk Road" and discussed Chinese financing for the modernization of Uzbekistan's irrigation infrastructure.

Trend's assessment is that China's position as Uzbekistan's largest source of foreign-invested enterprises is part of a much broader transformation in bilateral economic relations. The relationship has evolved from primarily trade-based ties toward deeper investment cooperation spanning energy, manufacturing, infrastructure, technology and agriculture.

For Uzbekistan, the growing Chinese presence provides access to capital, technology and industrial partnerships, while the diversification of projects could support the country's efforts to expand its manufacturing base and integrate more deeply into regional and global supply chains. At the same time, the concentration of foreign-invested enterprises among a handful of countries underscores the importance of continuing to diversify Uzbekistan's investor base.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s renewable energy share rises fourfold to nearly 8%
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 24. Kazakhstan’s renewable energy sector is expanding rapidly, with the share of renewables in the country’s electricity mix approaching 8% as new wind and solar capacity comes online and grid infrastructure is upgraded.

This was stated by the Ministry of Energy of the Republic of Kazakhstan.

According to the Ministry, over the past six years, the share of electricity generated from renewable energy sources (RES) has increased fourfold, from around 2% to nearly 8%.

The Ministry notes that RES accounted for 7% of total electricity generation at the end of 2025, producing 8.6 billion kWh out of approximately 123.1 billion kWh generated nationwide. With additional capacity commissioned in 2026, the current share is approaching 8%.

The expansion has been supported by government policy measures, renewable energy auctions, investment attraction, and the commissioning of new generating capacity. Kazakhstan currently has 172 RES facilities with a combined capacity of more than 3.8 GW. The portfolio includes 71 wind farms, 54 solar power plants, 44 hydropower plants and three biogas facilities.

In 2025, renewable facilities generated 8.6 billion kWh, equivalent to approximately 8.6 TWh and around 7% of Kazakhstan’s total electricity generation. During the year, nine new RES facilities with a combined capacity of 503.5 MW were commissioned. These included five wind farms totaling 387 MW, three solar plants totaling 90 MW, and one hydropower plant of 26 MW. The expansion has continued in 2026. Another 10 RES facilities with a total capacity of 245 MW are planned for launch, including four wind farms, five solar plants and one hydropower plant.

As of mid-August, seven facilities totaling 212 MW had already been commissioned, meaning approximately 87% of the planned 2026 capacity has entered operation. Renewable electricity generation is expected to reach 8.8 billion kWh by the end of the year.

The project pipeline extends considerably beyond these additions. Approximately 100 projects with a combined capacity of 3.6 GW are planned for implementation, while another 4 GW of large-scale RES projects are under development, including 1 GW of projects with energy storage systems. The growing volume of variable renewable generation is also increasing the importance of transmission infrastructure and energy storage.

In an exclusive interview with Trend, EBRD Director and Head of Energy Eurasia Sule Kılıc said the bank has mobilized 4.2 billion euros for Central Asia’s energy sector and financed more than 6.5 GW of installed renewable energy capacity in the region.

"We are the largest investors in renewable energy in Central Asia, having financed more than 6.5 gigawatts of installed renewable capacity to date and mobilised 4.2 billion euros for the region’s energy sector," Kılıc said.

According to her, the EBRD’s involvement goes beyond renewable generation to include modernization of electricity grids, which is necessary to integrate growing volumes of solar and wind power into national systems.

For Kazakhstan, the bank’s key partners include national grid operator KEGOC. Since the 1990s, the EBRD has supported seven KEGOC projects, most recently the Integration of the West Zone Project, which connects the previously isolated western power zone with the rest of the country through more than 600 kilometres of high-voltage transmission lines. Kılıc also said the EBRD is considering projects under Kazakhstan’s National Project for Modernisation of Electricity and Municipal Infrastructure.

A major new investment platform was launched in April 2026, when the EBRD and Kazakhstan signed a memorandum of understanding on the Just Energy Transition Investment Platform (QaJET). The platform is expected to mobilize up to 20 billion euros to deploy 10 GW of renewable capacity by 2035.

The first project under the platform is the 1-GW Mirny Wind project, developed by TotalEnergies and local partners. The project includes a 300-MW battery energy storage system with 600 MWh capacity. "The Bank mobilised around $550 million for the project. The inclusion of the battery storage component is a critical element in ensuring the sustainable integration of the project into Kazakhstan’s energy system," Kılıc said.

International companies are already playing a significant role in Kazakhstan’s renewable energy expansion, including TotalEnergies, China Power, Masdar and China Energy. Their participation is bringing additional capital and technologies into a sector where the development of generation capacity increasingly needs to be accompanied by investment in grids and storage.

Trend’s calculations show that the 212 MW of renewable capacity already commissioned in 2026 represents approximately 87% of the 245 MW planned for the full year. At the same time, the projected 8.8 billion kWh of renewable generation in 2026 would be about 2.3% higher than the 8.6 billion kWh generated in 2025. The combination of new generation, transmission upgrades, and storage is important for Kazakhstan’s longer-term energy targets. The country aims to increase the share of renewable energy to 15% by 2030 and up to 50% by 2050, including alternative energy sources.

The EBRD’s regional approach indicates that achieving these targets will depend not only on adding wind and solar capacity, but also on expanding the infrastructure needed to move and balance that electricity. For Kazakhstan, the parallel development of generation, high-voltage transmission and battery storage is therefore becoming a central part of the transition toward a more diversified power system.

World.title: People’s Artist of Azerbaijan Tofig Bakikhanov dies
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 24. People’s Artist of Azerbaijan Tofig Bakikhanov has died at the age of 96.

Tofig Bakikhanov was born on December 8, 1930, into the family of renowned tar player and People’s Artist Ahmad Bakikhanov. He received his first musical education at the ten-year music school (now the Bulbul Secondary Specialized Music School) affiliated with the Uzeyir Hajibeyli Azerbaijan State Conservatory (Baku Music Academy). In 1990, he was awarded the title of People’s Artist.

For his contributions to the development of Azerbaijan’s musical culture, he was awarded the Shohrat (Glory), Sharaf (Honor), and Labor orders, including the Order of Labor, 1st Class.

For more than half a century, Tofig Bakikhanov taught at the Baku Music Academy.

He was the author of three ballets, three musical comedies, 25 concertos, 20 sonatas, five symphonic mughams, eight symphonies, six symphonic poems, numerous chamber works, as well as more than 100 songs and romances.

World.title: "New Tashkent" project is a unique achievement of modern urban development - President Ilham Aliyev
World.content:

Of course, every time I visit Uzbekistan, I visit different places and see how Tashkent is becoming more beautiful, how its buildings, streets and infrastructure are being transformed, and how everything is being done with greater taste, care and quality, said President Ilham Aliyev at the award ceremony held in the presence of President of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev, Trend's special correspondent reports.

World.title: President Ilham Aliyev, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev lay foundation stone for “Azerbaijan” Park in New Tashkent (PHOTO/VIDEO)
World.content:
TASHKENT, Uzbekistan, August 23. On August 23, President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev and President of the Republic of Uzbekistan Shavkat Mirziyoyev laid the foundation stone for the “Azerbaijan” Park in New Tashkent, Trend's special correspondent reports.

A public space reflecting the rich culture, centuries-old history, and traditions of Azerbaijan will be created there. The park will contribute to further strengthening the bonds between the brotherly peoples of Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan.

The establishment of the “Uzbekistan” Park in Baku and the “Azerbaijan” Park in New Tashkent will serve as another symbol of the centuries-old friendship, mutual respect, and cultural affinity between the peoples of the two countries, as well as the strong and dynamically developing bilateral relations between Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan.

World.title: How has AI and tech changed your life? Australians share their stories
World.content:
Technology is creeping into every facet of our lives, for better or for worse is in the eye of the beholder, but it is certainly here to stay.

Australians are grappling with the prospects of AI replacing jobs, privacy breaches, misinformation and digital exclusion, while also benefiting from technology designed to make everyday tasks easier.

We want to hear your stories and experiences in our live blog below, where you can also put your questions to cybersecurity expert Mihai Lazarescu from Curtin University and the ABC's AI reporter Cam Wilson.

World.title: Runner smashes half-marathon record, heads straight to the football
World.content:
Yomif Kejelcha has smashed the half-marathon world record, running a staggering 56 minutes and 51 seconds at the Media Maratón Ciudad de Buenos Aires in Argentina on Sunday.

The Ethiopian shaved 29 seconds off the previous mark of 57:20, which had been set by Uganda's Jacob Kiplimo in Lisbon in March.

Kejelcha's time and that of the record he just beat are still subject to ratification by World Athletics.

The Media Maratón Ciudad de Buenos Aires is a World Athletics Label road race and took place under favourable conditions of 6 degrees Celsius and with a slight breeze.

As ever, the super shoe gets plenty of post-race love from Yomif Kejelcha. (Instagram: @maratondebuenosaires)

Tadese Worku (59:20) and Bereket Nega (1:00:20) of Ethiopia completed the podium.

"I'm over the moon," Kejelcha told World Athletics.

"I'm super happy and right now I don't feel any tiredness. The travel from Ethiopia was too long and I was tired the first days here, but later I felt better and today I was full of beans.

"I had planned to run conservatively over the early stages, but I felt good and decided to give it my all.

"This time is unbelievable. I can't describe it with words.

"I now hope to try the Argentinian meat, which has a very good reputation, and this afternoon I have been invited to watch the River Plate-Vélez football match. I'm very grateful."

At the historic Estadio Monumental, Kejelcha showed off his new record on a new River Plate shirt, although would have been disappointed as Vélez Sarsfield came from 2-0 down to draw 2-2 in their Argentine Primera División clash. Clearly Los Millonarios don't share Kejelcha's stamina.

Yomif Kejelcha showed off his record on a new River Plate kit at at the Estadio Monumental. (Instagram: @maratondebuenosaires)

Kejelcha's time allowed him to reclaim the record, which he previously held with a 57:30 in Valencia in October 2024.

The time is slower than that recorded by Kiplimo in Barcelona last year, when he ran what he described as "the perfect race" to stop the clock in 56:42.

But World Athletics did not ratify that time because race conditions did not comply with their regulations.

Kejelcha ran the race at an average pace of 2 minutes and 42 seconds per kilometre — which would give you a 5km parkrun time of 13 minutes and 28 seconds.

However, as was the case when he became the second man to run an official race marathon in less than two hours in London last year, he negative split the race, running the second half faster than the first.

Super shoes won't be banned despite 'technological doping' claims Lord Sebastian Coe says World Athletics has a duty to "enable" super shoe development despite concerns.

He set out behind two pacemakers, going through the first 5km at 13:45, while the second 5km was run in 13:34.

His subsequent 5km split was a remarkable 13:22, with the Ethiopian holding that pace through the next 5km, running it in 13:23.

Last April at the London Marathon, the 29-year-old two-time Olympian ran 1:59:41, finishing second behind Kenya's Sabastian Sawe, who set the world record with a 1:59:30.

In the women's race, Ethiopia's Fotyen Tesfay stormed to victory in 1:03:57, comfortably beating her two Kenyan rivals Nelvin Jepkemboi (1:05:06) and Catherine Amanang'ole (1:05:11).

World.title: National rental prices rise to half average Australian income
World.content:
The average apartment now costs half of the average Australian income to rent, with prices exceeding the 30 per cent housing stress mark even for six-figure earners, according to a new report.

Housing advocacy group Everybody's Home has found renting a unit now costs more than half the median take-home pay of a single worker in every Australian capital city.

The 2026 Priced Out report found apartments on average nationally cost $614 per week, making up 56 per cent of the take-home income of someone earning $70,000 — close to Australia's median income of $74,100.

Everybody’s Home spokesperson Maiy Azize said this was a "crisis that continues to get worse for the country's renters".

"We now see people earning really high incomes are still spending more than a third of their income on rent. If you are earning $130,000 a year, you are still spending more than a third on rent," she said.

"If you are earning an average income between $70,000 and $80,000 and living in a capital city, you are spending two-thirds of your income to afford the average rent.

" We are seeing across the board renters can't avoid rental stress anywhere in the country, which is dire. "

The report found northern WA, the Gold Coast and Sydney were the three most expensive places to rent, followed by the Sunshine Coast and Perth.

"For a long time Sydney was ground zero for the crisis and it is still really bad news, shocking if you are a renter in Sydney," Ms Azize said.

"This year one of the most expensive – the most expensive capital city in the country is Perth and WA across the board has some really dire results.

"The Gold Coast has been surging every year that we have done this report and it is getting expensive to rent on the Gold Coast, even if you are earning $130,000 a year, you can't afford to rent on the Gold Coast. You would need to be in a couple or a multi-income family to make that work."

The report found, for someone earning $70,000, median Sydney rent would take 69 per cent of their weekly pay, while even Adelaide — the cheapest capital — would cost more than half.

Changes and recommendations

Changes to housing policy in this year's budget were predicted by the government to result in a median rental increase of $2 a week.

However, Ms Azize said rents had been surging by about 10 per cent every single year.

"I think it's a bit of an insult to people's intelligence when the industry comes out and says that any rent increases from here are going to be down to these changes," she said.

"Any renter in Australia knows that they get whacked with a huge rent increase every single year."

However, she said changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax were positive overall.

"They're changes that we've been pushing for a really long time," she said.

"They're really good news for anyone who wants to make the housing system fairer, especially those renters who are trying to save to buy.

"But what these results show us is that the federal government and state and territory governments especially now really need to turn their attention to renters and taking some steps to limit rent increases because there's really only so much that people can afford to pay."

Rental prices have been surging over the past few years. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The report recommends several recommendations, including the Australian government committing to build 940,000 public and community homes over the next 15 years; introducing limits on the number and amount of rent increases during a tenancy and ending no-grounds evictions.

"For the past four decades we've seen the federal government especially really step back from funding housing, from playing a role, and they're leaving it entirely to the private sector," Ms Azize said.

"We can see that over that same period renting has become incredibly expensive.

"So we need to see the government step back in.

"When you look around the world at the countries that are actually doing a good job of turning around their housing crisis or better yet avoiding it altogether, they're the countries where the government is playing a really big role in providing housing. They're not just leaving it to the private sector."

World.title: KPMG to cut almost 400 jobs after audit leaks scandal
World.content:
Accounting firm KPMG says it will cut 27 partners and about 360 staff from its local arm, and revamp its structure as it grapples with lower revenue from lost contracts following the audit leaks scandal.

The company's revenue fell from $2.28 billion the previous year, to $2.26 billion in the 2026 financial year, and KPMG Australia chief executive John Sams expected more revenue falls.

KPMG has been unable to retain most of its ongoing government contracts after allegations KPMG audit partners misused client data and then mishandled a whistleblower's complaint about it.

In March, Labor senator Deborah O'Neill shared with parliament a whistleblower's allegations that confidential board papers from Lendlease were used to support bids for major audit tenders for Westpac and Dexus.

And earlier this month, the firm's current and former partners were hauled before a federal inquiry probing why the firm allegedly shared client information and ignored the whistleblower's allegations when they first surfaced.

Five former KPMG partners were grilled in camera: Julian McPherson (left), Kim Lawry, Martin Sheppard, Andrew Yates and Eileen Hoggett. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The job cuts at KPMG's Australian arm were widely expected as the firm reportedly sought financial support from KPMG International to remain solvent.

PwC review doesn't stop conflicts of interest Former Telstra chief Ziggy Switkowski has unveiled a review of PwC, but it's unlikely this is the end of an intense probe of its business and the way other consulting firms manage conflicts of interest.

KPMG is one of the "big four" accounting firms, which have taken a hit to their bottom line from getting fewer ongoing government consulting contracts, following the earlier tax leaks controversy at PricewaterhouseCoopers.

Mr Sams said in a statement the firm was cutting 5 per cent of its workforce, primarily in its consulting arm, "in response to continued economic weakness, difficult market conditions and the impact of the firm's conduct and whistleblower matters".

This includes 27 partners and about 360 employees.

"This is not a decision that has been taken lightly, and we know it will have a very real impact on people," Mr Sams said.

With demand for consulting remaining weaker, "most of the roles affected will be in our consulting business".

"Changes to our business and the professional services landscape have also reduced the need for some roles in business services," he said.

"Our immediate focus is on treating everyone impacted with care, dignity and respect. We are providing practical support and making wellbeing support central to the process."

More job cuts could follow

The company will also restructure so that the firm's mid-market and private deals team joins deal advisory and infrastructure, while its advisory team joins consulting.

Accounting firms could be split post KPMG scandal Accounting firms could be asked to split their lucrative consulting services from their audit functions, under a shake up of the industry being consulted on by the federal government.

These changes would align KPMG Australia more closely with its global advisory services.

The firm would also begin consultation on "a small number of award-based roles".

Mr Sams said more cuts could follow.

"The changes announced today are an important step in the longer work of renewing and rebuilding our firm," he said.

The firm was undertaking "internal and external reviews" in the wake of the whistleblower's allegations, which he said "will be completed in the coming months".

"Their findings will inform the next phase of our action plan and help ensure we take all necessary action," he said.

KPMG has faced months of scrutiny over its handling of a whistleblower complaint. (ABC)

Mr Sams thanked the firm's staff after a "very challenging year".

"They [KPMG employees] continued to deliver outstanding work for more than 13,000 clients, while supporting one another through a difficult period for the firm," he said.

" Our total revenue was slightly lower than last year, and below our expectations. "

Consulting takes a hit, audit and tax divisions grow

While consulting took a hit, revenue grew in four out of five divisions, led by audit and assurance, up 11 per cent, and tax and legal, up 10.9 per cent.

"We also continued to invest significantly in technology and build our AI capability, helping our people work more effectively and deliver better outcomes for clients."

But the firm needed to "be clear about the outlook".

ABC Business Daily The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news.

"We expect difficult market conditions to continue in FY27 and beyond," Mr Sams said.

"Economic growth is expected to remain subdued until at least 2028, affecting client investment and extending decision-making timeframes," he said.

"The professional services sector is also changing rapidly as client expectations evolve, AI reshapes the way services are delivered, and government spending on consultants remains lower.

"We also recognise the challenges created by our own failings, and the work we must continue to do to rebuild trust.

"While these conditions are likely to persist, we remain focused on what we can control. We will continue to monitor performance closely, act when needed and consider carefully how the firm needs to be set up for the future."

World.title: Racehorse injury rules under spotlight after jockey's death
World.content:
A coroner has recommended more stringent reporting standards for racehorses returning from injury after the death of a French apprentice jockey in the New South Wales Central West more than four years ago.

Marina Morel died during track work at Gulgong Racecourse on February 8, 2022.

The 30-year-old was riding Lina's Choice when the mare suffered a catastrophic leg injury while galloping past the winning post.

Morel was thrown to the ground before Lina's Choice rolled on top of her, causing blunt-force injuries to her head, neck and chest.

Morel was flown to Westmead Hospital in Sydney, where she died four days later.

Lina's Choice was euthanased at the racecourse.

An inquest into Morel's death examined whether a previous injury suffered by Lina's Choice contributed to the fall, and whether the jockey's death could have been prevented.

Marina Morel started as an apprentice jockey at the Gulgong Turf Club in 2021. (ABC News)

Horse appropriately managed, coroner finds

Morel came to Australia from France in 2014 to pursue her ambition of becoming a professional jockey and was working for Gulgong trainer Brett Thompson at BKB Racing at the time of the incident.

Lina's Choice suffered a ligament injury to her right front leg in March 2021.

Veterinarian Jack Holman recommended Lina's Choice rest for nine to 12 months but the mare returned to work after six months and 22 days.

Despite the earlier return, Deputy State Coroner Derek Lee found the rest period was consistent with academic literature for similar injuries and that Thompson appropriately managed the mare's return to work.

"Mr Thompson followed his usual practice for the management of horses returning to work from injury for Lina's Choice, which was appropriate," he said.

Brett Thompson has been a professional trainer for more than 15 years. (Supplied: Brett Thompson Racing)

Judge Lee also found there were no signs of lameness during the mare's recovery and no evidence that the way she returned to training or racing predisposed her to stress fractures.

He said evidence suggested the mare was also performing "well above expectations" in the lead-up to the fatal fall.

After returning to work, Lina's Choice participated in a barrier trial and two races at Wellington and Dubbo before Ms Morel's death.

Six days before the fatal incident, equine chiropractor Gary Christou detected some chest stiffness, and recommended Lina's Choice be monitored.

Judge Lee found that response was appropriate and that the stiffness alone did not indicate a veterinary assessment was required.

The coroner found Lina's Choice had nevertheless developed stress fractures in her left humerus, which resulted in the catastrophic fracture during track work.

"There is no evidence that the previous injury was associated with the stress fractures," Judge Lee said.

Marina Morel trained as a jockey in Sydney and Mudgee. (Supplied)

Calls for stronger safeguards

Judge Lee made several recommendations aimed at strengthening Racing NSW's oversight of horses returning from injury or extended breaks from training and racing.

He recommended Racing NSW develop and publish clearer guidance about what constituted a "major orthopaedic injury" that took into account the nature and extent of an injury, the treatment required and how long a horse was unable or not recommended to train or race.

Judge Lee also called for broader reporting requirements for trainers, including matters that could affect a horse's performance even where it appeared to have recovered before being nominated for a race.

Racing NSW requires horses that have not raced or trialled for 150 days or more to undergo an official veterinary examination and barrier trial before returning to racing.

Judge Lee called for that requirement to be formalised in a published policy and for Racing NSW to explore whether the 150-day threshold could be reduced, potentially to 60 days.

Morel's family attended the hearing remotely from France and had the assistance of an interpreter. Her mother wiped tears from her eyes at the conclusion of the hearing.

World.title: 'Disappointed' Hird congratulates McVeigh ahead of Bombers coach call
World.content:
Mark McVeigh appears set to be unveiled as Essendon's next senior coach, with fellow applicant James Hird congratulating his former teammate on the impending appointment.

Bombers legend Hird had been vocal in expressing his desire to return for another stint as coach, after Brad Scott was sacked in May.

Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham and Adelaide assistant Murray Davis were also in the mix.

But McVeigh, an assistant to Dean Cox at Sydney, is reportedly on the verge of being appointed, with an announcement expected as soon as tomorrow.

Mark McVeigh is in the box seat to be offered the Bombers job. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Interim coach Dean Solomon hands over the reins after the Bombers (2-21) completed the worst season in club history with a 10-point defeat to Port Adelaide on Sunday.

"Firstly, congratulations to Mark. He's a great friend of mine and I'm very proud of him that he's going to be named the coach, so good on him," Hird said on Nine yesterday night.

"From a personal point of view, it's very disappointing. I'm disappointed. I put my heart and soul into the effort, but obviously fell short and that's the way it goes."

Hird indicated he was yet to hear an official decision from Essendon, but said "maybe that's coming".

The 53-year-old ruled out returning to the Bombers in a different role, but said he still had the passion to coach.

James Hird, Dean Solomon and Mark McVeigh together in 2022 when they were all at the Giants. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Hird is director of coaching with VFL club Port Melbourne.

"We have a finals series to play," Hird said.

"We'll see what plays out at the end of the year with some other clubs who have contacted me and we'll see what happens."

McVeigh is reportedly set to present to the Essendon board again today, with an announcement imminent.

The 45-year-old played 232 games for Essendon and was one of the 34 players suspended over the club's devastating drugs saga, when Hird was coach.

McVeigh currently serves as Sydney's defensive coach, but could leave the club immediately to play a role in the Bombers' end-of-season exit meetings and list management decisions.

The second-placed Swans are preparing for a finals campaign while bracing for more fallout from the scandal that has rocked the club.

"That's one thing this football club's done well for a long period of time … be ready for the unexpected or if something does arise," Sydney coach Cox said last week about the potential of losing McVeigh to the Bombers.

"We've had those meetings [and] discussions. We're really clear on what will happen if he was or wasn't to get the [Essendon] position."

Two-time Essendon premiership champion and former captain Hird first took over as Bombers coach in 2010.

He was suspended for the 2014 season amid the fallout from the drugs saga, returned as coach in 2015 and resigned in August that year.

Hird had garnered plenty of support from Bombers fans in his latest bid to return as coach, after he narrowly missed out when Scott was appointed in 2022.
