World.title: Sugarcane farmers question APVMA paraquat ban
World.content:
Cane growers say a decision by the chemical regulator to ban them using controversial herbicide paraquat could lead to worse outcomes for the environment while they search for an alternative.

The Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA) released its review of paraquat and diquat in June, which significantly reduced the application rates allowed in most broadacre crops.

Chemical regulator approves paraquat use The Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority concludes its nearly 30-year review of the controversial but popular herbicide.

But sugarcane growers were given two years to phase out its use completely before the chemical would no longer be registered for use on their crop.

The APVMA said the review assessed each paraquat use pattern separately against current environmental safety standards and found an unacceptable risk to birds foraging in cane growing areas.

But Canegrowers chief executive Dan Galligan said growers feared the move could lead to worse environmental outcomes than those the regulator was trying to prevent.

"The lack of alternatives means there's a lot of stress and concern," he said.

" What it means is usually changing farming systems to something that's more expensive or sometimes even worse in terms of environmental outcomes. "

Bird health concerns

Paraquat is used early in the planting of the crop because it kills weeds quickly but does not linger in the soil, allowing the young cane to get established.

Mr Galligan said Sugar Research Australia was looking at suitable alternatives, but there was no timeline on when that would be delivered.

Dan Galligan is concerned about what the APVMA's decision will mean for sugarcane farmers. (Supplied: Canegrowers)

In the interim, he said changes to the farming system to achieve the same results would be "dramatic".

"Effectively, we're going to have to use more herbicides and possibly increase our sediment loss on farms, which is not really what we want to try and do," he said.

The APVMA acknowledged growers may need to change weed management practices, but said alternatives and the economic impacts of those changes were matters for growers, advisers, industry and state governments to manage.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the regulator said the use pattern in sugarcane posed acute and chronic exposure risks to birds foraging in treated areas.

"The supported sugarcane use patterns did not meet the required environmental safety standards," it said.

"Therefore [those use patterns] were not retained on approved labels," a spokesperson for the regulator said.

Adrian Crema grows sugarcane and bananas near Tully in Far North Queensland. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

But growers in Far North Queensland dispute the conclusion.

Tully farmer Bryce MacDonald said the APVMA's decision was "bizarre".

"I've never seen any bird die from paraquat," he said.

"In fact, I reckon there's more birds around than there ever was, and some other people have voiced that to me as well."

Nearby sugarcane and banana farmer Adrian Crema said growers did not understand why the risks could not be managed.

"I personally have never seen a dead bird as a result of spraying paraquat in a cane paddock," he said.

Without paraquat, the sugarcane industry will need to make changes. (ABC News: Yasmine Wright Gittins)

Growers using paraquat are able to adopt a minimal till farming system, which means they disturb the soil less and reduce run-off to the Great Barrier Reef.

"How are we going to grow sugarcane without paraquat?" Mr Crema said.

"Do they want us to go back to cultivating … to use more heavy residual chemicals which are more toxic to fish?

"There are a lot of confused cane farmers out there right now who want answers."

Approved uses

Paraquat has previously been linked to an increased risk of Parkinson's disease, although the APVMA's review found the evidence did not support a link between exposure through approved uses and the disease.

There is no timeline for when an alternative to paraquat for sugarcane will be available. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

Australia's peak body for Parkinson's disease disputes that finding.

Neurologists say warnings met with silence by chemical watchdog Dozens of neurologists are concerned "real world" human studies linking paraquat to Parkinson's disease are being overlooked as the regulator weighs up the future of the controversial weed killer.

Under the new restrictions, sugarcane farmers are still able to use paraquat on farm for fallow crops, headlands and fire breaks in the same paddock, but not on the sugarcane crop itself.

Mr MacDonald said that only added to the confusion and farmers should be trusted to use the product by the label.

"Farmers don't waste money. They don't waste chemicals. They use them conservatively," he said.

The APVMA said it did not assess crops based solely on where they were grown, and therefore different crops could receive different regulatory outcomes even when they were grown in similar regions.

World.title: Youth hub for vulnerable children at risk of closing
World.content:
A centre that keeps children off the streets, with a focus on tackling youth crime in one of Australia's most disadvantaged regional areas, is again at risk of closing its doors.

Gippsland Youth Spaces in Morwell has been a second home for at-risk and marginalised young people in the Latrobe Valley, in Victoria's east, for several years, providing free meals, laundry services, safe places to relax, social activities, training and pathways to re-engage with school and employment.

It was set up by the Labor government in 2021, but board member Jewel Burchell-Robins says it has had to beg for funding each year to continue.

She says if the youth space programs are shut down, at-risk young people will fall through the gaps.

"It's not only anti-social behaviour that we'll see, but also increases, unfortunately, in suicide or harmful and risky behaviours from young people because they don't have a safety net," she said.

The Latrobe Valley experiences high rates of youth crime and anti-social behaviour.

Last year, almost 2,500 incidents were committed by people aged between 12 and 29.

The youth unemployment rate is sitting at 10.2 per cent.

Jewel Burchell-Robins says she has already seen the impact of funding cuts at Gippsland Youth Space. (ABC News: Danielle Kutchel)

"The young people in our region don't have anywhere else to turn, and we have become a massive safety net for so many young people," Ms Jewel Burchell-Robins said.

She said that when the service began, it offered a full suite of programs to engage children.

"Having to cut back to the bare necessities and barely scraping by with such a shoestring budget has been a little bit heartbreaking, to say the least."

Ms Burchell-Robins worries about what the closure of Youth Space would mean for young people in the Latrobe Valley. (ABC News: Danielle Kutchel)

Dwindling offerings

Gippsland Youth Spaces originally operated in three locations, at Morwell, Wellington Shire and East Gippsland.

But now just Morwell remains.

The organisation has been surviving on grant money and donations from local businesses for several years, as ongoing government funding has slowly reduced.

Morwell car dealership owner Ray Massaro has been supporting the youth organisation through generous donations for several years.

Ray Massaro has been supporting Latrobe Youth Space financially for several years and says he wants to see the state government contribute more. (ABC News: Danielle Kutchel)

"They're not [in] gangs; these are kids that are bonding. You can see it. They're bonding and teaching and learning off one another … they've found their little tribe," he said.

" I'm passionate about supporting them, but I don't have that money. I'm holding on, treading water; eventually I can't tread water any longer. "

Youth Spaces executive officer Trevor Carstein said the service's days were numbered if more funding cannot be secured.

"It's great to have those networks and those partnerships [but] they're not life-saving," he said.

Trevor Carstein says the organisation is in a "dire" situation. (ABC News: Danielle Kutchel)

To recoup funds, the organisation has sold off its fleet of buses, which were used to transport young people to and from external activities.

External programs like camps and excursions have all been cut for the foreseeable future.

An annual trip to Parliament House to teach young people leadership skills through direct advocacy with politicians has also been cancelled.

But Mr Carstein said those cut-backs only buy the organisation "pieces of time".

"My projections are [we have] anywhere from 10 to 12 months," he said.

"It's dire because there's 2,300 young people currently signed up,

"That means we put those very vulnerable youth back out into nothing."

He said to be sustainable, the organisation needed about $500,000 a year to operate one centre with correct staff ratios and quality programs.

"This is a necessity for the Latrobe Valley."

Some of the young people supported by Latrobe Youth Space. (ABC News: Danielle Kutchel)

A spokesperson for the state government said more than $9 million has been provided to Gippsland Youth Spaces since it was established.

"This investment supported the organisation to build a more sustainable funding model, with the expectation it would operate independently beyond government funding," the spokesperson said.

"We continue to work with Gippsland Youth Space to identify further opportunities for a viable operating pathway for 2027 and beyond."

World.title: In the shadow of a palace, Beijing’s uncles defy a swimming ban to cool off
World.content:
WorldAsiaChina relations In the shadow of a palace, Beijing’s uncles defy a swimming ban to cool off Lisa Visentin August 24, 2026 — 11:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beijing: It’s just gone past 2.30pm on a sweltering August afternoon, and Wang Jianbao is gingerly descending the steps to the canal that runs past the Summer Palace. The 92-year-old comes here every day from crisp March through to chilly November, riding his tricycle for 40 minutes through Beijing’s western suburbs for a dip in the shadow of the UNESCO heritage-listed grounds. He’s not the only one. The unsanctioned swimming spot is not so much a secret, but a local haunt that doubles as an unofficial men’s shed for a regular group of seniors. Equipped with caps, goggles and floaties, they come here for the community as much as the exercise. Men take a dip in the canal just outside the Summer Palace grounds in Beijing. Fairfax Media Like the salty sea dogs who plunge into Sydney’s beaches each morning, a leathery set of Beijing uncles has been swimming here for decades.



“I am the oldest here. I have nothing to do at home, and it’s good physical exercise,” Wang says. He has swum in the area since his 20s, after coming to Beijing to find work as a bricklayer. No one knows the lore better than him. Years ago, when authorities tried to ban swimming in the canal, the locals staged a revolt after one swimmer was arrested and handcuffed, he says. The unsanctioned swimming spot doubles as an unofficial men’s shed for a group of regulars. Fairfax Media “All other swimmers sat down in front of the security guards’ vehicle so it couldn’t move. We blocked the vehicle until 11pm. “I told the head of security guard that the Summer Palace belonged to the people, not you: ‘Do you think you can stop people from swimming simply by installing a warning sign?’”



And with that triumphant anecdote complete, Wang slips into the water and sets off on a 400-metre paddle upstream. On this day, he is one of about 50 swimmers, most of them retired men, though a few women have come to cool off, too. The crowds are bigger than usual because the school holidays have coincided with the blistering dog days of summer called “sanfu” in China – the 10- to 20-day stretch where even cities in the country’s north such as Beijing bake in 35-degree-plus heat. Wang Jianbao, 92, rides his tricycle to the canal every day from March to November. Fairfax Media In the capital, the summer months see the public waterways transform into popular and free open-air swimming pools, often in defiance of no-swimming signs. This spot is just outside the south gate of the Summer Palace, in north-west Beijing. World.title: ‘The worst actress that ever lived’: Fleet St has the knives out for Harry and Meghan and this won’t end well
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family Opinion ‘The worst actress that ever lived’: Fleet St has the knives out for Harry and Meghan and this won’t end well Gary Nunn Contributor August 24, 2026 — 11:36am

August 24, 2026 — 11:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Already, the knives are being sharpened. Days after Harry and Meghan’s shock announcement of a UK return, the notorious British media is baying for blood. Here in the UK, as elsewhere, there is confusion over the return of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex after six years. Why take on this extraordinary pressure of moving back? Especially when there is little sign of any thaw in the hostility that they say drove them away? There is no apparent reconciliation with their family – King Charles was himself only informed of their return a few days ago. Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex meet people after viewing the floral tributes for the late Queen Elizabeth II outside Windsor Castle, in 2022. AP Harry just lost a major case against the British tabloids and, along with six other high-profile claimants, must pay an eye-watering £9.54 million ($18.16 million) towards the Daily Mail publisher’s legal costs. Even Meghan’s new acting role in Netflix series The Gentleman seems less than certain, as reports say it has been withdrawn “due to a public backlash”.



The UK public are not clamouring for the couple’s return to the fold. Polling by YouGov for The Sunday Times found that 51 per cent would oppose the duke and duchess returning as full-time working royals. Sky News polling found that 44 per cent opposed their return. The Sun headlined with one readers’ reaction that it was a “publicity stunt”, and amid a cost of living crisis 80 per cent of the tabloid’s readers say the Sussexes should fund their own security. Brits are, at best, divided by their return. As a British-born journalist who has written for the UK tabloid Harry sued – The Sun – and other Murdoch titles, I should be Harry’s bête noire. Yet I admire him. Duke and Duchess of Sussex, Harry and Meghan, at the Royal Children’s Hospital on a recent visit to Australia. The Age Harry impressively fought journalistic bullies, demonstrating in previous successful court cases that British tabloids were willing to drive people to paranoia through their inappropriate surveillance. The prince and his wife were two of the few people who had the money, profile and determination to challenge such unethical behaviour. Good for them. I don’t blame them for demanding privacy, then selling memoirs and Netflix shows telling their story on their own terms and making money for their own children. To me, they got the last laugh.



Except there’s nothing funny about how short our memories are. Have we learnt nothing from Diana’s death, The Leveson Inquiry into phone hacking or the tragedy of the bullying of Charlotte Dawson? Another perspective Opinion

Royal family It’s obvious what’s behind Harry and Meghan’s return to Blighty. It’s not to reunite with Will and Kate Kate Halfpenny Regular columnist Tabloid hounding and spiteful reporting ruins lives – and kills women. The pen is always mightier than the sword. Yet the UK tabloids remain blood-stained red tops. Have we forgotten Earl Spencer’s eulogy about his sister? “I always believed the press would kill her in the end… [they] have blood on their hands.” Can anyone truly blame Harry for fighting against such dark history being repeated with his wife? Have we forgotten, also, that the 2012 Leveson Inquiry, following the News International phone hacking scandal, found a UK press culture that ignored its own ethical code in the pursuit of stories through covert surveillance?



The less cynical view for the Sussex’s surprise UK return is one you won’t read much now the couple’s name is dirt on Fleet Street. They’re returning, perhaps, because they want the best life for their kids – educationally, financially and familially. The fantastic Invictus Games for wounded soldiers, founded by Harry, will be in Birmingham next year. And there’s a non-financial reason to ask for state-funded security: In Britain, private security staff cannot lawfully carry guns, pepper spray, batons or tasers, no matter what you pay them. Terrorist group al-Qaeda and other extremists have already threatened Harry, who twice served in Afghanistan, with murder. And how much bile will be stirred before Meghan’s life, too, is endangered via incitement to hatred? Especially at a time of rising British nationalism and violent jingoism. And it isn’t just the tabloids who pile on. Writing for The Times this weekend, columnist Camilla Long claimed the couple were tearing up their principles to “come back to a country they hate,” due to a “resentment and disappointment at the snobbery and structural racism that they think defines Britain”. She argues Harry wants to “destroy the monarchy” and that Meghan is “the worst actress that ever lived”.

World.title: Bullying case against Liverpool mayor ends
World.content:
A bullying case brought against Liverpool Mayor Ned Mannoun by his council’s unionised staff has been discontinued, with both parties accepting an end to the case after Mannoun read out a statement affirming his commitment to his council’s media policies.

The United Services Union, which represents about 600 workers at the council, lodged a claim in the Industrial Relations Commission in May this year after the mayor posted a Facebook video where he claimed the union had “bullied” the council’s deputy mayor, and included photos of union members taking industrial action. It claimed in the complaint that Mannoun’s actions placed members “in a collective position of risk and harm”, in an apparent “attempt to stoke community resentment against the union”. Mannoun rejected the allegations.

Liverpool Mayor Ned Mannoun arrives at the Industrial Relations Commission in Parramatta in May. Kate Geraghty

After several conciliation meetings, the union and mayor came to an agreement at the commission in late June.

“I affirm my commitment to the Liverpool City Council media policy,” he said at the Industrial Relations Commission hearing. He specifically affirmed clauses of the policy that require councillors engaging with the media to resolve personal differences privately and prohibit communication that could bring the council into disrepute.

World.title: A St Kilda dining icon will soon get a fresh start from a rising restaurant star
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outComing soon A St Kilda dining icon will soon get a fresh start from a rising restaurant star “St Kilda is the only place that makes sense for us.” Superstar chef Ellie Bouhadana, formerly of Hope St Radio, will open her first restaurant in a Barkly Street site that comes with 28 years of memories. Dani Valent August 24, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After a successful summer seafood pop-up at Stokehouse’s beachfront kiosk in St Kilda, and recent months cooking and eating her way around Morocco, Italy and the Netherlands, ex-Hope St Radio chef Ellie Bouhadana is launching her own restaurant. Dafina Seaside Grill will open in the storied Claypots site in St Kilda in early 2027, adding extra verve to an exciting time for the suburb, with Andrew McConnell’s Trader House taking over Stokehouse in spring and new developments happening on down-at-heel Fitzroy Street. Chef Ellie Bouhadana and husband Rapha Tamir will open Dafina Seaside Grill in the former Claypots site. Simon Schluter “St Kilda is the only place that makes sense for us,” says Bouhadana, who lives locally and is working alongside husband Rapha Tamir. “My parents brought me to Acland Street when I was a kid, for ice-cream, cakes and Luna Park. We came to Claypots, too. We couldn’t let it be gutted, maybe turned into a KFC.” Tamir’s grandparents came for regular Friday spaghetti marinara lunches and he remembers long meals under the courtyard’s bougainvillea. “It felt celebratory, with a casual, affordable approach to seafood,” he says.



1 / 3 The enormous octopus that once hung from Claypots’ ceiling. Erin Slattery 2 / 3 The bar of Claypots in January 2007, with seahorse door handles visible (right). Erin Slattery 3 / 3 Ellie Bouhadana and Rapha Tamir with the quirky Claypots doors. Simon Schluter Previous Slide Next Slide Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Renan Goksin opened Claypots in 1998, serving gumbos, chilli crab and simple grills. The atmosphere was bohemian, musical and charmingly chaotic. Neelam Sami took over in 2016 and Claypots remained a grungy slice of old-time St Kilda until it closed in February. Goksin has pointed out special features to the restaurant’s new custodians, who will retain some in their new fit-out. “He told me the bar is made from stolen pieces of the old St Kilda pier, so that’s non-negotiable,” says Tamir. Canvas sails are suspended from rope pulleys as de facto air-conditioning. Carved seahorses double as door handles. Walls are stuck with faux Sumerian tablets etched with cuneiform (the world’s oldest-known writing system), clustered around one that is apparently real. An enormous pressed tin octopus hangs from the ceiling – a head-scraping hazard, but also an icon. “We like the quirks and the energy but we’ll do our own thing,” says Tamir. “It’s going to be Ellie’s food, but we do feel attracted to St Kilda institutions and the Jewish immigrant story here.”



It will be the debut restaurant of chef Ellie Bouhadana (right), in partnership with Rapha Tamir. Simon Schluter Dafina is named for a Sephardi Jewish slow-cooked meat-and-grain dish that speaks to Bouhadana’s Jewish Moroccan heritage. “It’s a claypot cooked overnight in the communal fire, in the embers of the dying coals,” she says. In Jewish culture, foods are often slowly cooked on Friday night’s cooling fire, ready for the Sabbath when cooking is not allowed. “We’ll also do Moroccan-style brochette [kebabs], whole fish with cumin and garlic, lamb chops, dips and salad, lots of oil and vinegar, food for swiping with fresh-baked flatbreads.” Related Article How to make one of Melbourne’s favourite focaccias at home Bouhadana first came to attention for her lockdown pop-ups, including pasta parties and sandwiches sold from her driveway. She was the first chef at Collingwood wine-slash-listening bar Hope St Radio in 2021, and took the restaurant to a hat in the 2023 Age Good Food Guide. She left in 2024 and released her cookbook, Ellie’s Table, continuing with events and catering in Australia and overseas.



“I’ve been nervous to commit to a site,” she says. “But what I love about pop-ups is working with interesting people who become friends as we explore each other’s food and hosting style. It’s exciting to think about sharing my own hospitality. There’s a renewal in St Kilda, and we’re excited to put down roots and be part of that.” Dafina Seaside Grill opens early 2027 at 213 Barkly Street, St Kilda.

World.title: Dockers primed for finals despite loss while Eagles sweat on Harley tackle
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Dockers primed for finals despite loss while Eagles sweat on Harley tackle Paddy Sweeney Nine Sports Presenter August 24, 2026 — 11:21am

August 24, 2026 — 11:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to the Western Watercooler, where we digest the talking points from the weekend’s games – and the highlights, frustrations and silver linings WA footy fans can cling to as the season progresses. The Dockers ended their regular season with a 37-point loss, the heaviest of the season, against the rampaging Carlton. Harley Reid could be in trouble for a sling tackle while Brennan Cox could miss games with injury. Getty Images While they suffered their third defeat of the season, Fremantle had nothing to gain and clearly had one eye on finals, resting and managing players’ game-time. Meanwhile, the Eagles finished their 2026 campaign with an eleventh-straight defeat.



West Coast were outplayed from start to finish by the Hawks and while there’s been improvement this season, the year fell away in disappointing circumstances in the back half. Fremantle Dockers What went right? The home and away season. Fremantle compiled a 23-game stretch which stands above all in their 32-years. The minor premiership, for the second time.



A new benchmark of 14 straight wins. A perfect home record from 11 Optus Stadium games. On top of this, and arguably the most important part, has been the health of the list. As the saying goes, “the best ability is your availability”. Justin Longmuir has more often than not been able to choose close to his best side every week.



It’s built confidence in themselves, teammates and system, the year to date is proof. Fremantle enter finals as flag favourites – a position they thoroughly deserve. View post on X What went wrong? Brennan Cox’s calf issue. Injury and suspension were the two factors the Dockers were trying to avoid against the Blues.



Cox’s first-quarter setback is set to sideline him for Fremantle’s first final. This contributed to the Dockers conceding their biggest score of the season, 118. Cox has had a number of setbacks this season. He only returned from multiple games with a knee issue recently while also missed games mid-year due to injury. Silver lining: Stars waiting to return.



Jye Amiss, Sam Switkowski, Heath Chapman and Murphy Reid will all be ready for a qualifying final against Hawthorn. You can bet Justin Longmuir won’t be managing players’ minutes like he did against the Blues. Hayden Young (66 per cent), Luke Jackson (72 per cent), Shai Bolton (73 per cent), Andrew Brayshaw, Alex Pearce (75 per cent) and Caleb Serong (76 per cent) were all closely monitored and well below their average time on ground for the season. West Coast Eagles What went right? West Coast held off Hawthorn’s quest for a top-three finish.



The Hawks were gunning for third spot, setting them up for a qualifying final against a now decimated Sydney outfit with several Swans stars seasons over due to ongoing alleged sexual assault allegations. The Eagles found themselves down by 47 points in the second quarter with Hawthorn on track to leapfrog the third placed Brisbane. However, aided by wet and slippery conditions, the Eagles did enough to prevent the Hawks rising up the ladder, meaning they’ll begin their premiership quest with the toughest of assignments; Fremantle in Perth. What went wrong? Harley Reid’s sling tackle. The star’s fourth quarter incident, where Jai Newcombe’s head slammed into the turf, will most certainly attract attention from the MRO, potentially forcing Reid into a delayed start to 2027.



One of the Eagles improvements this year has been the ability to use handball to help a fast-paced transition. View post on X But yesterday, West Coast were handball happy, and in wet conditions, which only meant more pressure from the Hawks. The Eagles had 42 handballs to only 22 kicks in the opening term. Silver lining: Milan Murdock.



The mature-age recruit capped a brilliant debut season with one of his best performances of the year. The 26 year-old booted the Eagles first two goals and finished with an equal career-high three majors, to go with 24 touches. Murdock has become a mainstay in the side through his hard work, ability to provide pressure, play a role and hit the scoreboard. The East Fremantle product played 20 games in his first AFL season, earning a two-year extension.

After that, it rose in a mixture of $5000 and $10,000 increments. The home sold just above its reserve of $850,000. The underbidder was an investor, and the sellers recently retired and moved to Queensland.



Related Article Victoria residential property The Melbourne neighbourhoods where home buyers can find the biggest discounts “Properties that are around the $1 million price point are generally performing quite well,” Ray White Mount Waverley selling agent Jacob Biviano said. “The ones that are a little bit more tricky at the moment are the ones that are a higher price. “Homes that are ready to go, that are fairly new or don’t need much renovation work are still performing really well.” He described the market broadly as “consistent”. “We are obviously not in amazing times at the moment,” he said. “We are finding it quite consistent.”

World.title: ‘The worst actress that ever lived’: Fleet St has the knives out for Harry and Meghan and this won’t end well
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family Opinion ‘The worst actress that ever lived’: Fleet St has the knives out for Harry and Meghan and this won’t end well Gary Nunn Contributor August 24, 2026 — 11:36am

August 24, 2026 — 11:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Already, the knives are being sharpened. Days after Harry and Meghan’s shock announcement of a UK return, the notorious British media is baying for blood. Here in the UK, as elsewhere, there is confusion over the return of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex after six years. Why take on this extraordinary pressure of moving back? Especially when there is little sign of any thaw in the hostility that they say drove them away? There is no apparent reconciliation with their family – King Charles was himself only informed of their return a few days ago. Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex meet people after viewing the floral tributes for the late Queen Elizabeth II outside Windsor Castle, in 2022. AP Harry just lost a major case against the British tabloids and, along with six other high-profile claimants, must pay an eye-watering £9.54 million ($18.16 million) towards the Daily Mail publisher’s legal costs. Even Meghan’s new acting role in Netflix series The Gentleman seems less than certain, as reports say it has been withdrawn “due to a public backlash”.



The UK public are not clamouring for the couple’s return to the fold. Polling by YouGov for The Sunday Times found that 51 per cent would oppose the duke and duchess returning as full-time working royals. Sky News polling found that 44 per cent opposed their return. The Sun headlined with one readers’ reaction that it was a “publicity stunt”, and amid a cost of living crisis 80 per cent of the tabloid’s readers say the Sussexes should fund their own security. Brits are, at best, divided by their return. As a British-born journalist who has written for the UK tabloid Harry sued – The Sun – and other Murdoch titles, I should be Harry’s bête noire. Yet I admire him. Duke and Duchess of Sussex, Harry and Meghan, at the Royal Children’s Hospital on a recent visit to Australia. The Age Harry impressively fought journalistic bullies, demonstrating in previous successful court cases that British tabloids were willing to drive people to paranoia through their inappropriate surveillance. The prince and his wife were two of the few people who had the money, profile and determination to challenge such unethical behaviour. Good for them. I don’t blame them for demanding privacy, then selling memoirs and Netflix shows telling their story on their own terms and making money for their own children. To me, they got the last laugh.



Except there’s nothing funny about how short our memories are. Have we learnt nothing from Diana’s death, The Leveson Inquiry into phone hacking or the tragedy of the bullying of Charlotte Dawson? Another perspective Opinion

Royal family It’s obvious what’s behind Harry and Meghan’s return to Blighty. It’s not to reunite with Will and Kate Kate Halfpenny Regular columnist Tabloid hounding and spiteful reporting ruins lives – and kills women. The pen is always mightier than the sword. Yet the UK tabloids remain blood-stained red tops. Have we forgotten Earl Spencer’s eulogy about his sister? “I always believed the press would kill her in the end… [they] have blood on their hands.” Can anyone truly blame Harry for fighting against such dark history being repeated with his wife? Have we forgotten, also, that the 2012 Leveson Inquiry, following the News International phone hacking scandal, found a UK press culture that ignored its own ethical code in the pursuit of stories through covert surveillance?



The less cynical view for the Sussex’s surprise UK return is one you won’t read much now the couple’s name is dirt on Fleet Street. They’re returning, perhaps, because they want the best life for their kids – educationally, financially and familially. The fantastic Invictus Games for wounded soldiers, founded by Harry, will be in Birmingham next year. And there’s a non-financial reason to ask for state-funded security: In Britain, private security staff cannot lawfully carry guns, pepper spray, batons or tasers, no matter what you pay them. Terrorist group al-Qaeda and other extremists have already threatened Harry, who twice served in Afghanistan, with murder. And how much bile will be stirred before Meghan’s life, too, is endangered via incitement to hatred? Especially at a time of rising British nationalism and violent jingoism. And it isn’t just the tabloids who pile on. Writing for The Times this weekend, columnist Camilla Long claimed the couple were tearing up their principles to “come back to a country they hate,” due to a “resentment and disappointment at the snobbery and structural racism that they think defines Britain”. She argues Harry wants to “destroy the monarchy” and that Meghan is “the worst actress that ever lived”.

World.title: Bullying case against Liverpool mayor ends
World.content:
A bullying case brought against Liverpool Mayor Ned Mannoun by his council’s unionised staff has been discontinued, with both parties accepting an end to the case after Mannoun read out a statement affirming his commitment to his council’s media policies.

The United Services Union, which represents about 600 workers at the council, lodged a claim in the Industrial Relations Commission in May this year after the mayor posted a Facebook video where he claimed the union had “bullied” the council’s deputy mayor, and included photos of union members taking industrial action. It claimed in the complaint that Mannoun’s actions placed members “in a collective position of risk and harm”, in an apparent “attempt to stoke community resentment against the union”. Mannoun rejected the allegations.

Liverpool Mayor Ned Mannoun arrives at the Industrial Relations Commission in Parramatta in May. Kate Geraghty

After several conciliation meetings, the union and mayor came to an agreement at the commission in late June.

“I affirm my commitment to the Liverpool City Council media policy,” he said at the Industrial Relations Commission hearing. He specifically affirmed clauses of the policy that require councillors engaging with the media to resolve personal differences privately and prohibit communication that could bring the council into disrepute.

World.title: A St Kilda dining icon will soon get a fresh start from a rising restaurant star
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outComing soon A St Kilda dining icon will soon get a fresh start from a rising restaurant star “St Kilda is the only place that makes sense for us.” Superstar chef Ellie Bouhadana, formerly of Hope St Radio, will open her first restaurant in a Barkly Street site that comes with 28 years of memories. Dani Valent August 24, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After a successful summer seafood pop-up at Stokehouse’s beachfront kiosk in St Kilda, and recent months cooking and eating her way around Morocco, Italy and the Netherlands, ex-Hope St Radio chef Ellie Bouhadana is launching her own restaurant. Dafina Seaside Grill will open in the storied Claypots site in St Kilda in early 2027, adding extra verve to an exciting time for the suburb, with Andrew McConnell’s Trader House taking over Stokehouse in spring and new developments happening on down-at-heel Fitzroy Street. Chef Ellie Bouhadana and husband Rapha Tamir will open Dafina Seaside Grill in the former Claypots site. Simon Schluter “St Kilda is the only place that makes sense for us,” says Bouhadana, who lives locally and is working alongside husband Rapha Tamir. “My parents brought me to Acland Street when I was a kid, for ice-cream, cakes and Luna Park. We came to Claypots, too. We couldn’t let it be gutted, maybe turned into a KFC.” Tamir’s grandparents came for regular Friday spaghetti marinara lunches and he remembers long meals under the courtyard’s bougainvillea. “It felt celebratory, with a casual, affordable approach to seafood,” he says.



1 / 3 The enormous octopus that once hung from Claypots’ ceiling. Erin Slattery 2 / 3 The bar of Claypots in January 2007, with seahorse door handles visible (right). Erin Slattery 3 / 3 Ellie Bouhadana and Rapha Tamir with the quirky Claypots doors. Simon Schluter Previous Slide Next Slide Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Renan Goksin opened Claypots in 1998, serving gumbos, chilli crab and simple grills. The atmosphere was bohemian, musical and charmingly chaotic. Neelam Sami took over in 2016 and Claypots remained a grungy slice of old-time St Kilda until it closed in February. Goksin has pointed out special features to the restaurant’s new custodians, who will retain some in their new fit-out. “He told me the bar is made from stolen pieces of the old St Kilda pier, so that’s non-negotiable,” says Tamir. Canvas sails are suspended from rope pulleys as de facto air-conditioning. Carved seahorses double as door handles. Walls are stuck with faux Sumerian tablets etched with cuneiform (the world’s oldest-known writing system), clustered around one that is apparently real. An enormous pressed tin octopus hangs from the ceiling – a head-scraping hazard, but also an icon. “We like the quirks and the energy but we’ll do our own thing,” says Tamir. “It’s going to be Ellie’s food, but we do feel attracted to St Kilda institutions and the Jewish immigrant story here.”



It will be the debut restaurant of chef Ellie Bouhadana (right), in partnership with Rapha Tamir. Simon Schluter Dafina is named for a Sephardi Jewish slow-cooked meat-and-grain dish that speaks to Bouhadana’s Jewish Moroccan heritage. “It’s a claypot cooked overnight in the communal fire, in the embers of the dying coals,” she says. In Jewish culture, foods are often slowly cooked on Friday night’s cooling fire, ready for the Sabbath when cooking is not allowed. “We’ll also do Moroccan-style brochette [kebabs], whole fish with cumin and garlic, lamb chops, dips and salad, lots of oil and vinegar, food for swiping with fresh-baked flatbreads.” Related Article How to make one of Melbourne’s favourite focaccias at home Bouhadana first came to attention for her lockdown pop-ups, including pasta parties and sandwiches sold from her driveway. She was the first chef at Collingwood wine-slash-listening bar Hope St Radio in 2021, and took the restaurant to a hat in the 2023 Age Good Food Guide. She left in 2024 and released her cookbook, Ellie’s Table, continuing with events and catering in Australia and overseas.



“I’ve been nervous to commit to a site,” she says. “But what I love about pop-ups is working with interesting people who become friends as we explore each other’s food and hosting style. It’s exciting to think about sharing my own hospitality. There’s a renewal in St Kilda, and we’re excited to put down roots and be part of that.” Dafina Seaside Grill opens early 2027 at 213 Barkly Street, St Kilda.

World.title: Dockers primed for finals despite loss while Eagles sweat on Harley tackle
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Dockers primed for finals despite loss while Eagles sweat on Harley tackle Paddy Sweeney Nine Sports Presenter August 24, 2026 — 11:21am

August 24, 2026 — 11:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to the Western Watercooler, where we digest the talking points from the weekend’s games – and the highlights, frustrations and silver linings WA footy fans can cling to as the season progresses. The Dockers ended their regular season with a 37-point loss, the heaviest of the season, against the rampaging Carlton. Harley Reid could be in trouble for a sling tackle while Brennan Cox could miss games with injury. Getty Images While they suffered their third defeat of the season, Fremantle had nothing to gain and clearly had one eye on finals, resting and managing players’ game-time. Meanwhile, the Eagles finished their 2026 campaign with an eleventh-straight defeat.



West Coast were outplayed from start to finish by the Hawks and while there’s been improvement this season, the year fell away in disappointing circumstances in the back half. Fremantle Dockers What went right? The home and away season. Fremantle compiled a 23-game stretch which stands above all in their 32-years. The minor premiership, for the second time.



A new benchmark of 14 straight wins. A perfect home record from 11 Optus Stadium games. On top of this, and arguably the most important part, has been the health of the list. As the saying goes, “the best ability is your availability”. Justin Longmuir has more often than not been able to choose close to his best side every week.



It’s built confidence in themselves, teammates and system, the year to date is proof. Fremantle enter finals as flag favourites – a position they thoroughly deserve. View post on X What went wrong? Brennan Cox’s calf issue. Injury and suspension were the two factors the Dockers were trying to avoid against the Blues.



Cox’s first-quarter setback is set to sideline him for Fremantle’s first final. This contributed to the Dockers conceding their biggest score of the season, 118. Cox has had a number of setbacks this season. He only returned from multiple games with a knee issue recently while also missed games mid-year due to injury. Silver lining: Stars waiting to return.



Jye Amiss, Sam Switkowski, Heath Chapman and Murphy Reid will all be ready for a qualifying final against Hawthorn. You can bet Justin Longmuir won’t be managing players’ minutes like he did against the Blues. Hayden Young (66 per cent), Luke Jackson (72 per cent), Shai Bolton (73 per cent), Andrew Brayshaw, Alex Pearce (75 per cent) and Caleb Serong (76 per cent) were all closely monitored and well below their average time on ground for the season. West Coast Eagles What went right? West Coast held off Hawthorn’s quest for a top-three finish.



The Hawks were gunning for third spot, setting them up for a qualifying final against a now decimated Sydney outfit with several Swans stars seasons over due to ongoing alleged sexual assault allegations. The Eagles found themselves down by 47 points in the second quarter with Hawthorn on track to leapfrog the third placed Brisbane. However, aided by wet and slippery conditions, the Eagles did enough to prevent the Hawks rising up the ladder, meaning they’ll begin their premiership quest with the toughest of assignments; Fremantle in Perth. What went wrong? Harley Reid’s sling tackle. The star’s fourth quarter incident, where Jai Newcombe’s head slammed into the turf, will most certainly attract attention from the MRO, potentially forcing Reid into a delayed start to 2027.



One of the Eagles improvements this year has been the ability to use handball to help a fast-paced transition. View post on X But yesterday, West Coast were handball happy, and in wet conditions, which only meant more pressure from the Hawks. The Eagles had 42 handballs to only 22 kicks in the opening term. Silver lining: Milan Murdock.



The mature-age recruit capped a brilliant debut season with one of his best performances of the year. The 26 year-old booted the Eagles first two goals and finished with an equal career-high three majors, to go with 24 touches. Murdock has become a mainstay in the side through his hard work, ability to provide pressure, play a role and hit the scoreboard. The East Fremantle product played 20 games in his first AFL season, earning a two-year extension.

World.title: Mayors left disappointed by National ruling out bed tax
World.content:
Queenstown contemplates future of accommodation levy Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Auckland Council's economic agency Tātaki Auckland Unlimited questioned National's commitment to the tourism industry after being "dumbfounded" by National's announcement on Sunday ruling out a bed tax.

On Sunday the National Party ruled out the idea of a bed tax, promising that there will be "no new taxes" if it's re-elected.

It comes a fortnight after Prime Minister Christopher Luxon spoke publicly about the possibility of three new taxes under National - a bed tax, a bank tax and a fuel excise increase.

Director of destination Annie Dundas described National's move as a backwards step that put the city's major events and business pipeline at risk.

She said the industry had spent years working towards a sustainable funding solution, and the decision was at odds with the government's push to double the value of tourism exports by 2034.

"The big question is how committed is the government to supporting tourism?" she said.

Dundas said an accommodation levy let visitors contribute to the places they enjoyed and reduced the burden on ratepayers by returning funds to the regions where they were collected.

She said the country risked undermining popular destinations without sustainable tourism funding, with Auckland investing in an "astronomical" amount of hotel infrastructure over the past five years.

"If we can't demonstrate that we want visitors because we can't help market and fund and attract events, all of that investment is in jeopardy."

Dundas also questioned why anyone would want to spend on new tourism attractions and offerings when there was "no confidence" from the government to invest.

She said the international visitor levy did not give Auckland enough funding to attract major events, and a user-pays levy could have made a difference to regions across the country.

"We're just shortchanging ourselves and we want to protect our environment. We want to build great infrastructure. We want to host visitors, but we're just not funding things appropriately to do that as well as we should."

Regional Tourism New Zealand has called for political parties to back a nationwide accommodation levy ahead of this year's election to help cover costs and ease the pressure on ratepayers in popular destinations.

Mayors upset

The Auckland and Queenstown Lakes District mayors were both disappointed with National's announcement, with Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown hitting out at National for "walking away" from its commitment to the Auckland Regional Deal.

Brown said in a statement that Sunday's announcement raised serious questions about the government's commitment to the regional deal.

"The deal is meaningless if the government cannot honour even a relatively modest commitment to explore an agreed proposal.

"Ruling out the bed-night levy without offering any meaningful alternative to support the industry is deeply disappointing," he said.

The regional deal, signed in April this year, included the government committing to considering the accommodation levy policy in 2027.

Brown said the bed-night levy was a user charge, not a general tax.

"Taxes are unavoidable - you can avoid this by just not staying in a hotel.

"It would result in no additional rates or taxes on Aucklanders, while enabling Auckland to attract more events, support local businesses and grow the regional economy," he said.

Brown said the regional deal was an agreement between the Crown and the council.

"It should not be something one party can simply disregard."

Brown said he looked forward to discussing the issue with ministers responsible for the regional deal - Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop and Local Government Minister Simon Watts - at the next quarterly review of progress in September.

Luxon looking at 'other options'

Weekly interview with Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Speaking to Morning Report on Monday, Luxon denied reneging on both the signed deal with Auckland and the as-yet-unsigned one with Queenstown Lakes just for a clearer tax policy position.

"We were talking about exploring an accommodation levy to deal with the pressures and the costs associated with tourism in those regions.... we need to deal with it. We will deal with it, but we'll deal about it in a different way."

Christopher Luxon. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

He said National had looked at the bed tax idea, but "there's just no other way that... a couple setting off for a weekend in Queenstown or Auckland are not going to end up paying that bed tax.

"We're not the party that wants to chuck taxes or costs, unnecessary costs, on New Zealanders - and so that's why we say no new taxes."

Host Ingrid Hipkiss pressed Luxon on why he had reneged on the deal with Auckland.

"Because as part of exploring an accommodation levy, there's lots of other options that you would be exploring at the same time as well," he said.

Hipkiss replied: "Well, put those in the deal as well, put those in the agreement as well."

Luxon said that "as part of an exploration process, that's what we would be doing".

He would not say what other options National would consider, saying he did not want to "predetermine outcomes", but there were several options.

"We'll work with the councils and the mayors on that, but what we're not going to do - not going to do - is actually introduce a cost and a tax on New Zealanders that actually they end up paying rather than the tourists.

"We're very committed to finding the solution through that, and we need to do that because we've got some real pressure from tourism in some parts of the country - we're deeply, deeply committed to it, but we're also deeply committed to not having Kiwis pay a tax."

A 'complete u-turn'

Queenstown Lakes District Mayor John Glover told RNZ it appeared to be a "complete u-turn", after the government agreed to consider the accommodation levy for visitors in both the already-signed Auckland Regional Deal, and the deal for his region, which was almost signed a week-and-a-half ago - but had to be rescheduled due to National's crisis talks on the same day.

"It feels like policy making in a state of panic. I appreciate there's a campaign message about no new taxes, but the government particularly says it doesn't want to tax Kiwis for a weekend away.

"Well, what we just need to be clear about is that Kiwis are already being heavily taxed across the country, because every ratepayer that's in a tourism town is already having to pay for the cost of tourism, so to say they don't want Kiwis to be taxed is a bit of a rabbit hole to be going down," he said.

Glover said not being able to implement a bed tax would be "significant" for his region, where infrastructure was strained by the number of visitors each year - doubling the population during peaks.

"Things like car parks or waste collection, you know we've got some really expensive roads that go to the likes of the Routeburn track or Skippers Canyon, there might be five ratepayers live down there, but tens of thousands of visitors go there every year," he said.

"You would think we deserve governments that support tourism in this country, and they need to give council the tools to do that," Glover added.

Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell said she was "surprised" with the announcement, considering that the bed tax formed part of the Auckland Regional Deal.

"We're definitely sad to hear that because there's been so much hard work behind the scenes," she said.

"Councils without any alternative will have to continue to use ratepayer funds to invest in tourism offering," she added.

Tapsell said she and other mayors had also been pushing hard for more fair distribution of the International Visitors' Levy back to the regions, like Rotorua.

Deals now 'worthless'

Mat Woods, chief executive of Destination Queenstown, said it would be an understatement to call the National Party's decision a "massive blow".

He said "years of hard work" getting ready to implement the levy in 2027 had been rendered "worthless".

It was due to be signed the day National had its emergency caucus meeting to vote on Luxon's continued leadership and "would have been signed", Woods said.

"Districts like Queenstown and Wanaka, we desperately need an accommodation levy. And look, whether it's a tax or a levy, it is a user-pays charge. No one is forcing you to go on a holiday. But when you do go on a holiday, you do actually leave impacts on that district. And so that's where an accommodation levy is a fair way of actually looking at, how do we recoup some of those charges?

"Because the reality is we are already taxing people - we're taxing the local ratepayer for the impacts of tourism. So an accommodation levy is a fair way to actually apportion back some of that cost to the region."

Lake Wakatipu in Queenstown. Xinhua via AFP / Guo Lei

He said a $200 stay would have cost an extra $6, which in his words was "not a dealbreaker" for any tourist.

"They need to come back with something that actually will enable the regions to be able to cover this infrastructure to ensure that these are great places to live and great places to visit. At the moment, the only thing we actually have in place is the international visitor levy at the border - dollars that international visitors pay, excluding Australia. Now, Australia is our largest international market, so there is a big chunk of international market not paying at the border for that."

Woods was not sure what other options the government might suggest.

"I think if we looked at congestion charges, that's probably an indication of where we could look… I don't think there's been any discussions on that to date.

World.title: Auckland man charged in relation to major organised crime investigation
World.content:
An Auckland man has been charged in relation to a major organised crime investigation from five years ago linked to what police called "one of the world's largest organised crime takedowns".

In response to questions from RNZ on Monday, Detective Sergeant Bruce Howard confirmed a 46-year-old man had been charged in relation to Operation Equinox.

"He was arrested and remanded in custody on Saturday morning, when he was returned to New Zealand with two escorting officers following the end of his sentence in the United States."

Howard said the 2021 investigation involved about 400 officers, with 37 search warrants across Waikato, Bay of Plenty, Auckland, Central and Wellington Districts.

"It involved the National Organised Crime (NOCG), Armed Offenders Squad, Special Tactics Group, Asset Recovery, High Tech Crime, and came after coordination with domestic partner agencies and international law enforcement agencies.

"The latest arrest resulted in the man being charged with two counts of participating in an organised criminal group, three counts of importing drugs, 17 counts of importing methamphetamine and amphetamine, and three counts of importing ecstasy."

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

The man appeared in the Manukau District Court on Monday and was granted interim name suppression.

"This latest arrest shows we will not forget and alleged offenders will be held accountable for their actions. Drugs inflict misery on families and communities across New Zealand and those pushing these drugs are only interested in profiting off the massive harm they cause," Howard said.

"Targeting this organised criminal offending is an ongoing focus of New Zealand Police, and we will use every avenue available to us, including internationally, to stamp on this offending as hard as possible."

Operation Trojan Shield

In June 2021, New Zealand police announced its involvement in what was called "one of the world's largest organised crime takedowns".

Operation Trojan Shield was led by the FBI and co-ordinated with the Drug Enforcement Administration, AFP, Europol and other law enforcement agencies from more than a dozen countries.

Police said organised crime groups were using encrypted platforms to conduct international communications.

As part of that, Canadian-based encryption service company Phantom Secure was dismantled by the FBI in 2018. Another service, Sky Global, was dismantled in March 2021.

NZ police contacted the FBI in 2020 about a potential import into the country - the same year New Zealand became involved in the operation.

A special encryption platform was set up - ANOM - to access encrypted organised crime communications. Police said users unknowingly communicated on the system, operated by the FBI, for over 18 months.

The network had 57 devices in New Zealand using it and all were being used for criminal activities, Williams said.

World.title: Whale-watching boat carrying NZ Anglican Church delegates capsizes in Tonga
World.content:
A whale-watching boat carrying several New Zealand Anglican Church delegates capsized and sank in Tonga on Friday.

RNZ Pacific understands several passengers were briefly hospitalised, but there were no serious injuries.

Paramedics from New South Wales, who were in the country for a Rotary International training event, led the rescue.

"Before leaving, the Bishops, Chaplains and leaders of the group led a prayer, thanking and blessing the team for the help and support they had provided," a Rotary statement read.

"It was a very special and humbling moment for our team, and certainly not something we expected when we started the day."

The Diocese of Polynesia had recently finished their General Synod in Nuku'Alofa, with delegates present from across New Zealand and the Pacific.

World.title: Labour Party reveals its 2026 campaign slogan
World.content:
Labour has unveiled its 2026 campaign slogan: 'Better starts now.'

Leader Chris Hipkins made the announcement at a suburban home in Christchurch after taking a tumble in the latest poll.

The party has been repeating ad nauseum its focus on "jobs, health, homes and the cost of living" for the coming election campaign.

The announcement follows the latest RNZ-Reid Research poll showing Opportunity in a kingmaker position, and Labour down 1.8 points to its lowest result since the election.

Hipkins' preferred prime minister ratings also fell 2.6 points to 21.3 - leaving the opposition leader in the lead over National's Christopher Luxon but the gap narrowing with Luxon falling just 0.1 points to 19.9 percent.

"Labour's campaign obviously kicks up a gear today," Hipkins told Midday Report. "We'll have signs going up all over the country over the next two weeks and we've got more policy announcements to come.

"My message to Kiwis is pretty clear - better is possible, and better starts as soon as we change the government."

National campaign manager Simeon Brown said the slog was "the closest thing to a confession we will ever get from Chris Hipkins, because with 10 weeks until the election, he had better start now".

He added that Kiwis "do not need to imagine Labour's version of better, because they have already lived it. Six years, $120 billion more debt, new taxes, a cost-of-living crisis, and mortgage rates through the roof."

He claimed Labour was planning nine new taxes, which Hipkins dismissed as "lies", saying the only new tax they would campaign on was a targeted capital gains tax.

"We've ruled out all of the other taxes that the National Party are putting in all of their advertising materials. And I think the fact that they now are into this post-truth era where they just make things up shows how increasingly desperate they're looking."

Photos from Labour's slogan launch and erection of billboards in Christchurch, August 2026. Rachel Graham / RNZ

Labour on Sunday set out its fiscal strategy, promising a surplus in 2029/30 under the OBEGAL measure - the same timeframe as set out by the coalition's debt track when using that measure.

"That is the measure that Bill English, Stephen Joyce, Grant Robertson, Michael Cullen, all of them used - what's called the OBEGAL measure to track whether the government's in surplus or in deficit," Hipkins told Midday Report.

"We're going back to that. Nicola Willis couldn't achieve a surplus using that measure, so made-up her own. We're not going to do that."

Also on Sunday, National sought to differentiate itself from the left bloc by ruling out any new taxes as part of its election campaign.

However, that disappointed mayors and councils in Auckland and Queenstown Lakes, both of whom had signed regional deals with the government that included a commitment to investigate a bed tax - also called a bed-night levy or accommodation levy.

Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown has said the move has rendered the Auckland deal meaningless, while Destination Queenstown chief executive Mat Woods said calling it a "massive blow" would be an understatement.

The government had been set to sign the deal with Queenstown Lakes on the day of the caucus meeting where Luxon survived a second confidence vote, and it remains unsigned by the government.

Opportunities for Opportunity

Elsewhere in the interview on Midday Report, Hipkins would not rule out having Opportunity MPs, should they be elected, in a Labour-led government Cabinet.

"We're leaving all of those options on the table in terms of what the makeup of a future government could look like. It doesn't need to look as chaotic as the current government."

But he said having Te Pāti Māori MPs in Cabinet was "unlikely", citing the party's recent internal struggles.

World.title: Bougainville urged to prepare for El Niño-linked drought
World.content:
The Autonomous Bougainville Government (ABG) is urging people to prepare for a prolonged drought linked to El Niño.

In a statement, the ABG said there was an 80 to 90 percent chance of below-normal rainfall across Bougainville until the end of the year.

It said the Nissan Atolls and other vulnerable outer-island communities in Northern Bougainville would be prioritised for drought monitoring.

El Niño typically brings hotter and drier conditions to Papua New Guinea, increasing the risk of drought, water shortages, crop losses and food insecurity, particularly in the Highlands and remote island communities.

The PNG National Weather Service said a strong El Niño is firmly established and projected to persist into early 2027, bringing prolonged dry conditions across many parts of Papua New Guinea.

"The situation is being treated as an elevated drought and water-security risk, rather than normal seasonal conditions, with particular concern for water supplies, food gardens, food security and remote island communities," the statement said.

World.title: No charges over dog attack that killed Christchurch boy
World.content:
No charges will be laid over the death of a one-year-old Christchurch boy who was attacked by a dog at his home.

A police spokesperson said the death of Sonny-Charles Watson had now been referred to the coroner.

The boy was attacked by a cross-breed dog that lived at the Basingstoke St, Aranui, property on 14 August.

The city council said the dog was registered and had not previously come to its attention. On Monday a council spokesperson said the dog would be euthanised this week.

Local Government Minister Simon Watts previously told RNZ the government was reviewing the Dog Control Act to ensure councils had the tools to manage dangerous dogs.

"The news of this dog attack is devastating and my thoughts are with the child's family and everyone affected.

"Every New Zealander should be able to feel safe in their community and not fear being attacked by a dangerous and uncontrolled dog."

Watts said stronger penalties and greater powers for council officers were among the options being considered as part of the review.

World.title: Auckland detective pleads guilty to possessing objectionable publications
World.content:
An Auckland detective has pleaded guilty to possessing objectionable publications over nearly two years.

The officer, who will seek a discharge without conviction, will also be requesting permanent name suppression.

The officer, aged in his 60s, appeared in the Manukau District Court on Monday before Judge Richard McIlraith.

He initially faced 11 charges of possessing an objectionable publication between May 2023 and May 2024.

One of the charges alleged the officer had a "rape image", two charges say "child exploitation material", three charges say "child sexual exploitation" and five charges alleged the officer possessed "bestiality" material.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

On Monday, he pleaded guilty to an amended representative charge which said that between May 2023 and March 2025 he possessed an objectionable publication.

The officer's lawyer, Todd Simmonds, said he would be seeking a discharge without conviction as well as permanent name suppression at his sentencing in November.

Judge McIlraith declined media requests for a copy of the summary of facts until sentencing.

The officer was one of three police staff to be charged following a rapid review of staff internet usage sparked by the resignation of former deputy police commissioner Jevon McSkimming, after child sexual exploitation and bestiality material were found on his work devices.

Earlier this month, another Auckland police officer Matthew Rogers pleaded guilty to a representative charge of possessing an objectionable publication. He will be sentenced in October.

A Wellington-based officer, aged in his 50s, also faces 10 charges of possessing an objectionable publication between January 2024 and January 2025.

He has interim name suppression.

Acting Deputy Commissioner Tim Anderson earlier said each of the officers were being charged with multiple counts of possessing an objectionable publication, under the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act.

"Prosecution of our own staff is a serious but important step to take as it recognises the significance of the alleged offending that has been identified.

"I would like to acknowledge the professionalism and commitment by our investigators in the National Integrity Unit for their work to this point."

Anderson said the investigations had involved the analysis of a "significant volume of web activity".

"It is important we now let these matters progress to the court process, which limits the level of information we can provide at this point.

"These three police staff remain stood down from duties. Meanwhile, three investigations remain ongoing as part of the rapid review."

Police have investigated 22 cases, 12 have been resolved through either disciplinary action or performance management.

World.title: Police consider charges after violent North Shore group attack on teen girls
World.content:
Details of an horrific alleged attack on a pair of teens on Auckland's North Shore have been circulating online amid a plea for help from the public.

Police are yet to confirm what charges will be laid after the violent robbery and assault on two teenage girls in Takapuna on Saturday night.

They said they had identified most of the youths involved, aged between 12 and 17.

It is understood the victims had been hanging out with the group, before the group turned on them at around 9.30pm.

"The victims were separated and reportedly violently assaulted, before having their personal items stolen," Detective Senior Sergeant Mike Williams said.

The girls were able to identify a number of young people of interest at a bus station.

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

In a statement on Sunday, Williams said follow-up enquiries were being made and potential charges were being considered.

They were unable to confirm how many girls were involved in the attack.

A post that has been re-shared by community advocate Kaumosi Opie on social media alleges the two girls were beaten, stomped on, stripped down to their bras, spat on and filmed before their phones, clothing and other belongings were taken.

One of the victims is also alleged to have been knocked unconscious.

The group are alleged to have attempted to force the girls into public toilets behind a Katsubi restaurant, "apparently to prevent members of the public from seeing what was happening".

Police would not confirm these details when approached by RNZ.

An individual sharing on behalf of family of one of the victims is urging anyone with CCTV, dashcam or cellphone footage to share it with police.

"Any information, even something that seems minor, could help establish the movements and actions of those involved."

World.title: Former Roosters premiership star unveiled as PNG Chiefs' '007' signing
World.content:
Joey Manu has been unveiled as the much-hyped PNG Chief 007, with the two-time premiership winner to return to the NRL in 2028.

The Chiefs officially confirmed today the former Sydney Roosters utility signed a two-year deal with the club, which now boasts a backline that will be the envy of the NRL.

PNG had long hyped their seventh signing, with speculation Penrith superstar Nathan Cleary was bound for the club as their inaugural halfback.

But with a staircase at their home base showing each of their signings and "007" listed as "reserved", that honour will now go to code-hopper Manu ahead of the 2028 season.

Loading Instagram content

"We're thrilled to add Joey to our squad moving forward," Chiefs general manager Michael Chammas said.

"He is a world-class footballer with versatility across several positions and can change a game in a single moment with the skills he possesses.

"His experience and demonstrated success at the highest level will be a great benefit to our team and we can't wait to see him have a significant impact in the Chiefs jersey."

Manu joins a list that already includes Jarome Luai, Alex Johnston, Connor Watson, Zac Lomax, Brian To'o and Englishman Matty Lees.

But the move appears likely to have ended the 30-year-old's boyhood dream of representing the All Blacks.

To'o is still just the beginning for PNG Brian To'o is the fourth player to sign for Papua New Guinea who has played State of Origin in the past two years. It's a sign of things to come, with the NRL's richest club yet to truly enter free agency.

Manu left the NRL for an overseas rugby union career after the 2024 season, starting in Japan before a move to French team Racing 92 last year.

But his French rugby deal runs to the end of 2027, and New Zealand Rugby only selects players for the All Blacks if they play domestically.

Manu will be 33 by the time his Chiefs deal finishes.

Manu became one of the NRL's most prized utility players across 181 games, including the 2018 and 2019 premiership wins, with the Roosters.

He was named Dally M centre of the year in 2022 and won the Golden Boot award as the sport's best international player later that year.

The athletic New Zealand representative is equally adept in the centres and at fullback, and can also capably slot into the halves in a pinch.

On leaving the NRL after the Roosters' 2024 finals campaign, Manu offered no guarantees of ever returning to the 13-man code.

But any possible comeback had widely been expected to come with the Roosters, who scouted him as a teenager.

Instead, Manu becomes the latest jewel in the crown of the NRL's forthcoming 19th team, which can offer lucrative tax-free salaries to its signings.

PNG will be able to officially hit the market on November 1, with Cleary headlining a list of players who could still become free agents at that time.

The club has also been linked to Gold Coast utility AJ Brimson and Canberra second-rower Hudson Young, both of whom are State of Origin players, in recent weeks.

Isaah Yeo, Latrell Mitchell and Bradman Best are among other household names without deals beyond the 2027 season.

World.title: Aussie athletes continue top form with trio of medals at Diamond League
World.content:
Commonwealth Games champions Eleanor Patterson and Rose Davies have kicked on from their Glasgow triumphs, along with double silver medallist Jessica Hull, as Australia's athletes have continued to shine on the Diamond League circuit in Poland.

All three made the podium at the Diamond League Silesia meet in Chorzów overnight, with high jump champion Patterson soaring to third place, Glasgow 5,000/10,000 metre double winner Davies grabbing bronze in the 5,000m and Hull running her fastest race of the year to finish 1,500m runner-up.

But there was disappointment for Glasgow sprint hero Lachlan Kennedy, who after his Australian-record run for silver at Glasgow's Scotstoun Stadium, failed to make the 100m final in Chorzów.

Pride of place went to Olympic silver medallist Hull, who tried out new tactics, sitting back in the field in the Silesian Stadium and kicking for home at the top of the straight, only to be reeled in by Ethiopia's Tsige Duguma. She needed a 2026 world-leading time of three minutes and 55.06 seconds to pip Hull's 3:55.20.

"I got caught in the last few metres but it was a big step forwards in confidence today," said Hull, who is eyeing the inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest next month.

"That's the fastest I've run all year and we have some good races to come over the next few weeks."

Davies earned her second career Diamond League podium as she pursued Italian favourite Nadia Battocletti, fresh from her own 5,000/10,000 double at the European Championships.

Davies eventually finished third in 14:55.39, pipped by Ethiopia's Freweyni Hailu and Battocletti, who won in 14:54.09.

"Every race is a step forward and to come top three at a Diamond League shows I'm in good form," Davies said.

"I really look up to Battocletti, she's a great athlete and I would love to be like her."

Australia's Eleanor Patterson earned bronze during the women's high jump final. (Getty Images: Maja Hitij)

Patterson again defeated teammate, world champion Nicola Olyslagers, just as she had done in Glasgow when they took gold and silver.

It was a strong effort considering Patterson was battling illness, but she had to settle for third behind Ukrainian rivals, Olympic champion Yaroslava Mahuchikh and Iryna Gerashchenko.

Kennedy took his first strides back on the international circuit after his historic 9.85sec silver medal-winning run in Glasgow, but his 10.08sec run in the heats in Chorzów was not enough to earn him a place in the final, which was later won by Jamaica's world champion, Oblique Seville, in a searing 9.83sec.

"I didn't come out as well as I would've liked but I'm just trying to shake the rust off a bit. I'll get back into some training and better form — I'm happy," Kennedy said.

Triple Commonwealth pole vault champion Kurtis Marschall cleared 5.90m but it only earned him fifth place while his mate Armand Duplantis earned yet another effortless triumph with a 6.20m winner.

Queensland's two-time Diamond League champion Matthew Denny finished eighth in the discus (66.38m), as Lithuania's world record holder Mykolas Alekna won with a competition record 72.58m.

The international highlight was world champion Melissa Jefferson-Wooden handing Olympic champion Julien Alfred her first loss of the season to win the women's 100m, 10.78sec to 10.83.
